The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission finds that Judge Burrill demonstrates excellent organization, preparedness and willingness to learn. Judge Burrill conducts himself in a professional manner and shows empathy to those in his courtroom. Judge Burrill shows genuine interest in helping defendants that need support to improve their lives. Judge Burrill clearly explains possible consequences, reasons for posing certain questions and allows plentiful time for defendants to speak. The Commission commends Judge Burrill on these actions and attributes.

The Commission finds that Judge Burrill is thorough with the steps that need to be followed in each case and is skilled at working through his docket. Judge Burrill’s hard work and integrity are evident to the Commission. Based on the totality of the information reviewed, the Commission determined that Judge Burrill is an asset to the Mesa County Judicial system and consistently demonstrates the competencies required of a judicial officer.

Judge Burrill was appointed to the Mesa County Court in July of 2024, taking the bench in August 2024. Judge Burrill is from Madison, Wisconsin and attended the University of Wisconsin-Madison for his undergraduate degree, graduating in 2006. He attended the University of Iowa College of Law, earning his Juris Doctorate in 2010 and graduating with distinction. Prior to taking the bench, Judge Burrill was a Deputy State Public Defender from 2010-2024, practicing in both the Montrose and Grand Junction regional offices. While with OSPD, he served as both a county court and district court supervisor. Judge Burrill serves on the Mesa County Pretrial Committee, the local CJAC Committee, and is on the CCJA Legislative Advisory Group.

name: Nicholas Catanzarite
position: Fourteenth Judicial District - Grand County Court Judge
narrative: The Fourteenth Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission unanimously agrees 7-0, with three commission vacancies, that Judge Nicholas Catanzarite MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Catanzarite, observed him in Court, reviewed judicial performance data, written orders, survey responses, and reviewed a self-evaluation completed by his Honor. It was clear from the interview that Judge Catanzarite has grown significantly in his role since 2015 and excels as a valuable judicial officer in the 14th Judicial District. The Commission was disappointed by the lack of participation in the survey results and would encourage the public to participate in the future. Survey responses were statistically unrepresentative and lacked sufficient context to provide meaningful feedback to the Commission. Judge Catanzarite handles a combined docket of traffic cases, civil disputes including small claims, criminal, and misdemeanor cases. Judge Catanzarite possesses an excellent judicial temperament and treats those in his courtroom with patience and respect. He demonstrates a breadth of legal knowledge and has developed strong processes supporting judicial efficiency. Judge Catanzarite displays good control of his courtroom with pro se and represented litigants alike. The Commission is pleased that Judge Catanzarite has embraced virtual courtroom proceedings to support accessibility of the Courts. The Commission encourages Judge Catanzarite to require video appearance (as opposed to audio-only) whenever possible to promote traditional standards of decorum. Judge Catanzarite has developed his skill in delivering oral rulings for expediency and continues to strengthen his organization and clarity in oral rulings. The Commission commends his Honor for the quality of his written rulings as well. Judge Catanzarite has also demonstrated leadership in the judiciary as part of the CourtCall pilot program and addressing pro se litigants’ increasing use of Artificial Intelligence to generate pleadings which can strain judicial resources. The Commission appreciates his more than a decade of service to the 14th Judicial District and finds Judge Catanzarite ranks high in demeanor, control, fairness, and efficiency.
Based on all the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Catanzarite meets performance standards.

Judge Nicholas Catanzarite was appointed to Grand County Court in 2015. Prior to his appointment to County Judge, he practiced law in Grand County for 3 years with a focus on criminal defense, real estate, and family law. Judge Catanzarite earned his undergraduate degree from Michigan State University and his Juris Doctorate from the University of Denver in 2011.

name: Inga Haagenson Causey
position: Fifth Judicial District - Eagle County Court Judge
narrative: The Fifth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Inga Haagenson Causey in a 8-0 vote, with two commissioners absent, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission observed that Judge Causey is humble, patient, fair, compassionate, introspective, and possesses an impressive desire to learn. Entering her third year on the bench and doing the work of almost two judges in one of the busiest courtrooms in Colorado, she displays excellent management over her docket and has found strong footing within our judicial system. Judge Causey’s docket comprises approximately 78% criminal and misdemeanor, 10% civil litigation, 5% traffic, 5% small claims, 1% domestic relations, and 1% juvenile cases. Judge Causey reflects that she loves and is good at what she does – truly valuing hearing people in court, methodically setting up sustainable systems to keep pace with her large docket, growing community connections through the “Our Court” school-based program, and actively engaging in legislative advocacy to be engaged in the rapidly changing legal landscape. Judge Causey is diligent in her research and provides timely, understandable, and clear written and verbal orders. The Commission applauds her deep commitment to civic engagement within the community including her role in establishing a new Pretrial Services program to provide substance abuse and mental health support, proactively helping community members navigate the judicial system while ensuring community safety. The Commission recognizes Judge Causey’s efforts so far and encourages her to be more assertive in the governance of her courtroom. The Commission would also encourage Judge Causey to continue to find ways for self-health despite the busy schedule.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Causey, reviewed several of her written opinions, observed her in court, and considered survey results provided by 11 attorneys and 22 non-attorneys, which was a relatively small sample. Judge Causey received consistently positive reviews in her surveys from attorneys and non-attorneys, with slightly lower marks from non-attorneys. The partial year-to-year trend showed a slight increase in overall score despite the smaller survey sample size this year. The most consistent constructive feedback provided in the surveys reflect the need for a second County Court Judge to address the large docket and improve case management, and for Judge Causey to increase assertiveness in courtroom management.

Judge Causey graduated from the University of Colorado - Boulder in 1994, and Tulane University School of Law in 1999. She was appointed to the County Court bench for the Fifth Judicial District in December 2022. Prior to her appointment, Judge Causey served as a Magistrate Judge for the 13th Judicial District, and a Deputy Municipal Judge for the Towns of Minturn and De Beque. She also serves as an adjunct instructor for the Community College of Denver teaching Legal Research and Writing, Constitutional Law, Evidence, Criminal Law, Business Law and the Introduction to Law.

name: Jeremy Chaffin
position: Twenty-First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Jeremy Chaffin MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by a vote of 7-0. The Commission has one vacancy, one absent commissioner, and one recusal. The Commission considered multiple sources of information, including survey results, courtroom observations, interviews, the judge’s self-evaluation, and case management data. Survey results indicated that 100% of attorneys found Judge Chaffin meets performance standards, while non-attorney responses were more mixed; the Commission considered these results in the context of all available information.

The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission finds that Judge Chaffin demonstrates excellent legal knowledge and applies the law appropriately in the cases before him. Judge Chaffin is consistently well prepared, and issues prompt well-reasoned rulings grounded in law and fact. Judge Chaffin’s hard work and integrity are noted by both prosecutors and defense attorneys. The Commission has directly observed Judge Chaffin’s noteworthy dedication to the legal profession, ability to manage complex matters effectively while maintaining appropriate control over the courtroom proceedings, and timely issuance of orders moving cases forward in a timely and orderly manner.

The Commission also finds that Judge Chaffin exhibits a judicial temperament that is fair, respectful, compassionate, and professional. He treats parties, attorneys, litigants, and court staff with dignity, values their time, and actively works to solve problems humanely and creatively. Based on the totality of the information reviewed, the Commission determined that Judge Chaffin is an asset to the Mesa County Judicial system and consistently demonstrates the competencies required of a judicial officer.

Judge Chaffin received an undergraduate degree in Psychology from the University of Idaho in 2005 and earned his law degree from the University of Colorado School of Law in 2011. He worked as a Special Assistant Attorney General at the Colorado Attorney General’s Office in the Consumer Protection Section before clerking for Judge Nancy Lichtenstein at the Colorado Court of Appeals. In 2014 he moved to Grand Junction where he worked as a prosecutor with the 21st Judicial District until 2017. Prior to his appointment to the bench, he worked as an Assistant United States Attorney for the District of Colorado prosecuting federal crimes throughout western Colorado. Judge Chaffin was sworn in as a District Court Judge in the 21st Judicial District in December 2022.

name: Michelle Chostner
position: Tenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Tenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Michelle Chostner MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Chostner presides over a domestic relations docket and district court civil docket for the Tenth Judicial District. She is well prepared for cases before her bench. The orders she issues are well researched and thorough, though they are sometimes very long and would benefit from being more concise to encourage understanding. Her demeanor as a judge is calm and respectful; she strives to treat all court participants equally, bringing a sense of dignity to proceedings before her.

To evaluate Judge Chostner's performance, the Commission reviewed judicial performance data, written orders, surveys including comments from attorneys and non-attorneys, and a self-evaluation completed by Judge Chostner. The Commission also conducted in-court observations of the judge and personally interviewed her after compiling all other information. Judge Chostner appreciates the need for continued education and growth in her role as a judicial officer. She regularly conducts legal research, stays up-to-date on new laws, and she attends trainings in the areas of law she presides over. She also teaches courses in the law, and she serves on the judicial education subcommittee. Judge Chostner clearly cares about communicating the legal process to those not represented by attorneys, though some members of the commission are concerned that she may over-explain the process to ensure understanding and fairness which delays the proceedings unnecessarily.

Judge Michelle Chostner was appointed to the Pueblo County District Court bench in March of 2023. She received her bachelor’s degree from the University of Colorado, Boulder, in 2004, graduating summa cum laude, and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2008. After graduating law school, Judge Chostner worked at the Adams, Arapahoe, and Pueblo District Attorney’s Offices, where she was promoted to the role Senior Deputy District Attorney. In 2021, Judge Chostner was appointed as a Magistrate in Pueblo, where she handled truancy, civil, and probate matters. Judge Chostner enjoys spending time with her family and volunteering on various community boards, including the library board, and assisting with mock trial events.

name: Dina M. Christiansen
position: Thirteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance thanks the volunteers of the 13th Judicial District Commission and all Commissioners of Judicial Performance for their work evaluating Colorado Judges. We appreciate the time, diligence and concern the Commissioners put into this work. We especially appreciate the understanding of local needs and challenges courts face in districts across Colorado that the Commissioners bring to their work. However, as a result of a Rule 21 Complaint and independent review, the State Commission is taking the extraordinary step of issuing its own narrative and recommendation regarding Judge Dina M. Christiansen. The State Commission is not directing the District Commission to revise their evaluation narrative but offers this narrative to provide voters additional information to consider while voting.

The 13th Judicial District Commission conducted a retention election evaluation of Judge Christiansen in the spring of 2026. The District Commission concluded that Judge Christiansen did not meet performance standards and circulated a draft narrative to the judge as required by the rules. In response, Judge Christiansen submitted a Complaint under Rule 21 of the Rules Governing Commissions on Judicial Performance. In conducting an independent review, the State Commission found the District Commission had failed to complete the required “initial interim evaluation,” which is mandated by both statute and rule. The initial evaluation is an important part of Colorado’s judicial performance system. It gives a District Commission the chance to review a judge’s early work, identify concerns, and, if needed, require the judge to take part in a Judicial Improvement Plan. A Judicial Improvement Plan gives clear feedback, support, and guidance so a judge can improve before the retention year evaluation. Judge Christiansen did not receive early feedback or the opportunity for improvement through a structured plan. This left her without a fair chance to address concerns before her retention year evaluation. This failure is considered a “serious infraction of the rules and statutes,” and it requires the State Commission to issue its own narrative under Rule 21.

The State Commission understands that District Commissions operate on tight timelines, and that due to time constraints, this interim review did not occur. The State Commission cannot change or reverse the District Commission’s recommendation of “Does Not Meet Performance Standards.” The State Commission issues this narrative along with the District Commission’s to provide a clear and accurate explanation of what occurred, while at the same time recognizing the concerns raised by survey respondents and the District Commission.

The State Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0 with one commissioner absent and two vacancies, that Judge Dina M. Christiansen MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The State Commission also recommends that Judge Christiansen participate in a Judicial Improvement Plan to address the issues identified by survey respondents and the District Commission. This recommendation follows the State Commission’s independent review of the Rule 21 Complaint. This included interviews with Judge Christiansen, Chief Judge McGuire, and commissioners from the 13th Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance. The State Commission also reviewed Judge Christiansen’s self evaluation, several written decisions, the Colorado Supreme Court’s published opinion in In re People in Interest of G.D.M. (June 8, 2026), the judicial performance survey report, and observed courtroom proceedings. We encourage voters to explore additional resources at: Home | Colorado Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation Home.
Thirteenth Judicial District District Court Judge Honorable Dina M. Christiansen

The 13th Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that the Honorable Judge Dina M. Christiansen Does Not Meet Performance Standards. The Commission voted 5 to 2 that Judge Christiansen does not meet performance standards. The Commission currently has two vacancies, and one member of the Commission was recused. The local commission is in support of the State Commission’s narrative regarding Judge Christiansen.

The commission relied on the survey results, judicial observation, Judge Christiansen submissions, the meeting with the chief judge, and the interview to reach our decision. Commissioners recognized Judge Christiansen’s commitment to professional growth, her willingness to take on complex matters, and her efforts to expand judicial services within the district, including participation in competency court initiatives. Commissioners also noted positive feedback on her interaction with children and families, as well as her stated dedication to public service. Despite these strengths, the Commission identified significant concerns related to judicial temperament, legal analysis, and courtroom management. Multiple attorneys reported that Judge Christiansen can appear rigid, dismissive, or unnecessarily confrontational during hearings, particularly in more contentious matters. Commissioners were also concerned by reports that courtroom interactions take on a personal tone. The Commission also expressed concern regarding statements indicating Judge Christiansen may place substantial reliance on the perceived credibility or reputation of attorneys appearing before her when addressing unfamiliar areas of law. Commissioners believe judicial decision must be grounded in independent legal analysis and careful application of the law to the facts presented. The Commission additionally considered concerns raised regarding rulings that appeared rushed, insufficiently researched, or unsupported by adequate legal authority. While the Commission recognizes the demands placed on a relatively new district court judge, it remains concerned that efficiency and docket management may at times be prioritized over deliberate legal analysis, the development of a complete record, and thoughtful orders supported by the law.

After meeting with Judge Christiansen and reviewing the work Judge Christiansen has done over the last year and seven months, the commission has several concerns surrounding Judge Christiansen’s performance standards. Judge Christiansen received 29 survey responses (which reflects a 5.5% response rate from attorneys and a 0.39% response rate from non-attorneys) with an overall score of 2.9 out of 4. Of the survey respondents’ attorneys and non-attorneys agreed Judge Christiansen met performance standards. Judge Christiansen’s lowest score on the survey results is her application and knowledge of the law, this score was 2.7 out of 4.

Judge Christiansen received her law degree from the William S. Boyd School of Law at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and her undergraduate degree from the University of Utah. Judge Christiansen practiced primarily in domestic relations law (some criminal and probate law) from 2004 – 2019. In 2019, Judge Christiansen was hired to be a District Court Magistrate in the 8th Judicial District. She was appointed to be a District Court Judge on October 2, 2024. Since her appointment, Judge Christiansen created a statewide mandated competency court docket.

I respectfully disagree with the commission’s narrative as it is not based on objective data contained in my 2026 evaluation showing 93% of attorneys and 82% of non-attorneys state that I DO meet performance standards. Surveys regarding my performance directly contradict the commission’s views. Attorneys rated my overall demeanor a 3.3 out of 4.0. Attorneys rated me a 3.3 for giving proceedings a sense of dignity, 3.4 for addressing individuals respectfully, 3.2 in reacting to incidents in the courtroom appropriately, and a 3.3 for doing the necessary homework and being prepared. These results are publicly available for review at www.judicialperformance.colorado.gov.

name: Colleen Clark
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - Arapahoe County Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees, by a vote of 7-1, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Colleen Clark MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and to the public.

After meeting with Judge Clark, and after reviewing her prior work and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission determined that she meets judicial performance standards. Judge Clark was described as fair, calm, punctual, and courteous. Some respondents expressed concerns that Judge Clark can be at times slow to make rulings, appears to be visibly frustrated at times, and has opportunity to grow with how she engages with pro se litigants. Judge Clark, who currently presides over a criminal county court docket in Arapahoe County, has recently transitioned back to this docket from an 80/20 civil/small claims docket in Littleton, but brings over twenty years of prior experience in criminal law. Judge Clark assured the Commission that she is committed to all parties being treated with dignity and respect, punctuality, as well as her continued commitment to ensure all parties feel heard and respected. Judge Clark is excited about her return to the criminal docket, is confident in her ability to serve the citizens of Arapahoe County. The Commission concluded Judge Clark’s legal knowledge base is stable.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Clark, reviewed rulings she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and analyzed survey responses from both attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Clark. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in numbers, found mixed issues in some areas. The Commission found similar consistent with from past evaluations.

Judge Clark was appointed to the bench October 6, 2016. Prior to her appointment to the bench, she was a magistrate and a municipal court judge, and before that time, she worked as a prosecutor in many jurisdictions across the state and specialized in crimes against persons, mostly children. Judge Clark currently serves on the Colorado Supreme Court Task Force on Wellbeing and the Senior Judge Standing Committee, is a member of the National Association of Women Judges, is a member of the International Association of Women Judges, has served two terms on the board of the Colorado Women’s Bar Association. Judge Clark has provided trainings for the Sam Cary Bar Association, the Colorado Women’s Bar Association, the Colorado Judicial Institute and the Sturm College of Law in her previous term. Judge Clark was a member of the Leadership Cherry Creek 2020 class. She received her undergraduate degree in political science from the University of Rochester and her juris doctorate from Boston University.

name: Chantel E. Contiguglia
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (10-0) finds Judge Chantel E. Contiguglia MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Contiguglia was appointed to the District Court in Jefferson County on January 1, 2024. She presides over a mixed docket of criminal, civil and domestic relations matters. Judge Contiguglia has been described as prepared, fair, consistent, and respectful with good judicial demeanor and temperament. She is thoughtful and sets clear deadlines and expectations. Her case management was described as efficient; however it was noted her scheduling practices could be inflexible for trial and docket management, which has been perceived by some litigants to overlook practical needs of the parties. During her interim evaluation Judge Contiguglia was given this feedback and since that time, there has been improvement. Judge Contiguglia’s background is predominantly criminal defense work, which is reflected in her acumen with criminal law. Judge Contiguglia is committed to increasing her proficiency in civil and domestic relations law by seeking out colleagues with this expertise and attending continuing legal education in these areas. The Commission finds Judge Contiguglia meets performance standards and is pleased she has committed to increasing her proficiency in civil and domestic relations law.

The commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Contiguglia, reviewed orders she authored, observed her in court, reviewed the judicial performance survey responses from attorneys, non-attorneys, jurors and court staff, and received feedback from the chief judge of the 1st Judicial District, the Office of the District Attorney, and the Office of the State Public Defender. There was a limited number of survey responses for this evaluation period. Five appellate court judges responded to the survey and rated Judge Contiguglia high (4.0 out of 4.0).

Judge Contiguglia grew up in Walden, Colorado, a small town in Jackson County. She earned her Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Mesa State College and her Juris Doctorate from the University of Denver in 2006. Before her current appointment, she served as a County Court Judge in Arapahoe County for six years. Prior to that Judge Contiguglia spent over ten years with the Colorado State Public Defender’s Office. In addition to her public responsibilities, she remains committed to community service, frequently volunteering at local schools, mentoring young attorneys, and participating in programs that support access to justice.

name: William Culver
position: Sixteenth Judicial District - Otero County Court Judge
narrative: The Sixteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one commissioner abstaining and one commission vacancy, that Judge William Culver MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Culver presides over civil, criminal advisements, misdemeanors, traffic, and small claims matters in Otero County, Colorado. Judge Culver’s demeanor is described as, patient, fair, and understanding of people in the court room. Judge Culver has excellent docket control, consistently prepared for his hearings and executes exceptional oral and written orders. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview. Based on these findings, the Commission agreed that Judge Culver meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Culver, interviewed both the Public Defender and District Attorney, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, reviewed a self-evaluation, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had appeared before him. Although only 17 surveys were completed for Judge Culver, the Commission determined that the remaining sources provided a sufficient basis to issue this opinion.

Judge Culver has been appointed to the County Court since 2024. Before becoming a County Court Judge, Judge Culver was the elected district attorney for the 16th Judicial District. Prior to 2012, Judge Culver was a solo practitioner and focused on complex divorce proceedings and criminal defense. Judge Culver also litigated dependency and neglect cases, juvenile delinquency cases, civil cases and provided consultation in probate matters. Judge Culver graduated from Emory University School of Law in 1995 with a juris doctorate and Fort Hays State University in 1992 with a BA. Judge Culver is a member of the Colorado Bar, the Bar of the United States District Court for Colorado and the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals.

name: Caryn A. Datz
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Caryn A. Datz MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Datz presided over a juvenile delinquency and dependency and neglect docket until last year when she returned to a criminal docket. The Judicial Performance Commission observed Judge Datz conduct proceedings, reviewed selected written decisions, and analyzed survey results provided by attorneys, non-attorneys and appellate judges. The commission also interviewed Judge Datz, interviewed the Chief Judge of the 17th Judicial District, and representatives from the Public Defender’s Office and the District Attorney’s Office. The Commission reviewed judicial performance data and Judge Datz’s self-evaluation. After evaluating this information, the voting Commission members unanimously agreed that Judge Datz meets performance standards.

Judge Datz is considerate of all in her courtroom and provides written communications that are clear, thorough and well-reasoned. She gives participants an opportunity to be heard, while managing the proceedings and maintaining appropriate control over her courtroom. Citizens appearing in her courtroom find her to be well-prepared and thorough. She knows the law and applies it consistently and impartially. Her demeanor is professional, which promotes an atmosphere of respect and public confidence in her integrity. Judge Datz is articulate and displays an ability to express herself thoughtfully, a valuable skill in sensitive or difficult situations. She demonstrates that she is knowledgeable, professional and organized. She also actively participates in a number of community service activities and serves as an educator for several legal and non-legal organizations.

Judge Datz serves as a District Court judge for the 17th Judicial District covering Adams and Broomfield Counties. She was appointed to the District Court bench in August of 2018 by then Governor Hickenlooper. Prior to her appointment, Judge Datz was a Chief Trial Deputy for the 20th Judicial District Office of the District Attorney in Boulder County. A graduate of the University of Miami School of Law (2001), Judge Datz earned her undergraduate degree from the University of Wisconsin in 1998 with a B.A. in Spanish and English. She has taught as an adjunct professor at the University of Colorado School of Law and is an active member of several community organizations.

name: Andrea Eddy
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Andrea Eddy MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Eddy runs an energetic, positive and low-stress courtroom. She is known for being fair, clear and respectful. As a judge, she is consistent and manages her docket efficiently. Her empathy and grace help her meet people where they are, especially during emotionally charged situations. She listens closely and has the patience to allow people to express themselves without slowing down the pace of the courtroom. Judge Eddy values the rehabilitative nature of the court and the opportunity to help people. She is a hard worker, regularly volunteering to cover courtrooms for others, including working weekends to assist during a recent budget crisis. She values mentorship and is passionate about helping new attorneys through comprehensive rulings that explain her reasoning.

In evaluating Judge Eddy, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Eddy was appointed to the Denver County Court in July 2016. She serves on the court resource committee. Prior to her appointment, she served as a full-time magistrate for the Court and oversaw traffic court, first advisement court, domestic violence arraignment courts, and various specialty courts. For the prior decade, Judge Eddy served as a senior deputy district attorney in Denver, where she specialized in the prosecution of domestic abuse, child abuse and sex crimes. She is active with Volunteers of America. Judge Eddy earned her undergraduate degree from the University of California, Santa Barbara and her law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Jacob A. Edson
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Jacob A. Edson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and the public.

After meeting with Judge Edson and after reviewing his prior work and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous that Judge Edson meets judicial performance standards. Judge Edson has received praise for his demeanor, application of the law, communications and case management. Judge Edson is described as calm, diligent, kind, courteous and respectful. While a limited handful of respondents shared that Judge Edson’s records at times are a little lengthy, Judge Edson’s surveys reveal that he is viewed as thorough, hard-working, and unbiased. The Commission concluded that Judge Edson’s knowledge base is well above average. Based on the review considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Edson meets performance standards and should be retained.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Edson, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Edson. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any performance criteria. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings.

Judge Edson was appointed to the bench on July 1, 2023, by Governor Jared Polis. He previously served as a Magistrate in the 18th Judicial District; Chief Deputy District Attorney; Senior Deputy District Attorney; and Deputy District Attorney for the 18th Judicial District Attorney’s Office. Judge Edson earned his Bachelor of Science degree from Colorado State University in 1997, a Master of Business Administration degree from Colorado State University in 1999, a Juris Doctor from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2002, and Master of Criminal Justice degree from the University of Colorado-Denver in 2012. Judge Edson has been a mock trial coach for a local high school and has volunteered as a presiding judge or scoring panelist for high school mock trials here in Arapahoe County for the past two decades. He is an active or past member and participant in the Colorado Bar Association, the Arapahoe County Bar Association and Justice Sonia Sotomayor Inn of Court. In his spare time, Judge Edson is often found driving his three children to their sporting and social events and attending their local church.

name: Jay A. Edwards
position: Ninth Judicial District - Rio Blanco County Court Judge
narrative: The Ninth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that the Honorable Judge Jay A. Edwards MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Seven members of the Commission voted that Judge Edwards meets judicial performance standards, zero voted that he did not meet the standards, and one was not present to vote. There are two commission vacancies.

The Commission considered Judge Edwards’ performance over the past term by reading a selection of his legal opinions, observing him in court, reviewing his judicial performance survey reports from attorneys and non-attorneys, interviewing interested parties, reviewing the Judge’s self-evaluation, and interviewing the Judge. The Commission applied the following criteria when considering the Judge’s performance: his integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

The Commission found Judge Edwards’ legal opinions to be thoughtful, fair, and well-reasoned. Through court observations, interviews with interested parties, and survey reports, the Commission found that Judge Edwards holds a high level of integrity, knows and applies the law fairly, communicates well, holds a firm yet approachable temperament, and is of service to the legal profession and the public. Survey comments noted that Judge Edwards tends to speak and move through hearings quickly, but also that his courtroom management could be more efficient. He acknowledges that his case load has increased over the past year and is looking at ways to enhance efficiency to handle this increase. Because of the small number of survey responses, the Commission used the survey feedback to check on the Judge’s courtroom management through court observations and interviews with interested parties. Still, the Commission found Judge Edwards meets performance standards.

Judge Edwards was appointed to the County Court in 2023. From 2018 until his appointment, he served as the Meeker Town Judge. Before that, he practiced law in Rogers, Arkansas. He received his bachelor’s degree from Mesa State College in Grand Junction (now Colorado Mesa University) and his Juris Doctor from University of Arkansas School of Law.

name: John Eric Elliff
position: Second Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge John Eric Elliff MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Elliff currently presides over domestic relations matters in the Denver District Court. Judge Elliff meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which he is evaluated. The Commission commends Judge Elliff for mentoring newer judges, his preparation and knowledge of the law. Judge Elliff’s written decisions are well reasoned, comprehensive and clear. His notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include his professional judicial temperament, the clarity and promptness of his decisions, and his commitment to treating pro se litigants with respect. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Elliff displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Judge Elliff exceeded the Court’s productivity benchmark for civil and domestic relations cases.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Elliff and observed him during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions he authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with him. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Elliff in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 8 attorneys and 10 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Elliff. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Elliff meets performance standards.

Judge Elliff was appointed to the Denver District Court in January 2011. Prior to his appointment, he was a partner in the Denver office of Husch Blackwell, where he specialized in commercial and intellectual property litigation. Judge Elliff has remained actively involved in several professional and community service initiatives, including serving as a mentor for “Law School Yes We Can,” an organization that supports underprivileged minority college students interested in attending law school. He also mentors other judges, serves on the Colorado Supreme Court Civil Rules Committee, and participates in the Underfunded Courthouse Committee, which works with judges, state officials, and county commissioners to support improvements to court facilities in rural communities throughout Colorado. Judge Elliff received his undergraduate degree from Washington University in St. Louis and law degree from the University of Colorado Law School.

name: Katharine "Jenny" Ellison
position: Eighth Judicial District - Larimer County Court Judge
narrative: The Eighth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Katharine "Jenny" Ellison MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by a vote of 8-0 with one commissioner absent and one commission vacancy. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and public.

Judge Ellison is highly supportive of access to justice in her courtroom, making effective use of remote appearances to accommodate out-of-state parties, individuals in inpatient treatment, and those who live far from the Larimer County Justice Center. Judge Ellison maintains impartiality in her rulings and actively seeks input from her colleagues to help ensure balanced and fair decisions. She works diligently to make the legal process fair and understandable for pro se parties, while remaining mindful of her role as the neutral judicial officer. Judge Ellison has demonstrated strong legal writing skills in her opinions and orders. At the same time, she acknowledges that she can further improve the reasoning and articulation of her oral rulings. The Commission also appreciates her commitment to mentoring younger members of the legal profession.

For this evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Ellison, read a selection of her legal opinions, observed her in court, reviewed her judicial performance survey report, interviewed the chief judge for the district, the district attorney and head of the public defenders’ office for the district, reviewed case management statistics, and reviewed her self-evaluation. As to the survey data, a total of 16 individuals, 9 attorneys and 7 non-attorneys, completed the survey, which is a markedly low response rate. Given the significantly low response rates to the surveys overall, the Commission gave the appropriate weight to the survey responses in its evaluation.

Judge Katharine "Jenny" Ellison was appointed to the Eighth Judicial County Court bench by Governor Jared Polis on February 27, 2020. Before her appointment to the bench, Judge Ellison practiced civil litigation and she also served in the District Attorney’s Office in the Eighth Judicial District from 2004 to 2018, where her work focused primarily on appeals and juvenile law. Judge Ellison received her bachelor’s degree from Colorado College in 1999 and her Juris Doctorate from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2004.

name: Allison P. Ernst
position: Tenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Tenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-2, that Judge Allison P. Ernst MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Ernst presides over criminal cases as well as runs the Competency Court Docket in Pueblo, County which she was instrumental in implementing. Judge demonstrated a commitment to serving individuals with mental health needs, particularly through her work on competency matters. Judge Ernst’s demeanor is described as professional, respectful, compassionate, and thoughtful. She is diligent, knowledgeable, and thorough. Judge Ernst strives to make the right decisions, uphold the law, and ensure due process. Judge Ernst is very motivated and is involved in the legal community serving on numerous judicial committees and councils. Judge Ernst’s opinions reflect her knowledge of the law and are evidence of her ongoing learning by proactively educating herself and staying well informed of changes in the law. There is some concern that the judge’s sentencing practices may, at times, be more lenient than typical for comparable cases, with outcomes leaning toward the lower end of the range in certain matters. This has raised questions about consistency and proportionality, as well as whether those decisions consistently align with the seriousness of the offense, broader considerations of public safety, and public confidence in the judicial system.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Ernst, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had interaction in Judge Ernst’s court. A total of four (4) attorneys and ten (10) non attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Ernst. The Commission found the survey responses consistent with their independent evaluations. Based on these findings a majority of the Commission agreed that Judge Ernst meets performance standards.

Judge Ernst was appointed to the District Court in December 2016. She obtained both her undergraduate and law degree from Michigan State University. Directly after law school, Judge Ernst was awarded an Equal Justice Works Fellowship with Michigan State University’s Low Income Taxpayer Clinic. She then moved to Colorado and was hired by the Colorado State Public Defender’s Office in 2005 and worked as a public defender until 2011 at which time transition to private practice until she was appointed to the District Court.

name: Olympia Z. Fay
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Olympia Z. Fay MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Fay is a model of efficiency and has demonstrated the ability to clear inundated dockets and deliver justice in a timely manner. She balances warmth and kindness with a formality and professionalism that establishes decorum in the courtroom. She manages her docket in a way that ensures that all parties, including pro se litigants, have equal access to the court. She shows respect for everyone in the courtroom, including litigants, attorneys, witnesses, jurors and the general public. She has an expert knowledge of the law and is organized and well prepared. When asked, she provides feedback to guide new attorneys in their practice. A passionate believer in equal access to the courtroom, she has championed that cause in a way that elevates the community and the court. As a senior member of the bench, she encourages collegiality and a supportive atmosphere among judges, which has led to positive morale, collaboration and consistency throughout the court. She is responsive, approachable and well respected as a leader and colleague.

In evaluating Judge Fay, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Fay was appointed to the Denver County Court in January 2015. She serves on Court committees for human resources/employee engagement and community service and engagement. Prior to her appointment, she served as a Denver assistant city attorney for two years and as a deputy district attorney in Colorado’s 20th Judicial District. She began her legal career in private practice as a civil litigator, specializing in complex commercial litigation, securities litigation and intellectual property cases. She is an active member of the Colorado Women’s Bar Association, the Sam Cary Bar Association, the Colorado Bar Association and the Denver Bar Association and has earned awards for judicial excellence from the Colorado Judicial Institute and the Colorado Women’s Bar Association. She earned her undergraduate degree from Lenoir-Rhyne University and her law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Kolony L. Fields
position: Twenty-Third Judicial District - Douglas County Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds by a vote of 7-0, with one commissioner absent and two commission vacancies, that the Judge Kolony L. Fields MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Fields presides over a docket in Douglas County, including civil, misdemeanor, and traffic cases. Overall, Judge Fields scored higher than average for Douglas County Judges and demonstrated strong ratings in performance areas for fairness, demeanor, diligence, communications, case management, and application and knowledge of law. Comments received regarding Judge Fields were positive and mention her respectful demeanor to parties and her ability to care. Fairness, dignity, respect, and communication skills were among Judge Fields’s highest ranked categories. The commission commends Judge Fields in her courtroom demeanor and articulates oral findings.

The Judicial Performance Review Commission met with members of the District Attorney’s office, Public Defender’s Office, Probation Office, and the Chief Judge for feedback on Judge Fields. A personal interview was held with the Commission. The Commission also observed her in court and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys. Among the survey questions was “based on your responses to the previous questions related to the performance evaluation criteria, do you think Judge Fields meets judicial performance standards?” Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 89% answered yes; 11% answered no. Of the non-attorneys responding to the survey, 86% answered yes; 14% answered no. A total of 26 individuals responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Fields. Based on these findings, the Commission finds that Judge Fields meets judicial performance standards.

Judge Fields was appointed to the Douglas County Court in December 2019. She earned her B.A. from the University of Colorado, Boulder in 1999 and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2004. She started her career in the Office of the State Public Defender in Golden, Colorado where she worked until 2011. She left the Public Defender’s Office after being hired as a District Court Magistrate in Jefferson County, Colorado, a position she held from 2011-2019. Judge Fields has volunteered in mock trial competitions throughout her career as an attorney and a judicial officer. She is also involved in the Peer-to-Peer program through the Colorado Judicial Branch which provides guidance and support to other judicial officers across the state.

name: Sean Patrick Finn
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 7 to 1, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Sean Patrick Finn MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Finn is widely regarded as a highly knowledgeable and intellectually rigorous jurist. Attorneys and judicial colleagues consistently described him as well prepared, efficient, and very familiar with the law. The Commission found notable strengths in legal knowledge, administrative performance, and courtroom management. Judge Finn maintains an efficient docket, communicates clear expectations to counsel, and is recognized for his command of courtroom procedure and the law. He is also active in legal education, teaching judges, and attorneys throughout Colorado.

The Commission evaluated Judge Finn through courtroom observation, review of selected written decisions, survey responses (which, as with many judicial evaluations, were limited, with 44 total responses including 7 attorney responses), interviews with Judge Finn, the Chief Judge of the 17th Judicial District, and representatives from both the Public Defender’s Office and District Attorney’s Office, judicial performance data, and Judge Finn’s self-evaluation. The Commission found that Judge Finn demonstrates professionalism and a commitment to the judicial role. At the same time, some members of the Commission identified concerns relating to Judge Finn’s interaction with attorneys that warrant continued attention. The Commission discussed these matters directly with Judge Finn and it believes that increased sensitivity to how all participants experience proceedings in his courtroom will further enhance confidence in his fairness, impartiality, and professionalism.

Judge Finn has served as a District Court Judge in the 17th Judicial District, serving Adams and Broomfield Counties, since his appointment in 2018 by Governor John Hickenlooper. During this evaluation term, he presided over civil, domestic relations, juvenile, mental health, and criminal matters. Before joining the bench, Judge Finn served as a Senior Deputy District Attorney in Adams and Broomfield Counties and as Chief Trial Deputy and Chief Appellate Deputy in Boulder County. He earned his undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado and his law degree from Loyola Law School and remains active in legal education and professional training statewide.

name: Pierce L. Fowler
position: Third Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 7-0, with one commissioner vacancy and two commissioners absent, that Judge Pierce L. Fowler Meets Performance Standards.

As a District Judge Fowler presides over civil, criminal, domestic relations, and juvenile cases in the Third Judicial District, with most of his cases originating in Las Animas County and the remainder in Huerfano County. He receives very good marks for his demeanor in the courtroom and meets performance standards for his communications, fairness, case management, application and knowledge of the law. Some concerns were raised in the performance data and survey responses regarding promptness in ruling on pre-trial motions and issuing decisions in cases. Both attorneys and non-attorneys acknowledge he treats participants in the legal process with respect. Judge Fowler had little familiarity with criminal law prior to taking the bench but indicates he is more knowledgeable and comfortable in handling his criminal caseload, having now presided over many such cases including a significant number of jury trials. He has also committed to reaching out to other more experienced judges for guidance as needed in areas of the law where he has the least experience. Based on these observations, the Commission unanimously agrees that Judge Pierce Fowler meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted an in-person interview with Judge Fowler, reviewed written orders, observed him in court, reviewed a self-evaluation survey, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys. Judge Fowler meets performance standards and takes his responsibilities seriously and is dedicated to improving his performance.

Judge Fowler was appointed to the District Court on January 9, 2023. Prior to his appointment he was in private practice where he focused on civil litigation with a small firm in Denver and later opened his own family law practice in La Junta before relocating to Trinidad where he continued his private practice. Judge Fowler received his Juris Doctor (JD) from the University of Denver. He is an avid cyclist and engages in community food drives by handing out groceries and participates in other charitable events in Las Animas County.

name: Marika Frady
position: Fourth Judicial District - El Paso County Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission voted 10-0 that Judge Marika Frady MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

County Court Judge Frady currently presides over a docket that is 90% criminal and 10% civil. Her criminal docket consists of misdemeanors, traffic violations, and petty offenses. Her civil docket primarily consists of cases involving breach of contract, landlord/tenant disputes, and eviction. Attorneys and non-attorneys who appeared before Judge Frady commented favorably on how she works hard, strives to be fair and professional to each person in her courtroom, and is working to develop a good system to ensure that cases receive the attention they deserve but do not experience undue delays. Survey results were reviewed by the Commission. There were a total of 660 invitations sent to attorneys and non-attorneys; only 11 of them completed the survey. The extremely low response rate makes the results statistically invalid. Even so, Judge Frady received an overall score of 3.7 out of 4.0 for judicial performance.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Frady, reviewed several of her written orders, reviewed judicial performance data, and observed her in Court. The Commission also received feedback on Judge Frady from the Chief Judge of the Fourth Judicial District as well as representatives from both the local offices of the District Attorney and the Public Defender. Information from all sources consistently described her as a good judge who is learning fast, working hard, and making a positive contribution to the County Court. The Commission was particularly impressed with how Judge Frady’s hard work and focus on an efficient, but fair, process caused her division's caseload to drop from 850 to 450 cases on average. Her opinions are clear and well written. Despite being relatively new to the bench, Judge Frady has made a favorable impression on those who have appeared in front of her. Her efforts each day to approach her role as a judge with diligence, humility, and a commitment to continued learning are being rewarded with a solid start to her time on the bench.

The Governor appointed Judge Frady to the County Court on July 24, 2024. Before that, for 11 years she operated a solo legal practice, specializing in dependency and neglect defense in El Paso and Teller counties. Prior to working in private practice, she spent six years as a prosecutor. Judge Frady graduated from the University of Missouri in 2001, and in 2004 she received her law degree from the University of Colorado, where she served as President of the National Asian Pacific American Law Student Association. Judge Frady’s work ethic and commitment to justice will serve the County Court well in the coming years.

name: Rebecca Rankin Freyre
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Rebecca Rankin Freyre, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Colorado’s statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Freyre was appointed to the Colorado Court of Appeals in 2015 and has served with distinction for 11 years. She successfully stood for retention in 2018 and has now served a full eight-year term. The Commission finds her written opinions to be thoughtful, well-reasoned, and drafted with clarity that makes the information accessible to litigants, practitioners, and the public. We find her judicial demeanor at oral arguments to be respectful, engaging, and present. Judge Freyre served as the Deputy Chief Judge from January 2022 to January 2026. She currently chairs the PERA Board and sustains a broad range of civic and volunteer commitments to serve the legal profession and the public, including providing mentorship to law students and emerging judges. In summary, the Commission finds Judge Freyre to be an exemplary jurist and a valuable member of the Court of Appeals.

To conduct its evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Freyre, reviewed her self-evaluation, observed oral arguments, examined a selection of her legal opinions, and considered survey responses from attorneys and judges. Every survey respondent agreed that Judge Freyre meets applicable judicial performance standards. She received positive comments from respondents with respect to her strong writing skills, astute oral argument questions, strong legal analysis for reaching fair outcomes in gray areas, and her receptiveness and incorporation of feedback from her fellow judges.

Judge Freyre earned her undergraduate degree in Economics at Smith College and her law degree from the University of Denver College of Law. She began her career in law as a law clerk at a private criminal defense firm in Denver, Colorado before dedicating 25 years as a Deputy State Public Defender, working in the Appellate Division in Denver and the Trial Office in Arapahoe County before appointment to the bench in 2015.

name: William Young Furse
position: Twenty-Second Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance by a vote of 9-0 with one commission vacancy, finds that Judge William Young Furse MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Furse presides over a complex and increasingly diverse docket of criminal, civil, probate, domestic relations, juvenile matters, and appeals from the county court. His background as both a Public Defender and District Attorney gives him a balanced perspective on the judicial system. As with all judges, his legal knowledge is stronger in some areas than others, and he makes ongoing efforts to learn more through formal training and consulting with fellow judges. He communicates his decisions clearly after listening carefully to all parties, often following up to check understandings. His administrative performance is characterized as efficient, with opinions issued in a timely manner. His fellow judges consider him a team player who does his share, and they appreciate his willingness to take on additional workload when needed, including in more demanding types of cases. He demonstrates integrity by recusing himself when appropriate. His courtroom demeanor is consistently respectful, courteous, and considerate of others’ concerns such as anxiety about appearing in court or constraints in their schedules. He makes special efforts to be fair to those who represent themselves without lawyers. Outside the courtroom, he educates others about the judicial system and works to get assistance for people with fewer resources to access the judicial system.

The Commission evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Furse’s performance, the commission observed him in court, reviewed his opinions, considered his self-evaluation, reviewed responses to surveys sent to all persons who have appeared in court and to appeals judges, and received input from the District Attorney. It also conducted personal interviews with Judge Furse, Chief Judge Plewe, and the District Public Defender.

Before becoming a judge, Judge Furse served as a Deputy State Public Defender for the 22nd and 6th Judicial Districts. He also worked in private practice focused on criminal defense and served as a contract public defender for the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe. He served two terms as the elected District Attorney for the 22nd Judicial District, and following his term-limited service, he was Assistant District Attorney. He briefly returned to private practice until his appointment as a judge in 2023. Judge Furse works to increase community awareness and understanding of the judicial system through Leadership Montezuma. He also serves as a judicial representative on the district’s Access to Justice Program, which works to ensure that individuals can meaningfully access the courts regardless of financial resources. He is active in the local bar association. Judge Furse is a graduate of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and John Marshall Law School in Chicago.

name: Audrey A. Galloway
position: Nineteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Nineteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds, by vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that the Judge Audrey A. Galloway MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Galloway was evaluated on six criteria: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession. Judge Galloway receives high marks from both surveys and court observations in all six areas.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Galloway, reviewed her written opinions, observed her in court, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who appeared before her, finding that she exceeded expectations during this 4-year term. The Commission found that she adeptly manages a busy docket, while ensuring that litigants feel heard and understand the legal proceedings in her court. She exhibits a balanced perspective and temperament, making fair decisions. Judge Galloway has good control over courtroom proceedings, while also treating those who appear before her with professionalism and respect. Feedback received describes her as an excellent legal writer, and credits her for her intelligent written decisions. Judge Galloway communicates clearly and has a welcoming demeanor.

Judge Galloway was appointed to the District Court bench in May 2024. Prior to this appointment, she served as the Juvenile Magistrate in the 19th Judicial District for five years. Judge Galloway worked in private practice handling estate planning, probate, and domestic relations cases from 2014-2019 and served as a Deputy District Attorney in Weld County from 2008-2014. She earned a B.A. from the University of Notre Dame in 2001 in Government and International Studies and a J.D. from the University of Colorado Law School in 2006.

name: Sara Garrido
position: First Judicial District - Jefferson County Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of (10-0) that Judge Sara Garrido MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Garrido was appointed to the Jefferson County Court bench in April 2020. Her docket is a mix of civil (90%) and small claims cases (10%). Judge Garrido is responsible for a large volume of cases, many of which involve pro se (unrepresented) parties and emotional issues, such as evictions and contract disputes. Judge Garrido strives to treat all parties with dignity and respect, regardless of background, and communicates that all parties will be heard and treated with consideration whether they are attorneys or unrepresented parties. Survey results describe her as able to show compassion to parties while still following the law and issuing fair rulings. She is described as knowledgeable, decisive, patient, and highly organized. In this review period, Judge Garrido has improved her knowledge of evictions law and procedure to the point where she is consulted by other judges in the state on evictions issues. Judge Garrido and her staff ensure parties know what to expect when they come to court, through issuing written instructions and informing them of additional information sources such as the Court Resource Center and judicial website. She uses Webex to ensure accessibility to hearings. In the next review period, her goals include ongoing judicial education and continuing to improve court management procedures that demonstrate fairness and impartiality to both sides, particularly those cases in which one side is represented by an attorney and the other side is not.

The Commission conducted an interview with Judge Garrido, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, considered feedback from the Chief Judge, and reviewed the 2025 Judicial Performance Survey Report from attorneys and non-attorneys appearing before her. Based on the Commission’s evaluation, Judge Garrido meets or exceeds performance standards in all categories under review.

Judge Garrido received a Bachelor of Science in nursing from the University of Miami, Florida. She worked as an ICU nurse before starting law school at the University of Colorado School of Law, where she earned a Juris Doctor degree. Before taking the bench, Judge Garrido was a public defender in Jefferson County for 12 years, then opened a solo practice specializing in criminal, juvenile, and dependency and neglect law. She is a member of the Judicial Discipline Commission, the Access to Justice Housing Subcommittee, and the Housing Forms Subcommittee.

name: Lisa Gomez
position: Second Judicial District - Juvenile Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 9-0, with one Commissioner recusing that Judge Lisa Gomez MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Gomez presides in Denver Juvenile Court. Judge Gomez meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which she is evaluated. The Commission acknowledges Judge Gomez’s excellent knowledge of the law and her efforts to ensure public confidence and consistency in Juvenile Court. Judge Gomez’s written decisions are clear, concise, and well-reasoned. Her notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, is her knowledge of the law, the respect she shows for all participants in her courtroom, and her ability to balance decisiveness with empathy and compassion. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Gomez displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Judge Gomez exceeded 4 out of 5 of the productivity benchmarks for juvenile cases and the Commission is satisfied that she is working diligently to improve productivity.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system and also met with the Chief Probation Officer and a representative of the Denver Office of the Office of the Colorado State Public Defender regarding Judge Gomez’s performance. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Gomez and observed her during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions she authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with her. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Gomez in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 11 attorneys and 3 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Gomez. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Gomez meets performance standards.

Judge Gomez has been on the bench since 2015, when she was appointed as a Magistrate Judge in the Denver Juvenile Court. Governor Polis appointed Judge Gomez to the Denver Juvenile Court in March 2024. Prior to her judicial service, Judge Gomez was a Guardian Ad Litem at the Office of the Child’s Representative Respondent Parent Counsel and served as Truancy Defense Counsel and Contempt Defense Counsel at the State Court Administrator’s Office. She also practiced as a solo practitioner. Judge Gomez received her undergraduate degree from Metropolitan State College of Denver and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law.

name: Michael A. Gonzales
position: Twelfth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twelfth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (6-0), with two commission vacancies and two commissioners absent, finds that Judge Michael A. Gonzales MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The performance standards contemplate the judge’s integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Gonzales handles criminal, civil, juvenile and misdemeanor cases. In making its recommendation, the Commission reviewed surveys from attorneys and non-attorneys, including litigants, jurors, and others who have appeared before Judge Gonzales during the retention period. The Commission also reviewed Judge Gonzales’s self-evaluation and samples of his written work. Finally, the commissioners observed Judge Gonzales’s courtroom and conducted a personal interview. Of the attorneys responding, 100% agreed that Judge Gonzales meets performance standards. Of the non-attorney respondents to the survey, 89% agreed that Judge Gonzales meets performance standards.

The Commission felt that Judge Gonzales’s overall performance as a district court judge was well above the required standards. Surveys sent out by the Office of Judicial Performance Evaluation rate judges in categories of case management, application and knowledge of law, communication, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. The results of the surveys demonstrated that of all the judges in the 12th Judicial District up for review, his scores were consistently some of the highest in the District. This demonstrates Judge Gonzales’s commitment to self-improvement and ability to effectively communicate with the public. Judge Gonzales’s written and oral decisions are thorough, concise, and communicated efficiently. There were no concerns from the Commission regarding fairness or bias on the part of Judge Gonzales towards any party. The Commission observed Judge Gonzales's sincere dedication to his community and his aspiration to foster a deeper public understanding that the Court and the judiciary remain integral, accessible parts of that community.

Judge Gonzales took the district court bench in October 2011 and served as Chief Judge from January 2020 to July 2023. Prior to his appointment to the district court bench, Judge Gonzales served as a deputy district attorney for the 12th Judicial District for ten years before becoming the Alamosa County Court judge. Judge Gonzales received a Bachelor of Science degree in Political Science from Creighton University in 1993. He graduated from the University of Colorado School of Law in 1996. Off the bench, Judge Gonzales has been involved in coaching local youth sports, served on the board of directors for the Caring for Colorado Foundation from 2010 to 2016, and in 2022 he was appointed to the board of directors for the Robert Hoag Rawlings Foundation.

name: Brian Louis Green
position: Eleventh Judicial District - Park County Court Judge
narrative: The Eleventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 7-0, with two members absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Brian Louis Green MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Green presides over civil, criminal, misdemeanor, traffic, and small claims cases in his courtroom. In reaching its conclusions this commission interviewed Judge Green, observed him in several types of court hearings, and reviewed his written work from the past two years. In addition, the commission carefully considered his evaluations from attorneys and community non-attorneys. His evaluations were overwhelmingly positive as to his judicial performance. Especially noted in the evaluations were his qualities of patience, communication, knowledge and application of the law, and judicial demeanor. Judge Green brings integrity, a strong work ethic, and a wise understanding of human nature to the bench. Further, Judge Green possesses exceptional organizational skills. Judge Green is committed to providing a just and respectful courtroom experience to all who appear in front of him.

Significantly, Judge Green scored high in every category considered by the community evaluators. These categories included case management, application and knowledge of law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. Importantly, both attorneys and non-attorneys evaluated and gave Judge Green the highest score possible regarding giving participants respect, opportunity to be heard, listening to participants, and providing written and non-written explanations for decisions. He was perfect or close to perfect in many metrics surveyed. When asked about Judge Green’s strengths, the responses on the anonymous survey were overwhelmingly positive, and again noted Judge Green’s fairness, efficiency, and demeanor. As it relates to any perceived weakness, there were few comments, and even the single negative review found that Judge Green was fair despite grievances against the system in general. The Commission finds Judge Green to be knowledgeable and competent in the areas of criminal law and procedures. Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 100% answered “yes, meets performance standards”, 0% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 0% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Green meets or does not meet performance standards.
