Of non-attorneys responding to the survey, 100% answered, “yes, meets performance standards”, 0% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 0% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Green meets or does not meet performance standards. A total of three attorneys and eleven non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Green’s performance.

Judge Brian Green was appointed Park County Court Judge in 2007. Prior to that, he worked as a Deputy District Attorney with the 11th JD DA’s office, and as a research attorney for Lexis Nexis. He is a graduate of the University of Iowa Law School. Judge Green grew up in Penrose and Monument, CO. He enjoys hiking, cross-country skiing, photography, and travel.

name: Hilary Gurney
position: Fourth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District voted 9-0, with one absence, that Judge Hilary Gurney MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Since her appointment to the District Court bench two years ago, Judge Gurney has presided over civil and juvenile cases. Her strengths include demeanor, administrative performance, and integrity. She is described as a great listener, patient, calm, diligent and a team player. She has excelled as a juvenile judge. Without any prior civil litigation experience, an area for improvement for Judge Gurney is her knowledge of civil pretrial practice and procedure, although she is working hard to become more familiar with this area of law. The Commission discussed with Judge Gurney certain deficiencies in her civil orders, suggested sources for further development, and encouraged her to keep working. Judge Gurney was very receptive to the Commission’s feedback and suggestions, which the Commission greatly values. By all accounts, Judge Gurney is working hard to learn what is necessary to become a good district court judge in all disciplines.

To evaluate Judge Gurney, the Commission reviewed Judge Gurney’s self-evaluation, a sample of her written opinions, and the 2026 judicial performance survey results. The Commission also collected feedback on Judge Gurney from the Chief Judge of the Fourth Judicial District and from representatives of the local District Attorney’s and the Public Defender’s Offices. After collecting all this information and observing Judge Gurney in court, the Commission interviewed Judge Gurney.

Immediately prior to being appointed to the District Court bench in May 2024, Judge Gurney was a Magistrate in this judicial district, a position she held for two years. As a Magistrate, she helped create the district’s Competency Docket, to facilitate and expedite eligible candidates’ access to services. Before that, she was a Deputy Public Defender in Colorado Springs for fifteen years and in Steamboat Springs for one year. Judge Gurney earned her B.S. from the University of Michigan in 2003 and her J.D. from the University of Colorado Law School in 2007. She is a mother to young children and volunteers as a mock trial coach at a local college when her schedule allows.

name: Monica Haenselman
position: Twentieth Judicial District - Boulder County Court Judge
narrative: The Twentieth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 10-0, finds that Judge Monica Haenselman MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Haenselman has presided over criminal, traffic, civil, and small claims matters in the county court since 2023. This year, her colleagues selected her to serve as Presiding Judge, reflecting confidence in her leadership and judgment. She brings a high level of integrity and a strong sense of empathy to the bench, qualities that inform her thoughtful approach to each case. Judge Haenselman actively seeks out opportunities to strengthen her judicial skills and is receptive to constructive feedback, which she incorporates into her work. She has developed into a professional and decisive jurist who prepares extensively and manages her courtroom and docket efficiently and fairly.

The Judicial Performance Commission evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Haenselman’s performance the Commission observed her in court, reviewed opinions she authored, considered her self-evaluation, held a public meeting to invite comments, reviewed responses to a survey distributed to all persons who have appeared in her court, and reviewed comments from her colleagues on the bench. The Commission also conducted personal interviews with Judge Haenselman, the current and former Chief Judge, the District Attorney, and a representative of the Boulder defense bar.

Judge Haenselman was appointed to the Boulder County Court in April 2023. Prior to that, she served as a magistrate (2015-23) and family court facilitator (2007-15) for the 20th Judicial District. Earlier in her career, Judge Haenselman worked as an associate at LaBuda & Associates and as a commercial litigation associate at Sonnenschein Nath and Rosenthal. She received her law degree from Georgetown University Law Center and her undergraduate degree in Spanish and Latin American Studies from the University of Colorado.

name: Michael Patrick Halpin
position: Eleventh Judicial District - Custer County Court Judge
narrative: The Eleventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 7-0, with two members absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Michael Patrick Halpin MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

As the County Judge for Custer County, Judge Halpin presides over civil, criminal, misdemeanor, traffic, small claims and infraction cases in his courtroom. He is a non-attorney Judge who spent 14 years working courtroom security before becoming a county judge nearly four years ago. Judge Halpin’s 20 percent part-time position allows him time to study and prepare for his typical one day per week docket. Judge Halpin acknowledges that the brief dockets allow him to take motions under advisement giving him time to research legal matters and consult with other county judges before making a ruling. Judge Halpin emphasizes that he wants to make sure that people appearing before him have a full understanding of the proceedings before they leave his courtroom. Judge Halpin has attended training for non-attorney judges which has proven invaluable and created a network of peers. Regarding civil matters that come before him, Judge Halpin notes that his primary goal is getting parties together in court and helping them to resolve their issues. Even when he is not in court, Judge Halpin views live streams of other Colorado county judges, research statutes that apply to his docket, and takes advantage of continuing legal education courses. Judge Halpin works to treat everyone equally in his courtroom and gives no more weight to any party regardless of their status, race, influence in the community, or level of education.

Although invitations were sent out to both attorneys and non-attorneys appearing in Judge Halpin’s court, the survey responses were inadequate to be statistically meaningful. The Commission interviewed Judge Halpin and came away feeling assured that the citizens of Custer County are being well-served with Judge Halpin on the county court bench. The result was a unanimous vote by the Commission that Judge Halpin meets performance standards.

Judge Halpin became a P.O.S.T. certified Peace Officer for the State of Colorado after attending the Colorado State Patrol Training Academy in 1989. He was promoted to the rank of Technician and became a certified Technical Accident Investigator and Reconstructionist. He specialized in investigating and reconstructing serious injury and fatal crashes. Judge Halpin retired from the State Patrol and went to work for the Custer County Sheriff as a supervisor and oversaw court security. He worked exclusively in the Courts for more than 14 years before retiring after 34 years in law enforcement. Judge Halpin was sworn in as the County Judge for Custer County on December 1, 2022.

name: Kelly S. Hansen
position: Thirteenth Judicial District - Washington County Court Judge
narrative: The Thirteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that the Honorable Kelly S. Hansen MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Commission voted 7-0 Judge Hansen meets performance standards. Two of the members of the commission were not present for the voting and the commission has one vacancy.

After meeting with Judge Hansen, and after reviewing the work Judge Hansen has done over the last four years, the commission unanimously agreed that Judge Hansen meets performance standards. There were inadequate survey responses for Judge Hansen, therefore the commission was forced to rely on judicial observation, the submissions by Judge Hansen, the meeting with Chief Judge and the interview to make their decision. Judge Hansen effectively applies the law and is studious to stay up to date on any changes in the legislature. Judge Hansen treats people fairly in her courtroom and is dedicated to making sure her courtroom is efficient. Judge Hansen is a part-time judge in Washington County; she manages her judicial duties while also maintaining a private practice. Based on all of the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Hansen meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Hansen, reviewed the opinions she authored, observed her in court, and reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation. As previously mentioned, there were not enough survey responses for the Commission to review them. Judge Hansen is educated about this process and strives to be successful on the bench. The Commission addressed minimal concerns with Judge Hansen, Judge Hansen is dedicated to serving the citizens of Washington County. The Commission believes Judge Hansen will continue to strive for excellence while she is on the bench.

Judge Hansen is a 5th generation resident of Washington County. She was born and raised in Washington County. Judge Hansen lives in Akron with her husband and 2 sons. In 2004, she began practicing law in Akron. In 2011, she started her own law practice, Hansen Law LLC. Over the years, she has served the surrounding communities as follows: Stratton Municipal Court Judge; Stratton Town Attorney; Otis Town Attorney; Deputy District Attorney for the 13th Judicial District; Yuma City Attorney and Municipal Prosecutor; Akron Municipal Court Judge; Fort Morgan Municipal Court Deputy Judge; Sterling Alternate Municipal Judge; and Wray Municipal Court Judge. In 2016, she was appointed by Governor Hickenlooper to serve as the Washington County Court Judge. Judge Hansen continues to practice law full-time in Akron in the areas of real estate, estate planning, probate, business entities, and other miscellaneous areas. Judge Hansen enjoys waterskiing, sailing, reading, watching her sons in their many extracurricular activities, and spending time with family.

name: Elizabeth L. Harris
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Elizabeth L. Harris, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Colorado’s statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession and the public.

The Commission finds that her opinions are clear, well-written, and reasonably timely. At oral arguments, she is well-prepared, succinct in her questions, respectful, and seeks to draw out the issues most important to the Court’s decision-making process. Judge Harris received positive comments from lawyers about her preparation, intelligence, familiarity with the record on appeal, and knowledge of the law. Lawyers noted the length of time required for Judge Harris to issue an opinion as a weakness. Judge Harris received positive comments from fellow judges for her writing ability, her thoughtfulness and her engagement in committee work for Colorado Courts. Judges also noted Judge Harris’ timeliness in issuing decisions as a weakness. The Commission commends Judge Harris for her commitment to community service and the Court of Appeals/Supreme Court summer internship program. Such efforts beyond the daily work of the Court of Appeals demonstrate dedication to serving the legal profession and the public. In sum, the Commission finds Judge Harris to be a valuable member of the Court of Appeals.

To conduct our evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Harris, reviewed her self-evaluation, observed oral arguments, read a selection of her legal opinions, and considered survey responses from attorneys and judges. The Commission received survey responses from only 5 attorneys and 22 judges. Nevertheless, the Commission is confident in this opinion because 93% of responding judges and attorneys agreed, and all remaining sources of information available supported a finding that Judge Harris “Meets Performance Standards.”

Judge Harris is a graduate of Georgetown University and New York University School of Law. She began her legal career as a law clerk for the Honorable John Porfilio of the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit. After her clerkship, she spent five years at the Federal Public Defender’s Office in Colorado and then joined the law firm of Jacobs Chase, which was later acquired by Husch Blackwell. In 2013, she opened her own law firm where she focused on appellate litigation. She was appointed to the Colorado Court of Appeals in 2015.

name: Craig Peter Henderson
position: Twenty-First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-First Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission unanimously by a vote of 8-0 finds that Judge Craig Peter Henderson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Commission has one vacancy and one absent commissioner.

By all accounts Judge Henderson has made a smooth transition from being a county court judge to a district court judge. Judge Henderson demonstrates high levels of integrity and good communications skills. Judge Henderson cares about the people in his courtroom as people, not just cases he needs to get through. He takes the time to ensure parties understand what is happening in the courtroom. In criminal cases, he speaks to the defendants to ensure they understand the seriousness of their misconduct while also encouraging them to do better. Judge Henderson has worked throughout his career to improve his judicial temperament and now receives high marks in this area. Judge Henderson has improved his case handling to ensure cases are completed in a timely fashion but has received mixed reviews on issuing timely orders and managing his courtroom schedule. Judge Henderson has recognized his need to continue improving his docketing and calendar management. Judge Henderson has generally been complimented for his legal knowledge but has expressed his own desire for more training in domestic relations, dependency and neglect, and some civil matters and is looking to work such training into his schedule. Overall, the Commission believes that Judge Henderson meets performance standards and is a credit to the bench.

In reaching these conclusions, the Commission considered several sources of information. The Commission considered survey results, case management information, and Judge Henderson’s self-evaluation. The Commission also interviewed attorneys and the Judge, observed Judge Henderson in court, and read opinions he authored. The survey results and interviews were largely consistent with Judge Henderson’s self-evaluation. While there were only 20 survey respondents, they unanimously agreed that Judge Henderson was meeting performance standards.

Judge Craig P. Henderson grew up on the eastern plains of Colorado. He graduated from McPherson College and received his law degree from Washburn University, both in Kansas. In his career as a lawyer, Judge Henderson was mostly a prosecutor but also did a small amount of private practice. He made Mesa County his home in 2002 and worked for the Mesa County District Attorney’s Office as a prosecutor. He was appointed as a Mesa County Court Judge by Governor Bill Owens in 2006 and as a District Court Judge by Governor Jared Polis in 2024.

name: Thomas W. Henderson
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Thomas W. Henderson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and the public.

After meeting with Judge Henderson, and after reviewing his work and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous that Judge Henderson meets the judicial performance standards. His work is exceptional, with his overall performance strong enough to gain unanimous support from the Commissioners participating in the process. The Commission believes Judge Henderson effectively applies the law to the facts before him. He is also effective regarding case management, communication and administration. Judge Henderson is consistently described as respectful, fair, careful and reasoned, very knowledgeable in the Rules of Evidence, and able to handle complex cases. He is noted to have a very pleasant courtroom demeanor. Judge Henderson is the Arapahoe District Court’s Presiding Civil Judge. During a time of transition of many of the judges in the 18th Judicial District, Judge Henderson assisted with a smooth transition due to strong leadership and communication skills. He expressed one of his priorities was equal respect for those represented by counsel and pro se parties alike. He is cognizant of the need to take extra time with pro se parties to make sure they understand his rulings. Based on all the considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Henderson meets performance standards and should be retained.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Henderson, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Henderson. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any evaluation criteria. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings.

Judge Henderson was appointed to the District Court in 2023 after a 35-year career as a civil litigator. He earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from Whitman College in 1983 and graduated from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 1987. He has been married for 38 years and enjoys skiing, cheering for his wife’s alma mater at football games and supports the Denver Center for Performing Arts. He is very involved with the Arapahoe County Bar Association. He is the co-chair of the Access to Justice Committee and was the Bar Association’s president in 2020-2021. He frequently participates as a judge in the Bar Association’s annual high school mock trial competition.

name: James Hesson
position: Fourteenth Judicial District - Moffat County Court Judge
narrative: The Fourteenth Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission unanimously agreed 7-0, with three commission vacancies, Judge James Hesson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

It was clear from the interview that Judge Hesson is a dedicated judicial officer and is an asset to the 14th Judicial District in County Court. The Commission was disappointed by the lack of participation in the survey results and would encourage the public to participate in the future. Despite the nominal participation, those that did respond were generally complimentary of Judge Hesson. The survey results reflect that Judge Hesson has good judicial demeanor and litigants generally feel respected and heard. Judge Hesson handles a combined docket of traffic cases, civil disputes including small claims, criminal, and misdemeanor cases. He has grown his knowledge and comfort in handling cases beyond the criminal arena. Judge Hesson shows significant interest in meeting those who appear before his bench "where they are" and making the court process more accessible. Judge Hesson is a good communicator and makes great effort to ensure that those appearing before him understand as much of the process as possible. The Commission is pleased that Judge Hesson has embraced virtual courtroom options to promote efficiency and accessibility of the Courts. However, the Commission encourages Judge Hesson to firmly enforce traditional standards of decorum during WebEx proceedings. In deciding cases, Judge Hesson expressed his preference to issue written orders rather than verbal orders from the bench. With this in mind, the Commission would still encourage Judge Hesson to remain open to making some rulings from the bench where appropriate, for the sake of judicial economy and efficiency. Judge Hesson appropriately appears to value "getting it right" over "getting it done". So, while there were comments and notes regarding judicial efficiency or perceived lack thereof, the Commission recognizes that a cautious and thorough, if slower, approach to running a court is preferable to one that rushes through cases and is regularly found to be in error or overturned on appeal. While Case Management is important, the Commission believes that fairness, demeanor and similar considerations are of greater importance. Judge Hesson ranks high in these critical categories. Based on all the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Hesson meets performance standards.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Hesson, observed him in Court, reviewed judicial performance data, written orders, written comments from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Hesson, and reviewed a self-evaluation completed by his Honor.

Judge Hesson was appointed to the Moffat County Court in January 2024. He was a Deputy District Attorney for the 14th Judicial District Attorney’s Office since 2017. Judge Hesson earned his B.A. from the University of Dallas in 2013 and his J.D. from Baylor University School of Law in 2015.

name: William W. Hood III
position: Colorado Supreme Court
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Justice William W. Hood III, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Justice Hood has served on the Colorado Supreme Court since January 2014. The Commission finds that Justice Hood is courteous to attorneys and treats parties equally without regard to race, sex, or economic status. He demonstrates an admirable work ethic and issues decisions in a timely manner. During oral arguments, he is respectful of the attorneys and their allotted time, and he asks insightful questions. His opinions are well organized, and he has a clear writing style that makes the reader’s job easier. The Commission believes that Justice Hood is a valuable member of the Colorado Supreme Court.

To conduct our evaluation, the Commission interviewed Justice Hood, reviewed his self-evaluation, observed oral arguments, read a selection of his legal opinions, and considered survey responses from attorneys and judges. A total of 7 attorneys and 24 judges responded to the survey; overall, respondents affirmed that Justice Hood meets performance standards.

Before joining the Colorado Supreme Court, Justice Hood spent seven years as a judge on the Denver District Court. Before becoming a judge, Justice Hood was a litigation partner at a Denver law firm and served as a prosecutor for ten years in Colorado’s 18th Judicial District. Justice Hood graduated from the University of Virginia School of Law and Syracuse University. In 2014, the Colorado Chapter of the American Academy of Matrimonial Lawyers gave him its Distinguished Jurist Award. In 2011, he received the Denver Bar Association’s (DBA’s) Judicial Excellence Award. He is a 2007 graduate of the Colorado Bar Association’s leadership training program (COBALT). He has also taught several courses related to advocacy as an adjunct faculty member at the University of Denver Sturm College of Law.

name: Amanda C. Hopkins
position: Twelfth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twelfth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (6-0), with two commission vacancies and two commissioners absent, finds that Judge Amanda C. Hopkins MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The commission evaluated Judge Hopkins based on several criteria, including integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Hopkins presides over civil, domestic relations, juvenile, criminal, and water matters throughout the San Luis Valley. Judge Hopkins is a fair and impartial decision maker who “treats all matters, litigants, and parties with equal respect.” Attorneys and non-attorneys alike highlight Judge Hopkins's effective communication and active listening skills, noting her commitment to ensuring that all participants understand the proceedings and feel that their voices have been fairly heard. Judge Hopkins diligently prepares for her docket, stays up-to-date on case law and statutory changes, and issues thorough findings and orders. Due to her diligent preparation and understanding of the law, appellate judges from the Colorado Court of Appeals scored Judge Hopkins’s overall performance as a 3.6 out of 4. Furthermore, whether focusing on the remediation of generational trauma and educational neglect within her truancy docket or navigating the complexities of high-profile litigation with care, Judge Hopkins demonstrates an unwavering commitment to the community. Her administrative leadership as Chief Judge and her judicial approach reflect a sincere dedication to enhancing the legal outcomes and quality of life for all residents of the Twelfth Judicial District. One area of growth highlighted by attorneys, non-attorneys, and Judge Hopkins herself, is the timeliness of her decision making in civil litigation. Judge Hopkins acknowledged delays in issuing written orders and has sought further training and education to address this issue. Additionally, a few survey responses raised concern regarding Judge Hopkins’s understanding of water law, the rules of civil procedure, and the rules of evidence.

Based on the Commission’s overall evaluation, Judge Hopkins has demonstrated that she meets performance standards in all categories. In reaching this finding, the Commission interviewed Judge Hopkins, conducted numerous courtroom observations, and reviewed judicial performance data, which includes Judge Hopkins’s written orders, feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, and a self-evaluation done by the Judge herself. Because of the small number of survey responses, the Commission used the survey feedback to address concerns during Judge Hopkins’s interview and check the Commissioner’s independent findings.

Judge Hopkins was appointed to the bench in 2018 and named Chief Judge of the 12th Judicial District in 2023. She graduated from the University of Puget Sound in 2001 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in International Political Economy and received her Juris Doctor from Seattle University in 2006. Prior to joining the bench, Judge Hopkins worked for the Alamosa Office of the State Public Defender and became the managing deputy public defender of the office in 2011. In 2025, Judge Hopkins received the “Restorative Justice Champion” award from the Center for Restorative Programs for her work with families and schools appearing on her truancy docket.

name: Amanda Hunter
position: Eleventh Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eleventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 7-0, with two members absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Amanda Hunter MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Hunter presides over civil, domestic relations, juvenile, mental health, probate, and criminal cases in her courtroom. Judge Hunter's overall performance, as rated by people responding to the surveys, confirmed that she meets the performance standards. Comments included that she provides thorough and fair judgement in her decision making. Judge Hunter was found to be decisive and professional. The Commission reviewed a sampling of Judge Hunter’s opinions and found them to be clear and well written. Judge Hunter received high marks for understanding and applying the law, even in complicated matters. Judge Hunter has adapted well to the challenges and opportunities presented by the virtual environment and live streaming in her courtroom. The Commission observed Judge Hunter being patient, clear and concise with litigants and attorneys to ensure everyone in the courtroom understood the proceedings. In her interview Judge Hunter continued to show a high degree of understanding of the court’s processes, administration, and role in the community, as well as, a strong understanding of the power and corresponding responsibility the courts have to their constituents. Based on these findings the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Hunter meets judicial performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Hunter, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed surveys sent to attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Hunter. Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 89% answered “yes, meets performance standards”, 11% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 0% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Hunter meets or does not meet performance standards. Of non-attorneys responding to the survey, 61% answered, “yes, meets performance standards”, 28% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 11% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Hunter meets or does not meet performance standards. A total of nine attorneys and eighteen non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Hunter’s performance.

District Court Judge Amanda Hunter was appointed in November 2022 and sits in Park County. She is the Chief Judge of the 11th Judicial District and sits on the District’s Access to Justice Committee. Prior to her district court appointment, Judge Hunter served for seven years as the County Court Judge for Custer County and as a District Court Magistrate for Chaffee County. Prior to her judicial appointment, she practiced in criminal law. JudgeHunter has lived and worked in the 11th Judicial District since 2011. She earned her law degree from the University of Nebraska at Lincoln and a bachelor’s degree in business administration from the University of Iowa. Judge Hunter enjoys all the outdoor activities that Colorado has to offer but finds skiing to be her absolute favorite.

name: D. Cory Jackson
position: Seventh Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 9-0, with one Commission vacancy, finds Judge D. Cory Jackson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission on Judicial Performance evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. Judge Jackson satisfies all six criteria. To evaluate the judge's performance, the Commission observed him in court, reviewed opinions and orders, considered his self-evaluation, and reviewed survey responses prepared by both attorneys and pro se citizens who have appeared in his court. In addition, the Commission interviewed Judge Jackson, the District Attorney, and the Head of the Public Defenders.

While Judge Jackson’s docket consists of a variety of legal matters, he presides primarily over civil cases and juvenile matters. The Commission finds Judge Jackson to be well prepared and sensitive to the needs of all court participants. He works diligently to apply the law in each case before him. This judge is passionate about his profession, stating he finds time to serve as a member of the Colorado Pattern Civil Jury Instructions Committee, the Security Cash Fund commission, and the Statewide Panel on Consolidated Multidistrict Litigation. He conducts his courtroom in a moderate and balanced manner. The commissioners were impressed with Judge Jackson’s energy in managing his varied work responsibilities.

Judge Jackson was appointed District Judge for Colorado's Seventh Judicial District in 2017. He was appointed Chief Judge in 2024. As Chief, he is the administrative head of all district and county courts in the Seventh Judicial District. Before his appointment to the District Court, Judge Jackson served as Ouray County Court Judge and as Municipal Judge for Ouray, Ridgway and Telluride. Judge Jackson received his law degree from the University of Colorado Law School in 2005. His Bachelor of Arts degree with honors in economics is from Colorado College.

name: Lara M. Jimenez
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - Adams County Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 8-0 with two commissioners absent, that Judge Lara M. Jimenez MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Jimenez was appointed to the Adams County Court in January 2023 and presides over criminal felony (15%), misdemeanor and traffic (85%) cases. The Commission finds Judge Jimenez to be consistent, impartial, and fair. Her demeanor is professional and respectful to all parties before her, and she works hard to ensure that everyone is heard. Her manner conveys and promotes public confidence in her integrity. Additionally, she runs an efficient courtroom and manages her dockets well. She is committed to clarity in her communication, and her written decisions are concise and accurate, with accessible language. Judge Jimenez is hardworking, service-oriented, and committed to learning and growing. She demonstrates strong legal knowledge, self-awareness, and humility. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview with Judge Jimenez. Based on these findings, the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Lara Jimenez meets performance standards.

In reviewing the judicial performance of Judge Jimenez, the Commission conducted and reviewed a personal interview with her. The Commission also interviewed the Chief Judge of the 17th Judicial District, and representatives from the Public Defender’s Office and the District Attorney’s Office. Other elements of Judge Jimenez’s judicial performance review include her self-evaluation, judicial performance data, court observations, and legal opinions she authored. The number of judicial performance survey responses for Judge Jimenez were insufficient and therefore not reviewed per the judicial performance commission policies.

Prior to her County Court appointment, Judge Jimenez was a magistrate in the 17th judicial district and previously served as a magistrate for the City and County of Denver. Before her judicial career, Judge Jimenez was an associate attorney at Front Line Law and served as a Deputy District Attorney from 2011-2020. She earned her bachelor’s degree from Adams State University in 2006 and her Juris Doctor from the University of Colorado Law School in 2009. In addition to their judicial duties, Judge Jimenez is the President of the Adams and Broomfield Bar Association. She actively mentors' newer attorneys and is always willing to provide feedback after trial completion to attorneys who appeared before her. Judge Jimenez is also active at her children’s school and in their youth activities.

name: Tarryn L. Johnson
position: Fifteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fifteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds, based upon a unanimous vote of 6-0, with four commission vacancies, that Judge Tarryn L. Johnson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado judicial performance standards on which judges are evaluated are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Tarryn Johnson serves on the District Court Bench and presides over domestic relations, civil, criminal, juvenile, probate, and mental health matters in the Fifteenth Judicial District. Judge Johnson’s demeanor is described as patient and respectful. She uses language all parties can understand, explaining the process and her decisions. Judge Johnson moves her cases along timely and issues orders promptly, with her written decisions being both clear and concise. She treats parties fairly and does her homework to be fully prepared in the courtroom, although at times she could take care to ensure it is clear that any findings are based upon the record presented to her. Judge Johnson’s interview confirmed her knowledge of the law, her common-sense communication style, and her desire to make the best decision for the people who appear before her.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Johnson; reviewed opinions she authored and her responses to Judicial Performance questions; observed her in court; met with representatives from the District Attorney’s and Public Defender’s Offices; and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who have had interactions with Judge Johnson in the courtroom. Survey responses were low in number compared to those invitations sent out, but the Commission took the responses and comments seriously. Of the attorneys who responded to the survey questions, 100% of attorneys stated that Judge Johnson meets performance standards. Of those who were non-attorneys, 73% stated she meets performance standards while 18% stated she did not. Judge Johnson received an overall score of 3.2 out of a 4-point scale. In the interview process, the Commissioners asked questions relating to the responses on the surveys, responses from the Public Defender’s Office and District Attorney’s Office, and Judge Johnson’s personal judicial philosophy and desires as she serves as a District Court Judge.

Judge Tarryn Johnson was appointed as a District Court Judge in the 15th Judicial District in December of 2022. In August of 2024, she was named Chief Judge of the Fifteenth Judicial District. Prior to her appointment, Judge Johson was a Senior Deputy State Public Defender in the La Junta Regional Office, covering the 15th and 16th Judicial Districts. Judge Johnson received her undergraduate degree in Government from Adams State University and her Juris Doctorate from Texas Tech University School of Law. She has spoken in area high schools about the judicial branch of the government and has participated in mock trials in local schools. Judge Johnson also enjoys being a soccer coach and sponsoring soccer camps.

name: Michelle Jones
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Michelle Jones, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and to the public.

After meeting with Judge Jones, reviewing her prior work, and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous that she meets judicial performance standards. Judge Jones is repeatedly described as intelligent and thoughtful, patient, respectful, and fair with a balanced demeanor and strong intellect. Her writing is understandable and clear, citing appropriate case law, and giving sound, well-reasoned decisions. She makes it a priority to be patient with all parties, including all pro se parties, taking time to explain the procedure of what is happening and why, and setting expectations early in the proceedings. She is an active listener and ensures that all parties are heard when they come before her court. She has twice volunteered over the last few years to step in and bring challenging overburdened dockets up to speed, improving efficiencies, reducing the number of cases on the docket, and reducing the age of case and response time to motions in the division’s inbox. The comments surrounding Judge Jones and the work she has done are overwhelmingly positive. The comments refer to her as a good leader.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Jones, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Jones. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any evaluation criteria. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings.

Judge Jones was appointed to the bench effective January 10, 2023. She was born and raised in Grand Rapids, Michigan and attended Boston College where she double majored in political science and communications. She moved to Colorado in 2005 and attended University of Denver Sturm College of Law, from where she earned her juris doctor. After law school, she worked as a defense attorney, administrative law hearing officer, administrative law judge, and as a Magistrate for the 18th Judicial District serving both Arapahoe and Douglas Counties prior to her appointment to her position of District Court Judge. She frequently volunteers to present on educational panels, including at the Family Law Institute. She also volunteers annually for the Colorado Bar Association’s High School Mock Trial Competitions. She is active in her community and enjoys spending time with her family.

name: David N. Karpel
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge David N. Karpel MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and to the public.

After meeting with Judge Karpel, reviewing his work and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous that Judge Karpel meets judicial performance standards. Judge Karpel effectively applies the law to the facts before him, he is on top of his caseload and is very efficient. Judge Karpel’s courtroom demeanor is measured, direct, and calm. He is unbiased and treats participants with dignity and respect. Judge Karpel actively focuses on mentoring younger and inexperienced attorneys. Based on all the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Karpel meets performance standards and should be retained.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Karpel, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, reviewed comments received from interested parties during the evaluation process, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Karpel. Because of the small number of surveys responses, the Commission used the survey feedback to check the Commissioners’ independent findings. The overwhelming majority of attorney respondents agreed that Judge Karpel meets performance standards. Non-attorneys praised Judge Karpel’s performance consistently finding that he gives proceedings a sense of dignity, treats participants with respect, and has a sense of compassion and human understanding for those who appear in court.

Judge Karpel was appointed to the District Court bench in 2023. He graduated from the University of Colorado at Boulder, a law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law, and an MBA from the Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University. Following law school, he accepted a commission in the Navy’s Judge Advocate General Corps, serving as a prosecutor and defense counsel. He then served in the active reserves in a variety of commands and retired at the rank of Captain. He was a Senior Deputy District Attorney with the Denver District Attorney’s Office, followed by serving as federal prosecutor with the United States Justice Department’s Organized Crime and Gang Section in Washington, D.C. Judge Karpel participates in the “Law School Yes We Can Program” as a mentor to a University of Colorado student and in a program that brings Justices and Judges to speak at high schools in the Denver Metro area. Previously, he served on the CU Alumni Association Board as well as serving as Chair of the Board. He has also served on the Dean of the Leeds School of Business Advisory Board and the CU Foundation. Judge Karpel also participated in meals-on-wheels and served as a big brother in the Big Brother’s-Big Sister’s program.

name: Timothy Gerard Kerns
position: Nineteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Nineteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Timothy Gerard Kerns MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Kerns currently presides over a criminal docket in District Court in Weld County, Colorado. His performance was evaluated using the following statutory criteria: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission found that Judge Kerns generally excelled in each category. His personable demeanor produces a courtroom atmosphere focused on respect for everyone involved. His oral rulings from the bench clearly frame the legal issues and reflect a solid knowledge of the law. His written rulings are thorough and intelligently expressed. Furthermore, the Commission found his judicial style to be authentic and thoughtful, and appreciated his ability to adapt to the uniqueness of each case.

The Commission’s conclusions are based on observing Judge Kerns in court, a personal interview, reviewing opinions he authored, and reviewing survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had been involved in cases in his courtroom. Those survey responses produced an overall score of 3.8 out of 4, which is higher than the state average. Additionally, 100% of attorneys and 82% of non-attorneys responding to the survey stated that he meets performance standards. These high marks are consistent with the independent evaluations of Commission members.

Judge Kerns was appointed to the District Court bench in January 2011, after serving three years as a County Court judge. Prior to becoming a judge, he was a partner in a law firm that focused on mediation, family law, dependency and neglect proceedings, and general civil matters. He received his undergraduate degrees from Central Methodist College in 1991. He earned his law degree from the University of Missouri – Kansas City in 1994. Finally, Judge Kerns serves on several community boards, including the Weld County Pretrial Services Board, Weld County Bar Association Board, and Peer to Peer Judicial Coaching Board.

name: Victoria E. Klingensmith
position: Twenty-Third Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 6-1, with one commissioner absent and two commission vacancies, that Judge Victoria E. Klingensmith MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Klingensmith presides over civil and criminal matters in the District Court in Douglas County, Colorado. Judge Klingensmith’s demeanor is described as prepared, professional, respectful, fair, and knowledgeable about criminal and civil law. She brings clarity and answers to confusing, and often emotional and difficult issues by following the law. Her written decisions are clear, concise and well written. Judge Klingensmith works hard to stay up to date on new case law and procedures. Judge Klingensmith uses her natural intellect and efficiency to track new developments in the law, expand her practical and legal knowledge, and enhance the administration of justice in her court. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview. Judge Klingensmith’s’ opinions reflect her research and knowledge of the law along with a common-sense communication style. Based on these findings the Commission agreed by a 6-1 vote that Judge Klingensmith meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Klingensmith, reviewed opinions Judge Klingensmith authored, observed her in court, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had interaction in Judge Klingensmith’s court. Among the survey questions was “based on your responses to the previous questions related to the performance evaluation criteria, do you think Judge Klingensmith meets judicial performance standards?” Of the four attorneys responding to the survey, 25% answered yes; 75% answered no. Of the eleven non-attorneys responding to the survey, 82% answered yes and 18% answered no. A total of fifteen individuals responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Klingensmith.

Victoria E. Klingensmith was appointed to the District Court in September 2023. Judge Klingensmith received an undergraduate degree from the University of Denver and attended the University of Colorado School of Law. Judge Klingensmith spent approximately 19 years as a deputy district attorney for the 18th JD District Attorney’s Office. Judge Klingensmith is also an adjunct professor at the University of Denver School of Law.

name: Michael Kotlarczyk
position: Twentieth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twentieth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 10-0, finds that Judge Michael Kotlarczyk MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Since Judge Kotlarczyk’s appointment in 2024, he has presided primarily over civil cases. The Commission finds that Judge Kotlarczyk is well prepared for court with a polite, efficient, empathetic, and patient demeanor. He effectively balances running an efficient courtroom with ensuring that each party, including pro se parties, has ample opportunity to be heard and understood. Judge Kotlarczyk is well organized and employs effective case-management procedures that support the timely issuance of written orders and rulings. His orders and opinions are thoughtful, clear and concise, demonstrating thorough legal analysis and a strong command of the issues presented. Judge Kotlarczyk recognizes the impact that implicit bias may have on decisions and is careful to take steps necessary to be aware of and limit any such impact on his judicial conduct and decision making.

The Commission on Judicial Performance evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, integrity, judicial temperament and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Kotlarczyk’s performance, the Commission observed him in court, reviewed opinions he authored, considered his self-evaluation, held a public hearing to invite comments, and reviewed responses to a survey distributed to all persons who have appeared in his court. The Commission also conducted personal interviews with Judge Kotlarczyk, the District Attorney, the Chief Judge and representatives of the Boulder Defense Bar.

Judge Kotlarczyk was appointed as a District Judge in October 2024. Prior to his appointment, he served as a Senior Assistant Attorney General and Assistant Solicitor General in the Colorado Attorney General’s Office. Before entering public service, Judge Kotlarczyk was in private practice at Reilly Pozner LLP and Davis Graham & Stubbs LLP. Judge Kotlarczyk received his undergraduate degree from Drake University and graduated magna cum laude with a law degree from Georgetown Law. Judge Kotlarczyk serves as an adjunct professor at the University of Colorado Law School, teaching trial advocacy and serves on the Boulder County Bar Association’s Professional Committee. He continues to explore service opportunities in the community.

name: Timothy Lane
position: First Judicial District - Gilpin County Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (10-0) finds Judge Timothy Lane MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

On November 29, 2023, Judge Timothy Lane was appointed to the Gilpin County Court in the 1st Judicial District. He stands for retention in 2026 following a two-year provisional term. Described by his peers as a sound addition to the bench, Judge Lane is known to be a neutral arbiter, thoughtful and deliberate in his decision-making, knowledgeable in the law, and well regarded for setting high standards around preparedness and acting ethically. Those who have spent time in his court room, attorneys and non-attorneys, find him to be pleasant, professional, and a good listener. He is respectful of others and ensures that all parties have a voice and a clear understanding of the legal matters before them. For those individuals choosing to represent themselves (pro-se), this is an especially important characteristic.

Judge Lane is responsible for a high-volume, county court docket, which includes mostly traffic and misdemeanor criminal cases (75 percent). Civil and small claims cases make up the remaining docket (25 percent). The Commission’s performance evaluation process began with observations of Judge Lane in court and continued with the review of survey responses from non-attorneys, jurors and court staff. Feedback from the chief judge of the 1st Judicial District, prosecutors, and public defenders was considered, and commissioners conducted an in-person interview with Judge Lane. Individuals who completed surveys were asked questions involving case management, application and knowledge of law, communications, demeanor, diligence, and fairness. Judge Lane scored above average among those surveyed. Judge Lane was transparent with commissioners when asked to identify aspects of his job that warrant improvement. He noted his desire to develop additional expertise in civil law and civil procedure. Overall, the Commission is very pleased with Judge Lane’s performance. He is a dedicated jurist who has brought efficiency to the courtroom, a passion for staying current in evolving areas of the law, and a measure of consistency for the Gilpin County community.

Judge Lane is a graduate of Michigan Law School. He has worked in the 1st Judicial District Attorney’s Office, served as a staff attorney for the Colorado District Attorneys’ Council (CDAC), and as a legislative liaison at the Colorado Capitol prior to being nominated to the bench. A Colorado native, Judge Lane recently relocated from Golden to Gilpin County, where he and his family are active members of the community. He is a founder and former member of the Board of Directors for Gilpin Mountain Kids, Early Learning Center and is an avid outdoorsman who enjoys hiking, skiing, and golf.

name: Gretchen B. Larson
position: Twenty-First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Commission finds that Judge Gretchen B. Larson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by a vote of 8-0. The Commission has one vacancy and one absent commissioner. The Commission considered multiple sources of information, including survey results, courtroom observations, interviews, the judge’s self-evaluation, and case management data. Survey results indicate that attorneys rated Judge Larson very highly, while non-attorney responses were more mixed; the Commission considered these results in the context of all available information.

The Commission finds that Judge Larson demonstrates strong legal knowledge and applies the law appropriately in the cases before her. She is well-prepared, understands the issues presented, and issues rulings grounded in the law and facts. Commissioners noted her skill in the courtroom and her ability to manage complex matters effectively while maintaining appropriate control over courtroom proceedings and ensuring cases move forward in a timely and orderly manner.

The Commission also finds that Judge Larson exhibits a judicial temperament that is fair, respectful, compassionate, and professional. She treats parties, attorneys, litigants, and court staff with dignity and works to ensure that participants understand court processes and decisions. Based on the totality of the information reviewed, the Commission determined that Judge Larson consistently demonstrates the competencies required of a judicial officer.

Judge Gretchen B. Larson, a Colorado native, received her undergraduate degree from Southern Methodist University in 1989 and her law degree from the University of Colorado School of Law in 1993. She worked as a prosecutor with the 21st Judicial District (Grand Junction) from 1993 to 1999 and with the 9th Judicial District (Glenwood Springs) from 1999 to 2005. In March 2005, she returned to the District Attorney’s Office in Grand Junction until her appointment to the county court bench by Governor Bill Owens in July 2006 and to the district court bench by Governor Hickenlooper in November 2016.

name: J. Chris Larson
position: Twentieth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twentieth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 10-0, finds that Judge J. Chris Larson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Since Judge Larson’s appointment in 2024, he has presided primarily over civil cases. The Commission found Judge Larson to be hardworking, diligent, and thoughtful in his courtroom preparation and decision-making. He has implemented case-management practices designed to reduce delay and litigant expense, including providing oral rulings from the bench. He is committed to both substantive and procedural fairness and makes meaningful efforts to ensure that pro se parties understand the proceedings and have an opportunity to participate. Judge Larson’s demeanor and temperament further convey to litigants his commitment to fairness.

The Commission on Judicial Performance evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, integrity, judicial temperament and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Larson’s performance, the Commission observed him in court, reviewed opinions he authored, considered his self-evaluation, held a public hearing to invite comments, and reviewed responses to a survey distributed to all persons who have appeared in his court. The Commission also conducted personal interviews with Judge Larson, the District Attorney, the Chief Judge and representatives of the Boulder Defense Bar.

Judge Larson was appointed as a District Judge in May 2024. Prior to judicial service, Judge Larson was an attorney for the U.S. Department of Justice for more than twenty years where he served in leadership roles in Washington, D.C. and Colorado. Before joining the Department of Justice, Judge Larson was a law clerk for a federal District Court Judge. He received his law degree from the University of Michigan Law School and undergraduate and master’s degrees from Syracuse University. While at Syracuse, he attended the S.I. Newhouse School of Public Communications and the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs. He has participated in a variety of educational programs serving students from high school through law school, and he has worked to support expanded educational opportunities for individuals with intellectual disabilities. Recently, he began serving as the 20th Judicial District’s ex-officio representative to the Boulder County Bar Association.

name: Jennilynn E. Lawrence
position: Twenty-First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-First Judicial Commission finds that Judge Jennilynn E. Lawrence MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Four members of the Commission voted that Judge Lawrence met performance standards and four members voted that she did not meet performance standards. The Commission has one vacancy and one absent commissioner.

The Commission considered multiple sources of information, including survey results, courtroom observations, interviews, the judge’s self-evaluation, and case management data. Survey results indicated that 36% of attorneys found Judge Lawrence meets performance standards, while non-attorney responses were more mixed at 50%. In addition to attorney and non-attorney surveys, Judge Lawrence was evaluated by four judges on the Colorado Court of Appeals, who gave her an average rating of 3.8 out of 4. Due to the small number of overall surveys returned, the Commission considered these results in the context of all available information.

After meeting with Judge Lawrence and reviewing her work over the past two years and after assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was evenly split as to whether she meets judicial performance standards. Although much of her work is satisfactory, her performance was not strong enough to gain a majority of the Commission’s support. While many on the Commission found that Judge Lawrence has improved over the past year in administration and case management, others believe she is ineffective in knowledge of the law, communication and due diligence. It should be noted that Judge Lawrence is actively engaged in training and education and has logged 74 hours of continuing legal education over the past year. It should also be noted that she is relatively new to the district court bench, having been appointed in September of 2024. Judge Lawrence is currently meeting or exceeding state benchmarks for timely completing cases.

Judge Lawrence has 14 years of service as a judge on the Colorado County Court bench. Throughout her judicial career, Judge Lawrence has held leadership and service roles, including President of the Colorado County Court Judges Association and membership on statewide committees focused on judicial education, access to justice, and judicial well-being. Prior to her appointment to the 21st Judicial District Court, Judge Lawrence practiced as a trial attorney handling complex commercial litigation and is admitted to practice in Colorado, New Mexico, Wisconsin, and Florida. She earned a B.A. in English and Education from Fort Lewis College, in Durango Colorado, an M.A. in Interdisciplinary Education from Adams State University, in Alamosa Colorado and a J.D. from the University of Wisconsin–Madison.

name: Elizabeth D. Leith
position: Second Judicial District - Probate Presiding Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Elizabeth D. Leith MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Leith presides over matters in the Denver Probate Court. Judge Leith meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which she is evaluated. The Commission found Judge Leith to be an experienced and hardworking jurist who demonstrates judicial efficiency and exceptional judicial demeanor. Judge Leith’s written decisions are definitive, thorough, and well-reasoned. Her notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include her deep knowledge of probate and mental health law, her fair and respectful treatment of parties, and her ability to manage effectively complex and emotionally difficult cases. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Leith displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Because of the unique nature and complexity of mental health and probate cases, there are no productivity benchmarks.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system and also met with the Denver District Attorney, a representative of the Denver Office of the Colorado State Public Defender, and the Public Administrator of Denver Probate Court. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Leith and observed her during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions she authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with her. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Leith in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 35 attorneys and 8 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Leith. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Leith meets performance standards.

Judge Leith was appointed to serve as the Presiding Judge for Denver Probate Court in July 2011. Prior to her appointment, Judge Leith served as a Magistrate Judge in Denver District Court, an Assistant City Attorney for the Denver City Attorney’s Office, and a Deputy District Attorney in El Paso and Teller County. Judge Leith serves on multiple Supreme Court and judicial branch committees and is a judicial coach and mentor for other judicial officers. Judge Leith received her undergraduate degree from Metropolitan State University of Denver and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law.

name: Priscilla Loew
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 8-0 with two commissioners absent, that Judge Priscilla Loew MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Loew was appointed to the 17th Judicial District Court in May 2017 and presides over Civil (20%), Juvenile (20%), Probate (20%), and Criminal (40%) cases. The Commission finds Judge Loew to be thoughtful, professional, fair, and impartial. She is respectful to all participants who appear before her and her demeanor promotes confidence in her integrity. Additionally, she runs an efficient courtroom despite the strain on the judicial district overall due to the high volume of cases. Judge Loew demonstrates strong knowledge of the law and is committed to learning and growing. She consistently invites feedback after trials and participates in educational opportunities offered by the branch to stay current with the legislative changes in the law. She is extremely hardworking, serious, and passionate about her role as a public servant. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview with her. Based on these findings, the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Priscilla Jeffrey Loew meets performance standards.

In reviewing the judicial performance of Judge Loew, the Commission conducted and reviewed a personal interview with her. The Commission also interviewed the Chief Judge of the 17th Judicial District, and representatives from the Public Defender’s Office and the District Attorney’s Office. Other elements of Judge Loew’s judicial performance review include her self-evaluation, judicial performance data, court observations, legal opinions she authored, and the limited number of judicial performance surveys completed by attorneys and non-attorneys who have had court experiences with her. While the survey response rate continues to be low across the state, of the ten results received, it is notable that 100% of attorney respondents indicated ‘Yes,’ in response to whether she meets performance standards. Only one non-attorney responded with ‘No,’ while two did not respond to that question.

Judge Loew received her bachelor’s degree in history from Colorado State University and her Juris Doctor from the University of Denver College of Law. She worked at the Weld County District Attorney’s Office followed by the Denver District Attorney’s Office. Judge Loew was then hired as a magistrate in 2016 and appointed as a district court judge in 2017. She serves on the statewide juvenile rules committee and the Adams County Human Trafficking Task Force. Additionally, she is a board member of Colorado’s Sexual Offender Management Board and the Colorado Judicial Institute. She is also co-dean of Advanced New Judge Orientation, is part of the annual judicial conference planning committee, and volunteers in schools. Lastly, Judge Loew received the Colorado Women’s Bar Judicial Excellence Award in 2026.

name: Ryan P. Loewer
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0, that Judge Ryan P. Loewer MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Loewer serves as a District Court Judge and presides over a mixed docket of domestic relations, civil, and criminal cases. Judge Loewer’s demeanor is described as formal, professional, dignified and fair. Judge Loewer indicated to the Commission that he is working to balance the level of formality that he believes maintains decorum and expectations in his court with the need to make sure parties are not intimidated by the process. Judge Loewer makes a concerted effort to be organized and prepared for every court appearance and finds that assists him in efficiently managing his docket. Judge Loewer describes himself as hypervigilant in his efforts to avoid inappropriate bias and discrimination. As Judge Loewer gains additional experience, he recognizes he has room for improvement and is excited for the opportunities for growth that this provides. Judge Loewer’s orders are well written, thorough and reflect his attention to detail. Based on these findings the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Loewer meets performance standards and is an asset to the District Court.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Loewer, reviewed orders he authored, observed him in court, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys, non-attorneys, and appellate judges who had interaction in Judge Loewer’s court. The Commission also received information from the District Attorney and the Office of the Public Defender regarding their offices’ opinions and experiences with Judge Loewer. Judge Loewer was appointed to the District Court in August 2023.

Before presiding on the bench, he practiced criminal law for thirteen years as a deputy state public defender. He serves on the Colorado Judicial Education Committee, the Magistrate Wellness and Support Committee, and he presides as the district court judge for the 1st JD Fresh Start Program. He coaches other judges for the Colorado Judicial Peer-to-Peer Coaching Program. Judge Loewer is a graduate of and mentor for the Colorado Institute for Faculty Excellence—Judicial Education (COIFE-JE) and annually teaches at Advanced New Judge Orientation. He presents continuing legal education classes in the areas of overlapping issues of family and criminal law, indirect contempt practice, magistrate jurisdiction, rules of evidence, and attorney ethics. Judge Loewer attributes his interest in judging to his childhood hobbies of competitive livestock and dairy cattle judging.

name: Kerri Lombardi
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Kerri Lombardi MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Lombardi is the Denver County Court presiding judge and oversees the court’s overall administration, fiscal and budget responsibilities, employees, security and engagement with city and state partners. When she became presiding judge in 2024, she learned the business side of the court very quickly. She has been uniformly commended for her transparency and clear communication in handling recent budget issues, including holding several open forums to answer questions directly. She is a strong leader who shows up both literally and figuratively for employees and is a fierce advocate for the court, its people and its independence. She makes thoughtful decisions and demonstrates integrity while navigating systemic problems. She is known for not shying away from difficult issues and for tackling challenges straight on. In the courtroom, she is efficient, approachable, knowledgeable and commands respect.

In evaluating Judge Lombardi, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards. The Commission also interviewed many of the courts stakeholders and administrators that work closely with Judge Lombardi.

Judge Lombardi was appointed to the Denver County Court in 2015. In February 2024, she became the Court’s presiding judge. Prior to her appointment, Judge Lombardi served as a chief deputy district attorney in Denver for more than 20 years and specialized in cases involving domestic violence and crimes against children. She is a member of the Colorado Women’s Bar Association and the Colorado LGBTQ+ Bar Association. She earned her undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado Boulder and her law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Katharine E. Lum
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Katharine E. Lum, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Colorado’s statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Lum was appointed to the Colorado Court of Appeals in 2022 and has served for four years. This is her first time standing for retention. The Commission finds she embodies the qualities of an outstanding appellate judge and is a valuable asset to the Colorado Court of Appeals. Her opinions are fair and thoughtful, and she delivers well-reasoned decisions based on the law and facts. She is an exceptional judicial writer who conveys her opinions in a clear and accessible style understood by litigants, practitioners, and members of the public alike. She arrives well-prepared to oral arguments, and is engaged, present, and respectful in the Courtroom. She also serves as the Liaison to the 15th Judicial District. Beyond her duties as a judge, she participates in community service activities that advance the court’s mission.

The Commission conducted its evaluation of Judge Lum by considering her self-evaluation, observing her oral arguments, examining a selection of her legal opinions (including dissents), conducting an in-person interview with her, and reviewing survey responses submitted by attorneys and judges. Every survey respondent agreed that Judge Lum meets performance standards. She received positive feedback in regard to her strong listening, polite and respectful nature, and thorough preparation.

Judge Lum earned her JD from the University of California Berkeley School of Law. Prior to joining the bench, she was Of Counsel with Cooper Ramp Cage Bucar Lewis (and predecessor firms) where she specialized in domestic relations law at the trial and appellate levels; and she clerked for the Honorable Gregory J. Hobbs Jr. of the Colorado Supreme Court. She serves on the Supreme Court Standing Committee on Family Issues; as the Court of Appeals liaison and coordinator for a long-standing externship program with Colorado law schools; and as a board member of the Minoru Yasui Inn of Court.

name: Andrew Luxen
position: Second Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 9-0, with one Commissioner recusing, that Judge Andrew Luxen MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Luxen currently presides over criminal matters in the Denver District Court. Judge Luxen meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which he is evaluated. The Commission commends Judge Luxen for his knowledge of the law, his patience with courtroom participants and his commitment to maintaining courtroom dignity. Judge Luxen’s written decisions are clear, well-reasoned, and reflect thoughtful analysis of applicable law. His notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include his respectful judicial demeanor, his preparation, and willingness to give each party a fair opportunity to be heard. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Luxen displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Although Judge Luxen did not meet the productivity benchmark for criminal courtrooms, the results were largely influenced by unresolved cases inherited by Judge Luxen, not due to his delay. The Commission is satisfied that Judge Luxen is working diligently to improve productivity in his courtroom.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system and also met with the Denver District Attorney and a representative of the Denver Office of the Office of the Colorado State Public Defender regarding Judge Luxen’s performance.
