The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Luxen and observed him during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions he authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with him. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Luxen in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 25 attorneys and 15 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Luxen. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Luxen meets performance standards.

Judge Luxen was appointed to the Denver District Court in June 2022. Prior to his appointment, Judge Luxen served as Chief Deputy District Attorney at the Denver District Attorney’s Office and Deputy District Attorney at the Denver District Attorney’s Office. Judge Luxen currently serves as the District Court Judge Representative on the Colorado Sex Offender Management Board. He is also a member of the Colorado Judicial Institute’s Board of Directors and serves on the Executive Committee of the American Bar Association’s National Conference of State Trial Court Judges. Judge Luxen received his undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado and his law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law.

name: Thomas L. Lynch
position: Eighth Judicial District - Larimer County Court Judge
narrative: The Eighth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Thomas L. Lynch MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by a vote of 8-0 with one commissioner absent and one commission vacancy. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and public.

Judge Lynch believes in the importance of a streamlined and efficient courtroom. He has developed innovative processes to support these efforts. Examples include making local service providers available in his courtroom to assist in the use of Medically Guided Treatment Supervision and encourages utilizing free mediation services in landlord tenant cases. Judge Lynch employs specific processes and requirements for virtual appearances. He identifies limitations of the current virtual technology. Through his written procedures, he strives to ensure that courtroom decorum is maintained. Judge Lynch is currently participating in a pilot program for virtual appearances utilizing a new more secure and dedicated program developed exclusively for use in courtroom settings. The Commission believes that Judge Lynch is a competent and capable judicial officer. He is respectful and ensures that parties feel heard in his courtroom. His demeanor is calm and professional when addressing those appearing before him. The Commission believes that Judge Lynch is an asset to the Courts and the State of Colorado.

For this evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Lynch, read a selection of his legal opinions, observed him in court, reviewed his judicial performance survey report, interviewed the chief judge for the district, the district attorney and head of the public defenders’ office for the district, reviewed case management statistics, and reviewed his self-evaluation. As to the survey data, a total of 23 individuals, 11 attorneys and 12 non-attorneys, completed the survey, which is a markedly low response rate. Given the significantly low response rates to the surveys overall, the Commission gave the appropriate weight to the survey responses in its evaluation.

Judge Lynch was appointed as a Larimer County Court Judge by Governor Bill Ritter and took the bench in December 2010. His experience prior to the bench includes service as a deputy district attorney and non-legal work in the private sector. Judge Lynch received his Bachelor of Science degree in computer science and his Juris Doctor degree from the University of Wyoming.

name: Corinne Magid
position: First Judicial District - Jefferson County Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously by a vote of 10-0 finds Judge Corinne Magid MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Corinne Magid was appointed to the County Court in Jefferson County in March 2019. She presides over a mixed docket of criminal and civil law, with the majority being criminal, consisting of misdemeanor and traffic cases. Judge Magid is described as prepared, fair, kind, respectful, and compassionate. She listens to all in her courtroom and is thorough when making rulings. During the interim period Judge Magid was given feedback that she needed to assert her role in courtroom management of parties when necessary. She took this feedback and has made improvements. In 2024, Judge Magid began assisting in the county court civil division, which provided and continues to provide relief for its high volume of cases. Judge Magid is innovative and creative in improving systems. She has developed processes and implemented changes with small claims court, electronic search warrants, 48-hour bond hearings, county court staffing, and she created Spanish advisement processes that improved efficiency. Judge Magid volunteers for the Colorado Women’s Bar Association Lawyers Teaching for Change, which involves visiting elementary schools to discuss the legal system. She also participates in the district’s legislative committee to ensure compliance with laws and new legislation. The commission commends Judge Magid for her innovation and creativity and encourages her to continue with her efforts in systems improvement.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Magid, reviewed orders she authored, observed her in court, reviewed the judicial performance survey responses from attorneys, non-attorneys, jurors and court staff, and received feedback from the chief judge of the 1st Judicial District, the Office of the District Attorney and the Office of the State Public Defender. There was a limited number of survey responses for this evaluation period. Of the non-attorneys who responded, a good portion of those were jurors, whose feedback was positive. With all information considered, the commission finds Judge Magid meets or exceeds performance standards.

Judge Magid was appointed Jefferson County Judge in March 2019. Prior to her appointment, Judge Magid served as the Presiding Judge for the municipal courts of Golden and Northglenn and as a magistrate for Denver County Court. She has also worked as a law clerk for the Court of Appeals and as a prosecutor. Judge Magid received her undergraduate degree from Colorado State University in 2000 and her Juris Doctorate from Boston University in 2003. During this retention cycle, Judge Magid served as the Presiding Judge of County Court, a position for which she was nominated by her peers and appointed by the Chief Judge.

name: Zachary Ilya Malkinson
position: Twentieth Judicial District - Boulder County Court Judge
narrative: The Twentieth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 10-0, finds that Judge Zachary Ilya Malkinson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Malkinson presides over traffic, misdemeanor, civil, criminal, and small claims cases in the 20th Judicial District in Boulder, CO. His judicial temperament is engaged, respectful, and even-tempered. His courtroom is well managed and efficient. His decisions are thoughtful and well-reasoned, reflecting careful consideration of the issues and a strong command of the law. His written rulings and communication from the bench are clear and professional. Judge Malkinson is well-prepared and effectively balances the tension between managing his docket efficiently and giving each case the time that it requires. Survey results show that both attorneys and non-attorneys appreciate his understanding and application of the law, and the effort that he makes to explain it in his rulings.

The Judicial Performance Commission evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Malkinson’s performance the Commission observed him in court, reviewed opinions he authored, considered his self-evaluation, held a public meeting to invite comments, and reviewed responses to a survey distributed to all persons who have appeared in his court. The Commission also conducted personal interviews with Judge Malkinson, the District Attorney, and a representative of the Boulder defense bar.

Judge Malkinson was appointed to the County Court bench in January 2019. Prior to his appointment, he practiced as a partner in two Boulder law firms and as a solo practitioner where his law practice focused on criminal defense. Before entering private practice, Judge Malkinson was a trial attorney for the Alameda County Public Defender’s Office in Oakland, CA. Judge Malkinson attended Boulder High School, earned his undergraduate degree from the University of Iowa, and received his law degree from the University of California College of the Law, San Francisco (formerly UC Hastings) in 2001. He participates annually in the Colorado High School Mock Trial competitions, where he was the presiding judge for the February 2025 and 2026 sessions, speaks at Boulder County Bar Association events, and serves on the planning committee for the annual Judicial Conference.

name: Chelsea Malone
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Chelsea Malone MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Malone is known for her outstanding understanding of the law, is knowledgeable about procedure and runs a disciplined courtroom. As a judge, she has high standards for herself and others—she arrives to court well prepared and asks others to do the same. She is well respected for her courteous courtroom demeanor and her professionalism. She maintains appropriate boundaries with people who appear before her, while also mentoring new attorneys through constructive feedback. She demonstrated her expert understanding of court rules by revising the evidence chapter of a judge’s benchbook. Judge Malone’s intelligence is an asset to the statewide court system.

In evaluating Judge Malone, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Chelsea Malone was appointed to the Denver County Court in 2016. Prior to her appointment, she specialized in criminal defense, working as a solo practitioner. Her legal career began as a deputy public defender, where she represented clients charged with all levels of misdemeanor and felony crimes. Judge Malone is a board member of the Asian-Pacific American Bar Association of Colorado. She earned her undergraduate degree from the University of Wyoming and her law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Dawn Mann
position: Third Judicial District - Huerfano County Court Judge
narrative: The Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one commissioner absent and one vacancy, that Judge Dawn Mann Meets Performance Standards.

As a County Court Judge, Judge Mann presides over civil and criminal matters, including protection orders, evictions, money disputes, traffic, and misdemeanors in Huerfano County, Colorado. Judge Mann receives high marks for treating all courtroom participants with respect and fairness. Survey respondents from attorneys and self-represented litigants noted that she is courteous and treats all people in her courtroom with professionalism. Judge Mann is thorough in her written rulings and carefully applies the law to the cases she presides over. Judge Mann has expressed a continuing commitment to focusing on the timeliness of her orders and improving her case management. Based on these observations, the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Dawn Mann meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted an in-person interview with Judge Mann, reviewed written orders, observed her in court, reviewed a self-evaluation survey, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys. The survey results indicated that Judge Mann met performance standards in categories including Knowledge of Law, Communication, Diligence, Demeanor, and Fairness.

Judge Mann was appointed to the County Court in 2019. Prior to her appointment she was in private practice where she focused on general civil transactions and litigation including Probate Court and served as Guardian ad Litem for children. Judge Mann received her Juris Doctor (JD) from Nova University in Ft. Lauderdale, Florida in 1995 before she relocated to Colorado in 1998. Judge Mann enjoys supporting the local community by choosing to shop locally and by attending local events.

name: Michelle Martinez-Thomas
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Michelle Martinez-Thomas MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Martinez-Thomas is personable, professional and has a true passion for her work. She runs a supportive, rehabilitative courtroom, while also being capable of maintaining courtroom decorum and handling inappropriate behavior. She cares deeply about outcomes and justice. Judge Martinez-Thomas is a problem-solver who is creative, thoughtful and intentional in assigning meaningful and effective sentencing. She makes docket decisions based on the best use of everyone’s time. She is self-aware, a good communicator and values transparency. She works to improve whatever courtroom she is in and makes changes when needed. She is a willing teacher and worked to develop a brochure explaining the Denver County Court procedures and purpose in clear, understandable terms. She was ahead of her time in educating juries on implicit bias before it was mandated. She takes community service seriously and feels it is her duty as a judge to be visible in the community and serve as a role model.

In evaluating Judge Martinez-Thomas, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Martinez-Thomas was appointed to the Denver County Court in March 2020. She serves on the Court’s community engagement/community service committee. Prior to her appointment, she served as a magistrate in the 17th Judicial District, where she oversaw criminal, protection orders and domestic relations cases. Prior to becoming a magistrate, Judge Martinez-Thomas worked for the Colorado State Public Defender Office for 10 years. During that time, she was twice appointed to the Denver Mayor’s Latino Advisory Council and also received the Outstanding New Hispanic Lawyer award from the Colorado Hispanic Bar Association. She currently serves as a board member for the Colorado State University Foundation. Judge Martinez-Thomas is a Denver native and was a first-generation college student, starting at Front Range Community college and ultimately earning her undergraduate degree from Colorado State University. She later earned her law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Elizabeth Joan McCarthy
position: Second Judicial District - Juvenile Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Elizabeth Joan McCarthy MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge McCarthy is the Presiding Judge for the Denver Juvenile Court. Judge McCarthy meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which she is evaluated. The Commission commends Judge McCarthy for her commitment to improve the experience of all those who appear before her in Denver Juvenile Court. Judge McCarthy’s written decisions are clear, accessible, and well-reasoned. Her notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include exceptional communication and listening skills, a commitment to treating all participants with dignity and respect, and knowledge of juvenile law. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge McCarthy displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Judge McCarthy exceeded 5 out of 6 of the productivity benchmarks for juvenile cases and the Commission is satisfied that she is working diligently to improve productivity.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system and also met with the Chief Probation Officer, the Denver District Attorney, and a representative of the Denver Office of the Office of the Colorado State Public Defender regarding Judge McCarthy’s performance. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge McCarthy and observed her during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions she authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with her. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge McCarthy in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 10 attorneys and 4 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge McCarthy. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge McCarthy meets performance standards.

Judge McCarthy has been on the bench since 2019, when she was appointed as a Magistrate Judge in Denver Juvenile Court. Following her appointment as a Judge in January 2024, Judge McCarthy was appointed as the Presiding Judge for the Denver Juvenile Court in March 2024. Prior to her appointment as a Magistrate Judge, Judge McCarthy was a Senior Assistant Attorney General from 2016 to 2019, Assistant Attorney General from 2011 to 2016, and a Deputy District Attorney in Denver from 2008 to 2009. Judge McCarthy is a member of the Irving P. Andrews Inn of Court and the Women’s Bar Association. Judge McCarthy earned her undergraduate degree from Indiana University and her law degree from the University of Colorado Law School.

name: James R. McDonald
position: Seventh Judicial District - Hinsdale County Court Judge
narrative: The Seventh Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission unanimously agrees, by a vote of 9-0, with one Commission vacancy, that Judge James R. McDonald MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission interviewed Judge McDonald via zoom video conference on April 24, 2026, with various committee members observing him in Court, either in person or via electronic means. The Commission also spoke with representatives of the District Attorney’s Office and the Public Defender’s Office, and the Chief District Court Judge for the Seventh Judicial District.

Judge McDonald’s docket consists of civil and criminal cases. Judge McDonald was prepared for his hearings and generally did a good job of ensuring that all within his court room understood the proceedings and the matter at hand. Judge McDonald was observed as having a bit of an informal or colloquial approach, which while appreciated by some, was noted as being a bit too informal by others. It is clear to the Commission that Judge McDonald meets performance standards.

Judge McDonald was appointed to the Hinsdale County bench in May of 2020. He has been an attorney in private practice for nearly thirty years. McDonald was appointed as the Gunnison Municipal Judge in May 2005 and continues to serve as municipal court judge in five Colorado municipalities. He also serves as a weekend bond hearing magistrate for the State of Colorado. He received his undergraduate degree from the University of California at Berkeley, and his Juris Doctor from Vermont Law School.

name: Dennis L. McGuire
position: Fourth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 10-0 that Judge Dennis L. McGuire MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The judicial performance standards are: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge McGuire’s current docket consists of 50% domestic relations matters and 50% criminal cases. In his self-evaluation and in his interview with the Commission, he emphasized his commitment to maintaining strong knowledge in the areas of law relevant to the cases before him. Since his last evaluation, Judge McGuire has attended conferences and completed courses to further refining his competency in family law and his legal writing abilities. He recognizes that the matters he presides over often involve sensitive issues that naturally give rise to strong emotions and, at times, dissatisfaction with the outcomes. Nevertheless, he expressed a continued commitment to treating attorneys, litigants, and victims with dignity and respect in his courtroom. His opinions and rulings reflect not only his command of the law but also a deliberate, plain language approach that avoids legalese and ensures that self-represented litigants can clearly understand the court’s reasoning. A total of seven attorneys and fourteen non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys regarding Judge McGuire. The Commission found that, although limited in number, the survey responses were consistent with its independent evaluations. Based on these findings, the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge McGuire meets performance standards.

The Commission’s decision is based on a thorough process which included interviews with Judge McGuire, with the Chief Judge and representatives from the offices of the Public Defender and the District Attorney, as well as a review of the judge’s self-evaluation, written rulings, and survey report.

Judge McGuire was appointed to the District Court in July 2024. Prior to this appointment, he served as a County Court judge for several years and before that, a District Court magistrate judge. Prior to joining the bench, he was a Deputy State Public Defender. He received his undergraduate degree from Northern Arizona University in 1998 and his law degree from Case Western Reserve University School of Law in 2001. Judge McGuire is active in the community. In the past he has provided mentoring support for refugee families. He participates in the Judicially Speaking program, which is dedicated to enhancing students’ understanding of the judiciary and its role in the American legal system. He also is a member of the Fourth Judicial District Access to Justice Commission, where he serves on the Family Law Day and Legal Resource Day Planning Committees.

name: Jennifer Lynn Melton
position: First Judicial District - Jefferson County Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission agrees (9-0, one abstention) Judge Jennifer Lynn Melton MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Of the ten commissioners, one did not vote due to absence.

Judge Melton is a county court judge, appointed in July 2019, and presides over a mixed docket of criminal, misdemeanor, and civil cases. Judge Melton was observed to have an even-tempered and practical courtroom demeanor. Comments noted her fairness in sentencing, in which she takes into account criminal history, rehabilitation potential, financial situation, and future threat to the community. She is known and appreciated for her commitment to mentoring attorneys who are new to practicing law. The District Attorney’s Office and the Office of Public Defender commented that Judge Melton’s courtroom is a good place for new attorneys to learn as she takes time following trials to provide feedback if asked. Evaluations and feedback indicate Judge Melton can often move too quickly, specifically in the afternoon docket, and she needs to be more conscious of addressing Victim Rights Act (VRA) issues. Going forward, she has committed to slowing down the pace to ensure that all parties in her courtroom have adequate time for case presentation and understand the legal basis for her decisions.

Judge Melton’s evaluation was based on integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the community In evaluating Judge Melton’s performance, The Commission conducted a personal interview with her, observed her in the court, and reviewed the 2025-2026 survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys appearing before her. The Commission additionally received feedback from the chief judge, the District Attorney, and the head of the Public Defender Office. The Commission reviewed Judge Melton’s self-evaluation, and written rulings and orders she has issued.

Judge Melton attended Texas A&M University on an athletic scholarship for swimming. After graduation, she attended Texas Tech University School of Law on an academic scholarship. Following law school, Judge Melton clerked for the Honorable Max Osborne of the Texas Court of Appeals. In 1995, she moved to Colorado and practiced civil and domestic law with a small private law firm. In 2008 she was awarded contracts from the offices of Alternate Defense Counsel (ADC) and Respondent Parent Counsel (ORPC). Subsequently, she started her own solo practice specializing in criminal defense and dependency and neglect (child welfare) cases.

name: Michele Lynn Meyer
position: Nineteenth Judicial District - Weld County Court Judge
narrative: The Nineteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Michele Lynn Meyer MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Meyer currently presides over a criminal docket in County Court in Weld County, Colorado. Her performance was evaluated using the following statutory criteria: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission found that Judge Meyer generally excelled in each category. Judge Meyer has also demonstrated a willingness to adapt her approach as necessary for individual cases and to stay current with the legal landscape and docket needs. Her empathetic demeanor produces a courtroom where parties are truly heard and respected. Judge Meyer is also the presiding County Court Judge and dedicates significant time to training, mentoring, and supporting newer judges and colleagues.

The Commission’s conclusions are based on observing Judge Meyer in court, a personal interview, reviewing opinions she authored, and reviewing survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had been involved in cases in her courtroom. Those survey responses in 2025 produced an overall score of 3.6 out of 4. Additionally, 100% of attorneys and 75% of non-attorneys responding to the survey stated that she meets performance standards. The 2026 Survey responses produced an overall score of 3.4 out of 4, which is higher than the state average. Additionally, 75% of attorneys and 90 of non-attorneys responding to the survey stated that she meets performance standards. These high marks are consistent with the independent evaluations of Commission members.

Judge Meyer was appointed to the County Court bench in September 2007. Prior to becoming a judge, she was a deputy district attorney with Weld County. Judge Meyer obtained her law degree from the University of Denver and has an undergraduate degree from Colorado State University. Finally, Judge Meyer works as a mentor to other judges in Weld County.

name: Meegan Miloud
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 10-0 that the Honorable Meegan Miloud MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

After meeting with Judge Miloud, reviewing her work over the past three years, and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission unanimously determined that she meets judicial performance standards. Among her many accomplishments, she successfully managed a backlogged docket and brought it current. She accomplished this while maintaining an efficient and effective workflow. Judge Miloud is noted for her calm demeanor and good communication both in verbal interactions with court participants as well as in her written orders. She expresses understanding that parties that appear before her can be served best by having clarity and understanding of the process. To that end, Judge Miloud ensures that each party has ample time to ask questions and she provides proper instructions. Further, she maintains decorum in her courtroom. Judge Miloud is known for being well prepared. Her decisions are well-reasoned and she follows the law. She has plans to continue to develop her skills in civil law by attending conferences and courses as well as accessing the mentorship available in the district.

Judge Miloud has served three years on the bench after serving as a District Court Magistrate. Her docket consists of Criminal and Civil cases as well as Domestic Relations and some Probate cases. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Miloud, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments received from interested parties during the evaluation period, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Miloud.

Meegan Miloud is a Texas native. Judge Miloud enjoys reading, cooking, and playing tennis. She received her bachelor’s degree from the University of Oklahoma in 1998 and her juris doctorate from Texas Wesleyan University School of Law in 2001. Judge Miloud is a former District Court Magistrate in the 1st Judicial District where she presided over probate matters, domestic relations, and juvenile cases. She was formerly an Assistant District Attorney in Tarrant County, Texas and an Assistant District Attorney in Laramie County, Wyoming. Before taking the bench Judge Miloud was respondent parent counsel and Guardian ad Litem in cases of child welfare and adult mental health in the Denver metro area. Judge Miloud was Respondent Parent Counsel and a Guardian ad litem (GAL) for parents and guardians in Dependency and Neglect cases, counsel for Respondents in Mental Health, defense counsel and GAL for adult Respondents for Conservatorships and Guardianships and minors in Mental Health and Probate cases in the Denver metro area.

name: Pax Moultrie
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously finds by a vote of 9-0, with one commission absence and one commission vacancy, that Judge Pax Moultrie MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Colorado’s statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Moultrie was appointed to the Colorado Court of Appeals in January 2024, and this is her first time standing for retention as a Court of Appeals Judge. The Commission finds that her opinions are thoughtful, accessible, and well written. At oral argument, she has an excellent judicial demeanor, engages with the attorneys, and is respectful of all parties. The Commission commends Judge Moultrie for her service to the judicial branch’s well-being efforts to support judicial officers and employees as well as her efforts to educate the community about the courts. In sum, the Commission finds Judge Moultrie is a valuable addition to the Court of Appeals.

To conduct its evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Moultrie, reviewed her self-evaluation, observed oral arguments, read a selection of her legal opinions, and considered survey responses from attorneys and judges. Every surveyed respondent agreed that Judge Moultrie meets Colorado’s Judicial Performance Standards. She received positive comments from lawyers with respect to her courteous demeanor during oral arguments and her ability to write in plain language so that both lawyers and laypersons can understand her opinions. Judge Moultrie received positive comments from fellow judges, especially with respect to the valuable perspective she brings as a former juvenile court judge.

Judge Moultrie earned her bachelor’s degree from Washington University in St. Louis and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law. She began her legal career as a law clerk in the 1st Judicial District, which was followed by a clerkship with the Colorado Supreme Court. She then represented county departments of human services in dependency and neglect matters and juvenile delinquency matters. Before joining the Court of Appeals, she served as a district court judge for Denver Juvenile Court, where she presided over a docket consisting of dependency and neglect cases, juvenile delinquency cases, and adoptions. She also previously served as a magistrate in the 1st Judicial District. She is a member of several specialty bar associations, including the Sam Cary Bar Association and the Colorado Women’s Bar Association. She is a Fellow of the Colorado Bar Foundation and is a founding member of the Irving P. Andrews Inn of Court. Judge Moultrie has served as an appointed board member of law-related and community non-profit organizations and is currently active in the Colorado Judicial Branch’s well-being efforts to support judicial officers and employees.

name: Elise Myer
position: Ninth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Ninth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance by a vote of 7-0 with two commission vacancies and one commissioner absent, finds that the Honorable Judge Elise Myer MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission found Judge Myer’s legal opinions to be thoughtful, fair, clear, and well-reasoned. Through court observations, interviews, survey reports, and the Commission’s interview with Judge Myer, the Commission found that Judge Myer demonstrates exceptional integrity, strong legal knowledge, excellent communication skills, a calm and respectful judicial temperament, effective courtroom and administrative management, and meaningful service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission considers Judge Myer to be a model judge. She is prepared, fair, respectful, and thoughtful in her handling of matters before the court. She communicates clearly with attorneys, parties, and members of the public, and she maintains appropriate control of the courtroom while treating those who appear before her with dignity. The Commission found no meaningful concerns regarding Judge Myer’s performance. To the contrary, the Commission believes Judge Myer reflects the highest standards expected of the judiciary.

The Commission considered Judge Myer’s performance over the past term by reading a selection of her legal opinions, observing her in court, reviewing her judicial performance survey reports from attorneys and non-attorneys, interviewing interested parties including the district attorney and the district’s head of the public defender’s office, reviewing Judge Myer’s self-evaluation, and interviewing Judge Myer. The Commission applied the following criteria when considering Judge Myer’s performance: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. Judge Myer was appointed to the District Court in 2023. The Commission cannot recommend Judge Myer more highly, believes that she meets performance standards and is an asset to the 9th Judicial District, the Courts, and the State of Colorado.

Judge Myer was appointed as a district judge in the 9th Judicial District in June 2023. Prior to her appointment, Judge Myer was a public defender in the Glenwood Springs Regional Trial Office of the Office of the State Public Defender. She began her work as a public defender in June 2011 and, at the time of her appointment, was the managing attorney of her office.

Judge Myer received her bachelor’s degrees in Spanish and Sociology from Temple University in Philadelphia, PA, in 2004. She received her law degree from American University, Washington College of Law, in Washington, D.C., in 2010. She moved to Colorado shortly after finishing law school.

name: Dana Nichols
position: Nineteenth Judicial District - Weld County Court Judge
narrative: The Nineteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Dana Nichols MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Nichols currently presides over a County Court criminal docket in Weld County, Colorado. The Commission evaluated her performance on the following statutory criteria: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission based its conclusions on observing Judge Nichols in court, a personal interview, reviewing survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had been involved in cases in her courtroom, feedback received from the District Attorney’s Office and Office of the Public Defender, and reviewing a transcript, Court Order, and Appellate Order regarding a decision of the court. The Commission found that Judge Nichols was satisfactory in each of the statutory criteria, with 78% of attorneys and 88% of non-attorneys finding that Judge Nichols meets performance standards.

Judge Nichols received notable remarks for her demeanor on the bench and communication. She is observed to have a good judicial temperament and treats those who appears in her courtroom with kindness and respect. The Commission notes feedback suggesting Judge Nichols needs improvement in her legal knowledge, specifically ensuring her opinions are supported by the appropriate legal authority. Judge Nichols was receptive to this feedback, acknowledging that she needs to balance her use of plain language which facilitates clear understanding, to her obligation to safeguard the record with supporting legal authority. The Commission also acknowledges Judge Nichols’ contribution to the legal profession as a leader in the formation of a specialized Competency Court docket to help address mental health issues in County Court. Judge Nichols described this effort as a substantial undertaking but something that has been very important and rewarding. Her commitment to this endeavor is of great service to the legal profession and community.

Judge Nichols was appointed to the Weld County Court bench in 2007. Before her appointment, she served as a Deputy Public Defender for nearly 10 years in the Greeley, Pueblo, and Colorado Springs trial offices, as well as the Appellate division. She also spent three years in private civil practice in Denver with the firm of Kennedy & Christopher, P.C. Judge Nichols obtained her law degree from the University of Colorado School of Law and has an undergraduate degree in biological sciences from Colorado State University. Judge Nichols is a member of the County Court Judges Association (past president) and the Weld Chapter of the Colorado Women’s Bar Association. She previously served on state committees for the Colorado Rules of Criminal Procedure and the Colorado Senior Judge Program. She has authored chapters for the Colorado DUI Bench book. She currently serves on the Board for North Range Behavioral Health. Judge Nichols is currently assigned to Division 9, hearing all types of County Court cases including civil disputes, domestic violence, and DUI cases, and presiding over the Competency Court docket.

name: Jon J. Olafson
position: Second Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 9-0, with one Commissioner recusing, that Judge Jon J. Olafson MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Olafson currently presides over civil matters in the Denver District Court. Judge Olafson meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which he is evaluated. The Commission recognizes Judge Olafson for his strong case management skills and his commitment to the fair and efficient administration of justice. Judge Olafson’s written decisions are thorough and well-reasoned. His notable strengths, as observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include his civility and courtroom demeanor, his clear communication with courtroom participants, and his commitment to reducing courtroom bias. The Commission commends Judge Olafson for ensuring that proceedings are conducted efficiently and for his efforts to create an environment of fairness for all members of the community who appear before him. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Olafson displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Judge Olafson exceeded the Court’s productivity benchmark for civil courtrooms.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Olafson and observed him during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions he authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with him. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Olafson in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 41 attorneys and 4 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Olafson. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Olafson meets performance standards.

Judge Olafson was appointed to the Denver District Court in December 2023. Prior to his appointment, Judge Olafson practiced commercial and employment litigation, including as a partner at Buchalter, PC. Judge Olafson is active in service to the legal profession and broader community, serving as Secretary of the Board for the Center for Legal Inclusiveness, ex officio Director for Opera Colorado, an Advisory Board Member for the University of North Dakota College of Arts and Sciences, and President Emeritus for the Denver Philharmonic Orchestra. Judge Olafson received his undergraduate degree from the University of North Dakota and his law degree from Texas Tech University School of Law.

name: Meredith Patrick Cord
position: Fourth Judicial District - El Paso County Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (10-0) agrees that El Paso County Court Judge Meredith Patrick Cord MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Patrick Cord’s docket is 90% criminal and 10% civil cases. Her criminal cases are misdemeanors, approximately 65% of which are traffic and DUI cases. She is consistently described as knowledgeable, well-prepared, patient, and fair, and her written opinions reflect a careful command of the law. She maintains written case management orders, meets regularly with the attorneys assigned to her courtroom to build consistency amid high attorney turnover, and prepares her dockets a week in advance so that every matter receives appropriate attention. In her Commission interview, Judge Patrick Cord described keeping a note on her bench that reads, “This may be the most important day in this person’s life,” a philosophy Commissioners witnessed her honor firsthand, including in her patient and inclusive approach to the approximately 10 percent of her litigants who require Spanish-language interpretation. Judge Patrick Cord’s overall combined performance score on the 2026 Judicial Performance Survey was 3.7 out of 4.0, which is above average for County Court judges in the Fourth Judicial District. Her highest-rated category was communication at 3.8; diligence, demeanor, and fairness each scored 3.7; and case management and knowledge and application of law each scored 3.6. Although the Survey results are statistically invalid due to low response rate, 18 of 19 responders believe that Judge Patrick Cord meets or exceeds judicial performance standards. Judge Patrick Cord works hard to enhance public confidence in the judiciary. The Commission believes Judge Patrick Cord is a true asset to the Fourth Judicial District.

The Commission interviewed Judge Patrick Cord, observed her in court, reviewed her self-evaluation, written opinions, judicial performance data, comments from attorneys and non-attorneys, and the judicial performance survey results from 2026, which included 19 completed survey responses (2 attorneys and 17 non-attorneys). The Commission also spoke with the Chief Judge and representatives of the District Attorney’s Office and the Public Defender’s Office, all of whom reported positively on her performance.

Judge Patrick Cord was appointed to the County Court bench in January 2019. Before her appointment, she served as a District Court Magistrate in Colorado Springs for more than four years, handling domestic relations and child support matters. Prior to joining the bench, she was a shareholder at Johnson & Cord, P.C. practicing family law; she also served as an associate attorney at Kane, Donley and Johnson and the Marrison Law Firm, and as a prosecutor with the Fourth Judicial District Attorney’s Office. Judge Patrick Cord received her undergraduate degree from Ohio State University and her law degree from Case Western Reserve University School of Law in 2001. She serves on the Board of Directors of Court Care for the Pikes Peak Region and was recently appointed to the Colorado Commission on Judicial Discipline.

name: Amanda J. Philipps
position: Fourth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District Judicial Performance Commission voted 10-0 that Judge Amanda J. Philipps MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

District Court Judge Philipps currently presides over a docket that is 50% criminal and 50% civil. She previously handled a docket that was 50% domestic relations and 50% civil. She currently serves as the presiding judge in the court’s criminal cases, recognized for her deep knowledge and experience in criminal law. Attorneys and non-attorneys alike described her in survey responses as hard-working, calm and professional in demeanor, knowledgeable on the law, fair, and respectful. Survey responders rated her above 3.0 out of 4.0 on every metric measured. The two appellate judges who responded to the survey each gave Judge Philipps a perfect rating of 4.0. Although the Survey results are not statistically valid due to low response rate (only 23 people responded of 892 invited), the high marks comport with the other information the Commission collected.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Philipps, reviewed several of her written orders, reviewed judicial performance data, and observed Judge Philipps in Court. The Commission also received feedback on Judge Philipps from the Chief Judge of the Fourth Judicial District as well as representatives of both the District Attorney’s and the Public Defender’s Offices. She is described as “thoughtful,” “very fair and impartial,” and is said to have a “great judicial demeanor.” Her communication skills appear to the Commission to be excellent. Her opinions are clear and well written. The Judge proactively manages her cases so that they are efficiently heard and determined. Despite lacking a background in civil law, Judge Philipps has made significant progress in handling civil matters from inception through trial.

The Governor appointed Judge Philipps to the District Court on January 1, 2024. Before that, Judge Philipps was a Magistrate in the Fourth Judicial District, a Public Defender, and in private practice. Judge Philipps graduated from Middlebury College in Vermont in 2000 and from the University of Colorado Law School in 2004. Judge Philipps is committed to service in her community, giving her time and expertise to organizations that provide education and awareness on the impact of inequities within the judicial system. The Commission is impressed with Judge Philipps and believes that she is an important addition to the District Court bench.

name: Andrew C. Poland
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance (the Commission) unanimously agrees by a vote of 9-0 (One Commissioner recused because the Commissioner is a party to a case pending before Judge Poland) that Judge Andrew C. Poland MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Poland is a District Court Judge in Jefferson County, appointed on June 2, 2024, and presides over a mixed docket consisting of criminal (30%), civil (40%) and domestic relations matters (30%). Feedback for Judge Poland’s performance was provided by parties, attorneys, and jurors appearing before him in court and by peers, based on his integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the community. Feedback recognized Judge Poland’s steady growth during his first two years on the district court bench. He was recognized for managing his courtroom, having a fair and even temperament, being deliberate, clearly explaining his rulings, and being effective in case management. Judge Poland was also described as demonstrating meaningful growth in the role, with continued opportunity to further develop and refine his legal analysis as he gains experience across a broad district court docket. Judge Poland takes all feedback and suggestions for performance improvement seriously and collaborates with his mentors and staff to address issues. Judge Poland is active in many judicial and community service initiatives including serving on the Board of Governors for the 1st Judicial District Bar Association, coordinating projects through Jefferson County Open Space and volunteering for Jefferson County High School Mock Trials.

In conducting its evaluation of Judge Poland’s performance, the Commission conducted a personal interview, observed him in court, and reviewed the 2025–2026 survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys appearing before him. The Commission additionally received feedback from the chief judge, the district attorney, and the head of the Public Defender’s Office. The Commission also reviewed Judge Poland’s self-evaluation, and three orders involving matters for which he has ruled. After completing the above reviews, the Commission finds Judge Poland meets performance criteria.

Judge Poland is a native of Jefferson County, CO. He earned his Bachelor of Science degree in 2009 from Colorado State University and Juris Doctorate in 2011 from Thomas Jefferson School of Law. Prior to being appointed District Court Judge, Judge Poland practiced law privately from 2012 to 2023, focusing on juvenile defense and child welfare litigation. He served as an Instructor at Metropolitan State University from 2021 to 2023 teaching Legal Issues in Social Work Practice before serving as Magistrate in the 1st Judicial District from 2023 to 2024. His professional background reflects longstanding service to children, families, and the Jefferson County community.

name: Curtis Lane Porter
position: Fifteenth Judicial District - Prowers County Court Judge
narrative: The Fifteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds, based upon a unanimous vote of 6-0, with four commission vacancies, that Judge Curtis Lane Porter MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado judicial performance standards on which judges are evaluated are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Porter serves on the County Court Bench and presides over misdemeanors, traffic, and civil matters in Prowers County, Colorado. The Commission finds that Judge Porter meets or exceeds expectations in all areas. Judge Porter treats everyone in his courtroom with respect, he applies the law consistently and fairly, and he has a strong knowledge of the law applicable to the cases over which he presides. His dockets continue to run smoothly and efficiently. Based upon previous feedback, Judge Porter has taken steps to improve on the delay in issuing written orders, so that his orders are now generally issued timelier, while still being well-written, organized, and thorough. It is based upon these findings that the Commission agrees that Judge Porter meets performance standards.

In reaching its vote, the Commission reviewed Judge Porter’s self-evaluation and his written opinions, conducted a personal interview with Judge Porter, met with the Chief Judge of the district, considered comments from the District Attorney and Public Defender’s offices, conducted courtroom observations, and reviewed Judicial Performance Survey results. Generally, the Commission found the survey responses consistent with their own independent evaluations, with Judge Porter overall scoring above average in all areas according to survey responses.

Judge Porter was appointed to the Prowers County Court bench in June of 2016. Before this appointment, Judge Porter served as a Deputy District Attorney for the Fifteenth Judicial District, which is how he began his legal career. Judge Porter received his undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado in 2005 and went on to earn his law degree from the Brandeis School of Law at the University of Louisville in 2008. In addition to his work on the bench as a judge in Prowers County Court, Judge Porter also serves as municipal court judge for both Wiley and Lamar, Colorado.

name: Jonathan Bruce Pototsky
position: Ninth Judicial District - Garfield County Court Judge
narrative: The Ninth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 6-0, with 1 commissioner recusing, one commissioner absent and two commission vacancies, that Judge Jonathan Bruce Pototsky MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission reviewed several of Judge Pototsky’s opinions and found them to be thoughtful, fair, and well-reasoned. Comments from Judge Pototsky’s self-evaluation and interview suggest that he issues decisions in a timely manner, manages cases well, and maintains an active and engaging demeanor in the courtroom. The Commission agrees.

During live court observations, the Commission found Judge Pototsky to be open, concise, and effective in his communication. The Commission appreciates the length of time that Judge Pototsky has served on the bench and the clear expertise that he brings to his docket. As is common with many experienced jurists who manage busy dockets and difficult matters, the Commission discussed with Judge Pototsky the importance of continuing to ensure that all parties and attorneys feel heard and that proceedings reflect the court’s impartiality. The Commission found Judge Pototsky to be open to the discussion, receptive to feedback, and committed to maintaining the fairness and impartiality expected of the judiciary. The Commission has full confidence in Judge Pototsky’s continued ability to do so. The Commission believes that Judge Pototsky meets performance standards and is an asset to the Courts and the State of Colorado.

The Commission considered Judge Pototsky’s performance over the past term by interviewing Judge Pototsky, reading a selection of his legal opinions, observing him in court, reviewing his judicial performance survey report, interviewing the district attorney and the head of the district’s public defender’s office, and reviewing Judge Pototsky’s self-evaluation. The Commission applied the following criteria when considering Judge Pototsky’s performance: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Jonathan Bruce Pototsky was appointed to the Garfield County Associate Court bench in September, 2010 by Governor Ritter. Prior to taking the bench, he worked as a Deputy Public Defender in Michigan, a Deputy District Attorney in Colorado, and also was in private practice in the fields of family law, neglect/abuse, criminal defense, civil litigation and, real estate. He graduated from the University of Miami in 1987 with a BBA and from Thomas Cooley law school in 1991. He has been married for almost 34 years and together they have a son who is a professional screenwriter. In his free time, he likes to ski, hike, run, paddle board and visit beaches.

name: Bruce R. Raaum
position: Twenty-First Judicial District - Mesa County Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance the finds that Judge Bruce R. Raaum MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS and by a vote of 8-0. The Commission on Judicial Performance (Commission) was established with ten members, but presently has one vacancy and one absent Commissioner, leaving eight voting Commissioners. To reach its recommendation for retention of Judge Raaum, the Commission considered its interviews of Judge Raaum and of others who are familiar with him, courtroom observations, Judge Raaum’s self-evaluation, court case management data and survey results.

The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. The Commission finds that Judge Raaum demonstrates legal knowledge and applies the law appropriately in the cases before him. Judge Raaum is well prepared and issues prompt rulings grounded in law and fact. The Commission observed that Judge Raaum effectively manages a large volume of County Court cases while maintaining appropriate control and decorum over courtroom proceedings.

The Commission observed that Judge Raaum exhibits judicial temperament that is fair, respectful and professional. He treats parties, attorneys, and court staff with dignity, values their time and is committed to excellence in his role as a judge. The Commission determined that Judge Raaum demonstrates the competencies required of a judicial officer.

Judge Raaum received an undergraduate degree in History and Political Science in 1989 from North Dakota State University and a law degree from the University of Nebraska College of Law in 1992. From 1992 to 2007, he worked in the private practice of law in Mesa County in the areas of civil law, criminal and juvenile law and as a court appointed guardian ad-litem for children. He was appointed by Governor Bill Owens as a Mesa County Judge on September 12, 2006. He has presented perspectives in the area of pre-trial supervision and factors to determine bond and bond conditions at the Colorado Judicial Conference. He served on state-wide committees overseeing probation procedures, rules regarding Senior Judges and a weighted case-load study to determine the need for more County Court judicial officers. He spoke at a local conference on the subject of intimate partner violence. He was selected by his peers to serve as President-Elect of the County Court Judges Association and will be President in September 2026.

name: Christopher Rhamey
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (9-0, 1 abstention) finds that Judge Christopher Rhamey MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Rhamey was appointed to the District Court in Jefferson County on July 31, 2023. He presides over criminal, civil, and domestic relations cases. Judge Rhamey’s demeanor is described as calm, professional, and attentive. His approach to case management is effective, and he does not have any cases open that are over eighteen months old. Judge Rhamey issues orders on motions in a timely and efficient manner, often working into the night so that he can ensure the facts of the case are fresh in his mind while he is writing his orders. He is considered to be very knowledgeable about criminal law, and other judges seek his mentorship in this area. He prepares diligently for sentencing hearings and believes it is important to balance the risk to the community against the needs of the defendant while also considering the message it sends to the community. Judge Rhamey is still growing in his knowledge of civil and domestic relations law and is actively seeking mentorship and education in these areas. It is very important to Judge Rhamey that he always asks himself – and others – how he can improve in every aspect of his job, and the Commission believes that Judge Rhamey has been and will continue to be an asset to the judicial bench.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Rhamey, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, reviewed comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Rhamey. Survey responses noted Judge Rhamey’s knowledge of the law, preparation for hearings, and willingness to learn in areas with which the judge was less familiar. There were references that his tone in written orders could be harsh. The commission took extra care to examine the judge’s orders and concluded that Judge Rhamey’s tone was appropriate.

Prior to Judge Rhamey’s appointment to the bench, Judge Rhamey worked for the Adams County District Attorney’s Office where he specialized in child victim crimes and supervised nearly every unit in the office. He attended and played baseball for Pointe Loma Nazarene University in San Diego, California, then graduated from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2012. Judge Rhamey worked as a youth baseball coach before becoming an attorney and continues to coach baseball for his son’s Little League team. Judge Rhamey heads all wiretaps for Jefferson County and participates in Criminal Bench Bar meetings.

name: Alexandra Robak
position: Eleventh Judicial District - Fremont County Court Judge
narrative: The Eleventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 7-0, with two members absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Alexandra Robak MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Robak presides over civil, criminal, misdemeanor and traffic cases in her courtroom. Judge Robak is the only judge handling county court cases in Fremont County. In her seven years of experience, she has improved the efficiencies of handling a busy docket which a 2024 study indicated was 50 percent higher than typically assigned to a fulltime Judge. Surveys also continue to show Judge Robak earning high marks from people appearing in her court. Judge Robak emphasizes that she wants people to feel they have been treated fairly in her court by assuring them the opportunity to be heard and by showing mutual respect. Judge Robak has made strides to meet goals she set for herself four years ago including improving the efficiency of motion and revocation hearings as well as making recovery court align with national standards. Judge Robak is keenly interested in positive outcomes for people taking part in Fremont County’s Treatment Court. She is also working to change the perception about jury duty. Judge Robak wants citizens to recognize that jury service is important, which is why she personally thanks every juror for their service. Based on these factors the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Robak meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Robak, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed surveys sent to attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Robak. Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 67% answered “yes, meets performance standards”, 33% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 0% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Robak meets or does not meet performance standards. Of non-attorneys responding to the survey, 96% answered, “yes, meets performance standards”, 4% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 6% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Robak meets or does not meet performance standards. A total of three attorneys and twenty-five non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Robak’s performance.

Judge Robak was appointed to the Fremont County Court bench in January 2019. She received her undergraduate degree from the University of Michigan, and she graduated from Brooklyn Law School with a specialty in criminal law. Judge Robak worked for the Office of the State Public Defender in the 11th Judicial District prior to her appointment to the bench. She serves as the judicial officer on Fremont County's Recovery Court and the Competency Diversion Program (coming Summer 2026). When not on the bench, Judge Robak enjoys getting out into Colorado’s “Great Outdoors” with her husband and children.

name: Ann M. Rotolo
position: Fourth Judicial District - El Paso County Court Judge
narrative: The Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Ann M. Rotolo MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Rotolo’s docket is primarily misdemeanor cases and some (approximately 20%) civil cases. Survey respondents rate her performance overall at 3.5 out of 4.0, and 21 of 23 respondents believe she meets performance standards. Judge Rotolo’s strengths include her deep legal knowledge from many years of experience, communication skills, and demeanor. When participants in the legal proceedings seem overwhelmed, she attempts to slow the proceedings and offer additional explanations. This ensures that each person appearing before her is equipped and empowered. The Commission received concerns that Judge Rotolo may overstep her judicial role and become overly involved in case resolution prior to trial. Judge Rotolo explained that she does encourage parties to negotiate a satisfactory resolution in appropriate cases because, as the saying goes, “When two elephants fight, it’s the grass that suffers.”

The Commission’s decision is based on a thorough process that included interviews with Judge Rotolo, Chief Judge Sokol, and representatives from the offices of the Public Defender and the District Attorney, as well as a review of the judge’s self-evaluation, written rulings, and survey report.

Judge Rotolo has served on the County Court since her 2008 appointment by Governor Bill Ritter. She graduated with honors from Miami University in Ohio and earned her J.D. from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 1991. Before taking the bench, she worked as a deputy county attorney, in private practice, and as a magistrate. Judge Rotolo sat on the Colorado Judicial Disciplinary Review Board for almost 17 years. She recently resigned from the State Personnel Rules Committee after over 13 years and the ComCor Board after over 5 years. She participates in Teen Court.

name: Cheryl Rowles-Stokes
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - Arapahoe County Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Cheryl Rowles-Stokes MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and to the public.

After meeting with Judge Rowles-Stokes, and after reviewing her work over the last four years, and after assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous as to whether she meets judicial performance. Judge Rowles-Stokes knows the law and is conversant with it and she is a mentor to young attorneys, helping them improve their skills. Judge Rowles-Stokes is patient with those who appear before her. She runs an efficient courtroom. She listens carefully to arguments, and her records are accurate. Judge Rowles-Stokes was described as extremely knowledgeable about the law, wanting to share that knowledge, especially with young lawyers. She is also clear about her reasoning and expectations. Judge Rowles-Stokes is passionate about the law. She works hard, helps other divisions and judges. She is fair and respectful. It was suggested that she should train new judges. She was well-spoken and informative and addressed the participants in a friendly, professional manner. Jurors reported that Judge Rowles-Stokes “…was professional, impartial, and handled every aspect of the case in a way that made me, and my fellow jurors feel composed, and comfortable to accomplish our part of the proceedings”. Based on the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Rowles-Stokes meets performance standards and should be retained.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Rowles-Stokes, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and analyzed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Rowles-Stokes. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any evaluation criteria. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings.

Judge Rowles-Stokes was appointed January 4, 2012. She earned her undergraduate degree from Colorado Christian University in Human Resources Management, a master's degree from Jones International University in Business Communications, and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law. Prior to joining the bench, she was a Chief Deputy District Attorney for the 18th Judicial District Attorney, the Vice President of Human Resources for High-Speed Access Corp., and the Director of Human Resources and Legal for Rifkin & Associates. When not on the bench, Judge Rowles-Stokes dedicates her free time to serving the community as a board member of the Sam Cary Scholarship Endowment Fund, which awards scholarships to students at the University of Colorado and the University of Denver Schools of Law, and enjoying life with her friends and family, which includes eight grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. She also clears her mind by working on cars for family and friends.

name: Jeffrey Dean Ruff
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge Jeffrey Dean Ruff MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Ruff has spent 100% of his time on the bench in the past year on an exclusively criminal docket. The reviewed information confirmed that Judge Ruff is almost universally considered to be fair. His demeanor conveys his empathetic qualities, and he is praised as being kind and respectful of those who appear before him. He is diligent and well-prepared for proceedings in his courtroom. The Commission found these themes to be consistent with what Commission members observed and reported across evaluation methods.

For this evaluation, the Commission interviewed the judge, read and reviewed a selection of his legal opinions, observed the judge in court, and reviewed judicial performance survey reports submitted about him. The Commission also reviewed his self-evaluation and interviewed the district attorney and head of the public defender’s office for the district. There have been concerns over the past two years about the Judge’s case management. The Commission specifically considered this issue. It noted that while there are ongoing concerns about him timely and effectively managing his docket, his focus on improving has produced results which the Commission finds encouraging. Given that much of the criticism appears to be derived from open court proceedings, the Commission believes that ongoing efforts to balance fairness and giving litigants an opportunity to be heard with the need to efficiently manage court time will lead to even more positive improvement.

Judge Ruff was born and raised in Billings, Montana and attended the University of Montana where he obtained a B.A. in 1996 and his Juris Doctorate in 1999. He then moved to Colorado where he began his law practice until appointed to the District Court bench in 2024. Judge Ruff’s background includes working with organizations and individuals with substance abuse and mental health struggles, and with survivors of violence. Going forward he is seeking to find community service activities appropriate for a judicial officer, and the Commission supports his efforts in that regard.

name: Tamara S. Russell
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Tamara S. Russell MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

During most of this term, Judge Russell presided over a mixed docket including criminal, civil, and domestic relations cases. However, in February of 2026, Judge Russell’s docket switched to an all-criminal docket. Judge Russell is a highly experienced Judge and is noted to be balanced and respectful to both attorneys and litigants in her courtroom. She strives to treat each person in her courtroom equally with dignity, respect, and fairness. She demonstrates a good command of the law and the rules of evidence, and her orders are typically well-reasoned and detailed. She stays current with changes in the law, something she prioritizes and makes significant effort to do. Judge Russell aims to balance her efforts to manage court time effectively and efficiently with her judicial philosophy of allowing all parties to fully state their positions in her courtroom and be heard. Even if a litigant disagrees with her rulings, she works to have the parties feel that they are understood and that they, in turn, understand her rulings. This aim has, at times, potentially come at the expense of docket management, a component of her performance that she continues to hone.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Russell, reviewed orders she authored, observed her in court, reviewed the 2020-2025 judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys appearing before her, received feedback from the Chief Judge of the District, as well as the District Attorney and Public Defender Office Head. The 2026 survey results had a very limited number of responses, but a significant majority of attorneys and non-attorneys opined that Judge Russell meets performance standards. 11 appellate judges responded to the performance survey and rated Judge Russell highly (3.5 out of 4.0).

Judge Russell was raised in rural Indiana and graduated from Indiana University with honors. She attended CU Law School and graduated in 1987. Most of her career has been spent in the courtroom; she worked for an insurance defense firm after law school and then became a deputy district attorney in Adams County. Subsequently, she became Chief Deputy City Attorney in Lakewood, Colorado, which lasted until she was appointed to the Jefferson County District Court bench on October 1, 2005.

name: Chelsea Williams Ryan
position: Eighth Judicial District - Jackson County Court Judge
narrative: The Eight Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Chelsea Williams Ryan MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by vote of 8-0 with one commissioner absent and one commission vacancy. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

The Commission finds that Judge Ryan exhibits thoughtful, fair, and well-reasoned decision-making. Information obtained through her interview and self-evaluation reflects a judicial officer who strives to issue rulings in a timely manner, promote engagement by all parties, and treats litigants with dignity and respect. Courtroom observations of Judge Ryan confirm clarity in her communication, openness in her interactions, and maintaining appropriate courtroom decorum. She conducts proceedings in an organized and understandable manner and ensures that parties have the opportunity to be heard. Judge Ryan shows patience, professionalism, and respect toward litigants, attorneys, and court personnel. The commission appreciates her sincere and sustained commitment to the fair and impartial administration of justice, as well as her understanding of the impact of judicial decision-making on the communities she serves.

For this evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Ryan, reviewed a selection of her written opinions, observed her in court, interviewed the chief judge for the district, the district attorney, and the head of the public defender’s office, and reviewed her self-evaluation.

Judge Chelsea W. Ryan was appointed to the Jackson County Court bench on July 16, 2019. Prior to her appointment, Judge Ryan practiced as an associate attorney with Miller and Associates Law Offices in Denver, Colorado, where she focused on administrative and appellate law. Before entering private practice, she served as a Deputy Public Defender in the First Judicial District. Judge Ryan also worked as a law clerk for the Honorable Judge Stoker in Twin Falls, Idaho, following law school.
