She earned her bachelor’s degree from Marquette University in 2008 and her Juris Doctor from Gonzaga University School of Law in 2011, graduating cum laude as a Thomas More Scholar. Judge Ryan has been admitted to the Idaho and Colorado Bars since 2011.

name: Nancy Woodruff Salomone
position: Twentieth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twentieth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance, by a vote of 10-0, finds that Chief Judge Nancy Woodruff Salomone MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Salomone has presided over criminal, civil, domestic relations, and probate dockets in the 20th Judicial District during her nearly nine years on the bench. As Chief Judge, she has responsibility for not only her own cases but also the administration of the county and district courts within the District. The Commission finds Judge Salomone to be sharp, organized, empathetic, and highly skilled at legal analysis. Judge Salomone has advanced innovations in court processes, including in her work presiding over the post-judgment Adult Integrated Treatment Court focused on substance abuse issues, as well as in her work presiding over the recently formed pre-judgement Competency Docket. She is valued for her firm and fair management of the courtroom, her balanced concern for both victims and the accused, and her diligent administration of the 20th Judicial District.

The Judicial Performance Commission evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. To evaluate Judge Salomone’s performance the Commission observed her in court, reviewed opinions she authored, considered her self-evaluation, held a public meeting to invite comments, and reviewed responses to a survey distributed to all persons who have appeared in her court. The Commission also conducted personal interviews with Judge Salomone, the District Attorney, and a representative of the Boulder defense bar.

Judge Salomone was appointed as a District Judge in October 2017. Prior to her appointment, she practiced as a partner in a Boulder law firm, as a solo practitioner, and as a deputy state public defender in Denver. As Chief Judge, she represents the District while engaging with court-involved organizations and the legal community. Some examples include recurring meetings with court sub-agencies, local law enforcement, Boulder County leaders, and directors of the court’s partner agencies. She convenes local leadership councils and participates in the statewide Chief Judge Council. She is a member of statewide committees including the Multidistrict Litigation Panel, the Criminal Benchbook Committee, and the Judicial Equity Project. She speaks at local schools, and she previously provided coaching assistance to a local high school mock trial team. Judge Salomone earned her undergraduate degree from the University of California at Los Angeles in 1994 and her law degree from the University of Michigan Law School in 1998.

name: Brittany Schneider
position: Fourteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fourteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agree, 7-0, with three commission vacancies, that Judge Brittany Schneider MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

It was clear from the interview that Judge Schneider is a dedicated judicial officer and is an asset to the Court. Judge Schneider has settled into her role as the chief judge in the 14th Judicial District and continues to improve in her role as both chief judge and a district court judge. She works hard to serve the judiciary and earn the respect of those that appear in her courtroom. The Commission was disappointed by the lack of participation in the survey results and would encourage the public to participate in the future. Despite the nominal participation, survey results and comments reflect that Judge Schneider works hard to serve the judiciary and treat those that appear in her courtroom with respect. Judge Schneider handles a combined docket of domestic relations, civil, juvenile, and criminal matters. Judge Schneider continues to increase her knowledge and appears comfortable handling a diverse case load. Judge Schneider demonstrates integrity, legal knowledge, good communication skills, good judicial temperament, good administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public. Judge Schneider continues to improve in the area of timely issuance of written civil orders and remains committed to efficiency. The Commission is pleased that Judge Schneider has embraced virtual courtroom options to promote efficiency and accessibility of the Courts. However, the Commission encourages Judge Schneider to firmly enforce traditional standards of decorum during WebEx proceedings. Based on all the aforementioned considerations, the Judicial Performance Commission recommends that Judge Schneider meets performance standards.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Schneider, observed her in Court, reviewed judicial performance data, several of her written orders, written comments from attorneys and non-attorneys, and a self-evaluation done by the Judge.

Judge Schneider was appointed as a judge to the 14th Judicial District Court in November 2023. She was appointed as chief judge in the 14th Judicial District in 2024. Previously, Judge Schneider was a Moffat County court judge in the 14th Judicial District. a deputy district attorney in the 14th Judicial District, assistant public defender in the Wyoming Office of the Public Defender, owner of the Law Office of Brittany Schneider, and deputy district attorney in the 9th Judicial District Attorney’s Office. She earned her undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado – Colorado Springs in 2008 and acquired her juris doctorate from the University of Oregon School of Law in 2011.

name: Karl L. Schock
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Karl L. Schock, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Colorado’s statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Schock was appointed to the Colorado Court of Appeals in 2022 and has served for four years. The Commission finds that he has the qualities of an excellent Court of Appeals judge. His written opinions are clear and easy to understand. At oral argument, he is respectful, curious, and well-prepared on both the facts and the law. He also serves on committees that work on model criminal jury instructions and probation services, which helps improve the courts.

To reach its decision, the Commission interviewed Judge Schock; reviewed his self-evaluation; watched several oral arguments; and read many of his opinions, concurrences, and dissents. It also reviewed survey responses from attorneys and judges. Every person surveyed agreed that Judge Schock meets Colorado’s judicial performance standards. Many praised his clear writing. Some noted that his separate concurrences and dissents show care in his work. Others said his questions at oral argument made them feel he took their legal issues seriously.

Judge Schock earned his undergraduate degree from Northern Arizona University and his law degree from the University of Colorado in 2006. He then clerked for Judge Michael Murphy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit. After clerking, he joined the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck until 2015 when he served as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Appellate Division before being appointed to the bench in 2022.

name: Isaam L. Shamsid-Deen
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Isaam L. Shamsid-Deen MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Shamsid-Deen is direct and efficient in his courtroom. He is considered a team player by his colleagues and is known to be hardworking and diligent. Since joining the bench, he has handled difficult cases and new areas of law well. He is self-aware and, as a newer member of the court, is willing to seek guidance from other judges. He has a continuing focus on mastering the technical aspects of his work and growing as a judge. As he gains experience, it is expected that he will add even more value to the court. Judge Shamsid-Deen is passionate about being visible in the community, being relatable as a judge, and representing the court well. He takes his position on the court seriously and strives to be a role model in the community.

In evaluating Judge Shamsid-Deen, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Shamsid-Deen was appointed to the Denver County Court in June 2023. He serves on the Court’s information technology committee. Prior to his appointment, he served as a senior deputy district attorney in Denver, where he prosecuted organized crime, embezzlement and adulty felony cases. From 2009 to 2012, Judge Shamsid-Deen was a compliance investigator with the Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies’ Civil Rights Division. He is a past member of the National Black Prosecutors Association where he served as its Rocky Mountain regional director. His memberships include the Sam Cary Bar Association, Colorado Women’s Bar Association, Colorado Hispanic Bar Association, and the Asian Pacific American Bar Association of Colorado. Judge Shamsid-Deen earned his undergraduate degree from Colorado State University and his law degree from the University of Denver.

name: Theresa Slade
position: Twenty-Third Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 70, with one commissioner absent and two commission vacancies, that Judge Theresa Slade MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Slade presides over a mixed docket in Elbert County and, during her current term, has served in Douglas, Arapahoe, and Elbert Counties, where she managed a broad range of case types including criminal, civil, domestic relations, juvenile, mental health, and probate matters as her assignments shifted over time. She demonstrates a professional and respectful courtroom demeanor and conducts proceedings in a manner that promotes order and clarity. She is able to address complex, sensitive, and emotionally difficult issues with care and precision. Her written decisions are generally clear, concise, and well reasoned. Judge Slade is a diligent judicial officer who manages a demanding docket and remains attentive to changes in the law and courtroom practice. She applies her legal knowledge and experience to ensure that matters are handled efficiently and appropriately. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview. Her opinions reflect a structured approach to legal analysis and a clear communication style. Based on these findings the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Slade meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Slade, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non attorneys who had interaction in Judge Slade’s court. Among the survey questions was: “Based on your responses to the previous questions related to the performance evaluation criteria, do you think Judge Slade meets judicial performance standards?” Of the attorneys responding, 82% answered yes; and 18% answered no. Of the non attorneys responding, 60% answered yes and 40% answered no. A total of twelve attorneys and ten non attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Slade.

Judge Slade was appointed to the District Court in August 2012. She earned her bachelor’s degree from Colorado State University and her law degree from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law. Before joining the bench, she practiced in the 18th Judicial District as a Deputy District Attorney, Alternate Defense Counsel, Respondent Parent Counsel, and Guardian ad Litem, and she also served as a municipal and magistrate judge. She previously owned and operated Slade & Associates, where she practiced criminal and juvenile defense and represented parents and children in dependency and neglect matters. During her judicial career, Judge Slade has served on statewide and local committees, including the Colorado Supreme Court Juvenile Rules Committee, the Colorado Victims Assistance (COVA) Board, the Colorado Restorative Justice Committee, and the Elbert County Community Management Board. She has volunteered extensively, including presenting legal education programs, coaching high school mock trial teams, participating in Constitution Day presentations, speaking in schools, and assisting with CASA volunteer training.

name: Judith Smith
position: Second Judicial District - Denver County Court Judge
narrative: The Denver County Court Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 5-0 that Judge Judith Smith MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Smith is upbeat and approachable and creates a positive and cordial atmosphere in her courtroom. She is a true problem solver and has frequently shown a willingness to explore novel solutions. In her courtroom, she uses plain language, shows empathy and ensures that everyone has the opportunity to be heard. She speaks directly with litigants and takes the time to ensure that people in her courtroom understand the reasoning behind her decisions. She is a legal scholar and is often sought out by colleagues for her advice and expertise. Judge Smith has a strong understanding of technology and was instrumental in the court’s recent transition to a comprehensive web-based system that increases efficiency across the court, allows for real-time note entry and reduces the use of paper. Judge Smith has a reputation for her intelligence, work ethic and positivity.

In evaluating Judge Smith, the commission did extensive live, livestream and recorded courtroom observations, conducted a personal interview with the judicial officer, and reviewed case management data and the judicial officer self-evaluation, with supporting documents when submitted, to inform its decision for meets/does not meet performance standards.

Judge Smith was appointed to the Denver County Court in September 2018. She serves on Court committees for information technology, judicial retention and appeals index. Prior to her appointment, Judge Smith spent 14 years as an assistant United States attorney for the District of Colorado where she led the special prosecutions section and established the cybercrime and national security section. Before that, she was a Denver deputy district attorney where she specialized in juvenile prosecutions. She began her career in private practice with a global law firm and also clerked for a federal judge in the 10th Circuit Court. Her memberships include the Colorado Women’s Bar Association and the Colorado LGBTQ+ Bar Association. Judge Smith earned her undergraduate and law degrees from the University of Colorado Boulder and her Master of Laws degree from Columbia Law School.

name: Erin Lynn Sokol
position: Fourth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Chief Judge Erin Lynn Sokol MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

During this term, Judge Sokol has presided over both domestic relations and felony criminal dockets. She currently presides over a felony criminal docket in addition to her administrative responsibilities as Chief Judge. Chief Judge Sokol’s demeanor is described as respectful and dignified. She is clear with her answers to confusing and difficult issues. Her written decisions are also clear and professionally written. Her judicial temperament is particularly calm in demanding situations. Chief Judge Sokol spends time tracking new developments in the law, while also expanding her practical and legal knowledge. In addition to all her judicial responsibilities, she reliably completes all her administrative duties as Chief Judge of the district. Based on these findings, the Commission unanimously agrees that Chief Judge Erin Sokol meets performance standards.

The Commission members observed these qualities during the evaluation period. They met with representatives of the District Attorney’s and Public Defender’s offices for feedback on her performance. The Commission also interviewed Chief Judge Sokol, reviewed opinions she has written, and observed her in court. Surveys were collected, but due to low completion rates, no surveys were provided to the Commission.

Chief Judge Sokol was appointed to the District Court on August 1, 2017. She earned her undergraduate degree from the University of Michigan in 1996 and her law degree from Georgetown University Law Center in 1999. Before joining the bench, she practiced law in private firms in Washington, D.C. and Colorado Springs. Since her appointment, she has presided over civil, domestic relations, and felony criminal dockets. She was appointed to the role of Chief Judge of the Fourth Judicial District in early 2024 and continues to serve in that role to date. Chief Judge Sokol has been active locally by giving presentations to Leadership Pikes Peak, school groups, the Girl Scouts, college students, the El Paso County Citizen College, and other community organizations and groups. She has also volunteered to preside over high school and college mock-trial competitions, as well as Teen Court trials among other community service activities.

name: Kelley R. Southerland
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0 with two commissioners absent, that Judge Kelley R. Southerland MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

During the period under review, Judge Southerland demonstrated exemplary performance across all areas of judicial responsibility. She brings exceptional energy, dedication, and professionalism to her work and displays a deep commitment to serving the community in which she lives and works. Judge Southerland is respected for her integrity, fairness, and calm judicial temperament, consistently treating litigants, attorneys, and court staff with patience, respect, and dignity. Since being on the bench, she has done rotations in juvenile and domestic relations where she combines strong legal knowledge with an acute understanding of the complex social, mental health, and resource related challenges facing families. Judge Southerland strives to promote accountability while encouraging positive outcomes. Judge Southerland is also highly collaborative, contributing meaningfully to a cohesive bench and actively engaging in boards and statewide initiatives that support the judiciary and the public. Her written work reflects careful legal analysis and a commitment to legally correct outcomes, even in difficult or emotionally charged cases. As in many high volume jurisdictions, the timeliness of written orders remains a systemic challenge due to heavy caseloads and limited judicial resources; nevertheless, Judge Southerland is thoughtful and conscientious in managing these demands and remains committed to balancing efficiency with quality decision making. Overall, Judge Southerland exemplifies the highest standards of judicial service and is an outstanding jurist whose leadership, work ethic, and devotion to the rule of law make her an exceptional asset to both the court and the community.

In reaching its recommendation, the Commission considered multiple sources of information, including a personal interview with Judge Southerland, courtroom observations, a review of her written decisions, and judicial performance surveys. Survey responses were overwhelmingly positive, though of the nearly three thousand survey invites that were sent out, only fourteen responded. Most of these fourteen people noted her fairness, compassion and patience on the bench. The only negative responses were about the timeliness of orders, an area where Judge Southerland strives to improve, but also is exceptionally challenging for the entire bench due to a lack of judicial resources.

Judge Southerland was appointed as district court judge in the 17th Judicial District effective January 10, 2023. Before her appointment to the district court, Judge Southerland served as a magistrate in the 17th Judicial District beginning in 2017. In her practice before joining the judicial branch, Judge Southerland's career as an attorney spanned 15 years of dedicated service to children and families. She served in various legal roles in the juvenile and domestic relations courts. Judge Southerland is a graduate of Wesleyan College in Macon, Georgia, University of Denver Sturm College of Law, and Iliff School of Theology.

name: Kellie L. Starritt
position: Seventh Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Seventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 9-0, with one Commission vacancy, that Judge Kellie L. Starritt MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

The Commission observed Judge Starritt to have an excellent demeanor, and to be patient, professional, polite and respectful to parties and counsel, and to maintain control of her courtroom. The Judicial Performance Survey and the Commission’s interviews demonstrate that Judge Starritt is organized, prepared for court proceedings, and takes time to research issues with which she is unfamiliar. Judge Starritt told the Commission she wants to issue rulings more promptly in the general civil and criminal cases on her docket. To accomplish that, Judge Starritt regularly meets with a Colorado Judicial Department mentor for guidance on managing her caseload more effectively, and also for suggestions on being more proactive in addressing pretrial disputes and unprofessional behavior in her courtroom. Judge Starritt presides over civil, criminal, domestic relations, juvenile, mental health and probate cases in Gunnison County, and in domestic relations cases in Montrose County. The Commission observed Judge Starritt in court and interviewed the District Attorney for the 7th Judicial District, the Head of the 7th Judicial District Public Defender’s Office, and the Chief Judge of the 7th Judicial District. The Commission also personally interviewed Judge Starritt on April 14, 2026, and reviewed Judge Starritt’s Judicial Performance Survey, her Self-Evaluation, and three of her written orders.

The comments in the Judicial Performance Survey were overwhelmingly positive, with a total of 11 attorneys and 13 non-attorneys responding to the Survey. Ten of the attorneys responding to the Survey opined that Judge Starritt meets performance standards, and three of the non-attorney responders opined that Judge Starritt meets performance standards. The Commission notes that 24 total Survey responses are a small sample size and takes that into account in weighing the Survey responses relative to its own interviews and observations. The Commission ultimately unanimously concludes that Judge Starritt meets judicial performance standards in all six of the statutory criteria, which are: integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and to the public.

Judge Starritt was appointed as a District Court Judge in July 2024. Prior to her appointment, she served for seven years as a District Court Magistrate handling domestic relations cases for the 7th Judicial District. Before then, Judge Starritt served as a Guardian Ad Litem in child welfare cases and as a county attorney and was in private practice for over 15 years. Judge Starritt presently serves on the Access to Justice Committee for the 7th Judicial District, serves as a committee co-chairperson on the statewide Children’s Justice Act Task Force, and leads the Domestic Relations Best Practices Group for the 7th Judicial District. Judge Starritt received her undergraduate degree from Marquette University and her law degree from the University of Wyoming.

name: Natalie G. Stricklin
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Natalie G. Stricklin MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and the public.

After meeting with Judge Stricklin, reviewing her prior work, and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission was unanimous that Judge Stricklin meets judicial performance standards. Judge Stricklin is a clear communicator who treats all courtroom participants with respect. Her courtroom is marked by clarity, professionalism, respect, and attentiveness reflecting Judge Stricklin’s strong commitment to fairness and accessibility in the judicial process. She is praised for her preparation and command of the law. Her rulings are well reasoned and grounded in thoughtful analysis of the facts and applicable legal principles, and she is willing to reconsider a ruling when presented with a persuasive legal argument. Based on all the information reviewed, the Commission finds that Judge Stricklin meets and often exceeds performance expectations. Judge Stricklin’s professionalism, fairness, and dedication to continuous improvement support the Commission’s unanimous recommendation that Judge Stricklin meets performance standards and should be retained.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Stricklin, reviewed rulings she authored, observed her in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Stricklin. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any evaluation criteria. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings.

Judge Stricklin was appointed to the District Court bench in December 2023. She graduated with distinction from the University of Michigan in 2003 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in psychology and Magna Cum Laude from Michigan State University College of Law in 2007. Following graduation, she accepted a position as a Deputy State Public Defender with the Office of the Colorado State Public Defender working in the Greeley Regional Office from 2007 to 2010 and the Arapahoe Regional Office as a Senior Deputy State Public Defender from 2010 to 2015. After several months in private practice handling criminal defense and family law cases, Judge Stricklin accepted a position in November 2015 serving as an Assistant Federal Public Defender for the Districts of Colorado and Wyoming. She has volunteered for the Arapahoe County High School Mock Trial Competition for three years and with the courthouse Take Your Kids to Work Day activities last year. She has also been a guest lecturer at DU Law School’s Women in the Law class and CU Law School’s Jury Selection and History class. In her spare time, she cheers on her daughter’s desire to participate in every extra-curricular activity available.

name: Grant Sullivan
position: Colorado Court of Appeals
narrative: The State Commission on Judicial Performance finds that Judge Grant Sullivan, by vote of 9-0 with one commissioner absent, and one commission vacancy, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The judicial performance standards include integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Sullivan began service on the Colorado Court of Appeals in January of 2024. The Commission found the judge’s written opinions to be consistently well-reasoned, fair, and thoughtfully articulated, demonstrating a strong command of the law and clear judicial reasoning. Although Judge Sullivan joined the Court of Appeals in January 2024, the Commission notes a strong and confident transition into the role of appellate judge. The judge has proactively established systems to manage workload efficiently and collaborates regularly with judicial colleagues, reflecting a dedication to continuous improvement and excellence in service.

As part of this evaluation, the Commission conducted a thorough review of Judge Sullivan’s performance. This included an in-depth interview with the judge, a review of selected legal opinions, courtroom observations, analysis of the judicial performance survey report, and a review of the judge’s self-evaluation. Judge Sullivan was observed to be clear, open, and highly effective in communication, and consistently maintained courtroom decorum. While appropriately assertive in managing proceedings, the judge’s tone and demeanor remained balanced, reflecting impartiality and professionalism. These qualities contribute meaningfully to the public’s confidence in the judiciary. Judge Sullivan’s self-evaluation and interview reflected a deep commitment to timely, transparent, and respectful engagement with all parties, an approach that aligns with courtroom observations and stakeholder feedback. Judge Sullivan practiced law as a trial and appellate litigator with the Colorado Attorney General’s Office, specializing in constitutional law, voting rights, election law, tax, administrative law, and appeals. He previously practiced law with the Denver office of a national firm and served as a Supreme Court Fellow with the National Association of Attorneys General. He clerked on both the Colorado Court of Appeals and the Colorado Supreme Court. Judge Sullivan earned his Juris Doctorate from the University of Colorado Law School and his Bachelor of Business Administration degree from the University of Texas at Austin. In addition to his duties as a judge on the Court of Appeals, Judge Sullivan participates in the Court of Appeals’ “Courts in the Community” program and serves on numerous court committees (including the Judicial Department’s Reclassification Review Board, an Appellate Rules Subcommittee, and a planning committee for the annual Colorado Judicial Conference). He also volunteers as a guest coach and judge for the CU Mock Trial and Moot Court programs and volunteers with the Food Bank of the Rockies.

name: Tamara McSherry Sullivan
position: Twelfth Judicial District - Costilla County Court Judge
narrative: The Twelfth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (6-0), with two commission vacancies and two commissioners absent, finds that Judge Tamara McSherry Sullivan, Costilla County Court Judge, MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The commission evaluated Judge Sullivan based on several criteria, including integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

The evaluation of Judge Sullivan reflects a strong alignment between her personal judicial philosophy and the feedback provided by the legal community and the Judicial Performance Commission. Judge Sullivan’s self-evaluation emphasizes that her decade of experience with Colorado Legal Services in the San Luis Valley deeply informed her commitment to "promoting access to justice" and "maintaining patience and neutrality". These self-identified strengths are directly echoed in the performance survey results, where respondents specifically praised her patience, professional demeanor, and "nuanced understanding of the human element in legal disputes". Furthermore, her background in managing a legal office translated into high marks for "organizational aptitude" and "administrative performance". Ultimately, the Commission’s unanimous (6-0) finding that she meets performance standards serves as a strong validation of her goal to provide a "fair and respectful courtroom environment for all individuals."

In her capacity as the Costilla County Court Judge, it is imperative to clarify that Judge Sullivan's judicial mandate does not grant her any authority regarding the management, operational oversight, or policy formulation of the Costilla County Sheriff’s Office or any other law enforcement agencies. This separation of powers ensures that her role remains focused on the fair and neutral administration of justice within the courtroom. Consequently, she is not involved in the administrative decisions or broader law enforcement activities currently occurring within Costilla County.

A native of Cortez, Colorado, Judge Sullivan obtained a Bachelor of Arts in English from Regis University in 2006, followed by a Master of Arts in Environmental Law and Policy from Vermont Law School in 2007. She subsequently earned her Juris Doctor from the University of Denver in 2012. Before her appointment to the Costilla County Court, Judge Sullivan practiced as a staff attorney with Colorado Legal Services within the San Luis Valley.

name: Tayler M. Thomas
position: Tenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Tenth Judicial District Commission finds by a majority vote that Judge Tayler M. Thomas MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. Of the 10 voting Commissioners, 7 voted “meets performance standards” and 3 voted “does not meet performance standards”.

Currently, Judge Thomas presides over a Domestic Relations and Civil Docket. Judge Thomas has been a judge for three years. Judge Thomas is well-organized, prompt in her rulings, and is proactive in ensuring her docket runs smoothly. In an effort to become a better judge, including working on better formulating her court orders that integrate the law and facts, Judge Thomas routinely seeks advice from a senior judge and employs a research attorney. Judge Thomas takes advantage of learning opportunities, including trainings offered by the judicial branch and the Colorado Bar Association. Although improving, the Commission finds Judge Thomas continues to lack impartiality. Judge Thomas, at times, favors one litigant over another, based, in part, by the litigants’ attorneys. The Commission is confident Judge Thomas will continue to work on this bias.

The Commission on Judicial Performance evaluates judges on six standards: legal knowledge, communication, administrative performance, integrity, judicial temperament, and service to the legal profession. To adequately evaluate Judge Thomas on these standards, the Commission interviewed Judge Thomas, Chief Judge Gregory Styduhar, the public defender’s office head, and the District Attorney. Additionally, the Commission observed Judge Thomas in the courtroom, and reviewed written public comments, and reviewed written orders drafted by Judge Thomas. While Judge Thomas volunteers at her daughter’s school and in the past has served as a mentor for a middle school student, the Commission would like to see Judge Thomas become more involved in community service activities in Pueblo such as engaging in efforts that directly inform citizens about the courts, promotion of transparency, and building trust between the Pueblo court and the Pueblo community.

Judge Thomas was appointed to the district court bench in May of 2023. Prior to becoming a judge, Judge Thomas was employed at the 10th Judicial District public defender’s office for six years. Judge Thomas received her Juris Doctorate from Creighton University School of Law in Omaha, NE and her bachelor’s degree from Colorado State University-Pueblo. Judge Thomas is a native Pueblo resident who enjoys family time, cooking, and traveling.

name: Darren L. Vahle
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 7-0, with one member abstaining, one member absent, and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Darren L. Vahle MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance and service to the legal profession and to the public.

After meeting with Judge Vahle, reviewing his work over the last six years, and assessing feedback from attorneys and non-attorneys, the Commission agreed that Judge Vahle meets judicial performance standards. His work presiding over a criminal district court docket received praise for his demeanor, prompt decisions, knowledge of the law, fairness, diligence and case management. The Judge was described as smart, understanding the law, and managing caseloads effectively, as well as being calm, fair, diligent, courteous and a team player. At times Judge Vahle can be critical and make undue comments, but he assured the Commission that his aim is not to be critical but to maintain a high standard in the court; he takes his values and the consideration of others as foremost. The Commission concluded that Judge Vahle’s knowledge base is well above average, that he is a trusted peer, and a key pillar for many.

The Commission conducted personal interviews with Judge Vahle, reviewed rulings he authored, observed him in court, reviewed comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Vahle. Attorney and non-attorney respondents, although low in response numbers, found no performance issues in any area. Most of the Commission found this to be similar to past evaluations.

Judge Vahle was appointed to the County Court bench by Governor William Ritter in June 2008 and to the District Court bench by Governor John Hickenlooper in July 2018. He was raised in Arapahoe County and graduated from Arapahoe High School. He graduated cum laude from Westmont College with a Bachelor of Arts degree in psychology. Following graduation, he worked at a juvenile detention center and at the Denver Children’s Home before enrolling at the University of Denver Sturm College of Law. He graduated a semester early in the top 10 percent of his class and went to work for the District Attorney’s office in the18th Judicial District. Judge Vahle volunteers in his community coaching varsity boys’ volleyball at Littleton Public Schools, as well as for a local volleyball club during their fall season. He serves his church playing drums on the worship team and serves on the church’s security team. Judge Vahle is a regular blood and platelet donor and is also a blood drive coordinator. He has been a volunteer judge for the Arapahoe County High School mock trial competition for over 15 years.

name: MaryAnn "Mariana" Vielma
position: Seventeenth Judicial District - Adams County Court Judge
narrative: The Seventeenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 8-0, with two commissioners absent, that Judge MaryAnn “Mariana” Vielma MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Vielma presides over criminal, misdemeanor, and traffic matters in County Court for the 17th Judicial District of Colorado. Judge Vielma’s demeanor is respectful, professional, dignified, and fair. She brings clarity and answers to confusing, and often emotional and difficult issues. Her written decisions are clear, concise, and well-written. Judge Vielma is an extremely hard worker and is dedicated to being the best county court judge she can be for her community. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview. Judge Vielma’s written opinions reflect her knowledge of the law and common-sense communication style. Based on these findings, the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Mariana Vielma meets performance standards.

In reviewing Judge Vielma’s judicial performance, the Commission conducted interviews with members of both the District Attorneys’ Office and the Public Defenders’ Office, conducted a personal interview with Judge Vielma, reviewed legal opinions she authored, and observed her in court. There were an insufficient number of judicial performance survey responses regarding Judge Vielma, and so, according to the judicial performance review policies, none were reviewed. During this term, Judge Vielma received the 2023 Judicial Excellence Award from the Colorado Judicial Institute.

Judge Vielma was appointed to the County Court in July 2020. She received her undergraduate degree from the University of Texas at El Paso, and her law degree from the University of St. Thomas School of Law. Prior to her appointment, she served as a magistrate, an Assistant County Attorney, Senior Deputy District Attorney, and District Court Law Clerk. She has been and is currently a leader in the legal profession and community, serving on boards or committees of the Colorado Women’s Bar Association, the Colorado Hispanic Bar Association, Diversity on the Bench Coalition, and the Colorado Commission on Judicial Discipline. Judge Vielma received the Judicial Excellence Award from the Colorado Judicial Institute in 2023. She is an active member of the Adams/Broomfield Bar Association, the 17th Judicial District Access to Justice Committee, and the Colorado Bar Association Leadership Training Program.

name: Dayna L. Vise
position: Eleventh Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eleventh Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by vote of 7-0, with two members absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Dayna L. Vise MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Vise presides over civil, domestic relations, juvenile, criminal and misdemeanor cases in her courtroom. In evaluating Judge Vise’s performance, the Commission reviewed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys, observed her courtroom, conducted a personal interview, and read opinions she has authored. Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 100% answered “yes, meets performance standards”, 0% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 0% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Vise meets or does not meet performance standards. Of non-attorneys responding to the survey, 75% answered, “yes, meets performance standards”, 19% answered “no, does not meet performance standards”, and 6% had no opinion regarding whether Judge Vise meets or does not meet performance standards. A total of five attorneys and sixteen non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Vise’s performance. Survey comments indicate that Judge Vise is knowledgeable, respectful of court participants, and fair. The Commission agrees with these comments based on observations of Judge Vise in the courtroom.

In her interview, Judge Vise demonstrated a clear commitment to professionalism. She stays informed of changes to the law by reading weekly published court opinions and engaging in continued legal education beyond requirements. Judge Vise makes consistent efforts to treat all litigants and defendants fairly and considers district and state-wide data in all sentencing decisions. She endeavors to provide clear and understandable orders. Based on these findings the Commission unanimously agrees that Judge Vise meets judicial performance standards.

Judge Vise grew up in Loveland, Colorado. She earned her B.A. and her law degree from the University of Colorado-Boulder. Prior to her appointment as District Court Judge on October 1, 2024, she worked as a District Court Magistrate for the Eleventh Judicial District; as a senior managing attorney for Polansky Law Firm, PLLC; as an appellate attorney and trial attorney with the Colorado Public Defender’s Office; and as a law clerk for the Honorable Daniel C. Hale. Judge Vise is active in the legal community, serving on the Colorado Bar Association’s Criminal Law Section Executive Committee and participating in local bar events. She is a member of the Colorado Bar Association, Women’s Bar Association and the local Heart of the Rockies Bar Association. She volunteers as a mock trial judge for high school and CU mock trial competitions and volunteers with local animal welfare and outdoor/recreational organizations.

name: Sarah Block Wallace
position: Second Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Second Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 9-0, with one Commissioner recusing that Judge Sarah Block Wallace MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Wallace currently presides over civil matters in the Denver District Court. Judge Wallace meets all aspects of the performance criteria on which she is evaluated. The Commission found Judge Wallace to be a thoughtful, hardworking, and highly engaged jurist who demonstrates a strong commitment to the fair and efficient administration of justice. Judge Wallace’s written decisions are clear, thorough, well-reasoned, and definitive. Her notable strengths, observed by the Commission and described in survey responses, include her strong case management skills, her professionalism and courtroom demeanor, and her ability to manage complex and high-profile matters with diligence, composure, and care. Survey respondents and the Commission also noted Judge Wallace’s commitment to maintaining courtroom dignity, treating participants respectfully, and ensuring proceedings are conducted efficiently and professionally. The Commission, based on its observation and analysis of survey responses, did not identify any evaluation category in which Judge Wallace displayed a notable weakness as to the performance criteria. Judge Wallace exceeded the Court’s productivity benchmark for civil courtrooms.

The Commission met with the Chief Judge of Denver District Court to discuss challenges facing the court system. The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Wallace and observed her during court proceedings. It also reviewed opinions she authored, comments received from interested parties during the evaluation, case management data, and judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who interacted with her. The surveys reflected personal opinions regarding Judge Wallace in the categories of case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness. A total of 39 attorneys and 12 non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Wallace. The overall information and data reviewed supports the Commission’s recommendation that Judge Wallace meets performance standards.

Judge Wallace was appointed to the Denver District Court in January 2023. Prior to her appointment, she was a partner at Ballard Spahr LLP, where her practice focused on commercial litigation and complex civil matters. Judge Wallace is active in service to the legal profession and broader community, through her leadership with the CU Law Alumni Board, mentoring law students and interns, participation in legal education programs, and regular involvement in mock trial and professional development activities. Judge Wallace received her undergraduate degree from Colby College and her law degree from the University of Colorado Law School.

name: Daniel Walzl
position: Twelfth Judicial District - Alamosa County Court Judge
narrative: The Twelfth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (6-0), with two commission vacancies and two commissioners absent, finds that Judge Daniel Walzl MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The performance standards contemplate the judge’s integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Walzl presides over a busy courtroom that addresses cases across a range of areas, including civil law, criminal law, misdemeanors, traffic and small claims. Both attorneys and individuals representing themselves appear in front of him. He also had a busy jury trial schedule in 2025, with eighteen jury trials held in his court.

The 2026 Judicial Survey Report for Judge Walzl had an overall rating of 3.4, up from his previous rating of 3.1 in 2025. Judge Walzl’s personal stated value is that he endeavors to reflect the community of Alamosa’s expectations and standards in the courtroom while applying rules and laws fairly. He recognizes that Alamosa County court is a high volume, high conflict courtroom. He has a fair expectation that attorneys act professionally and come prepared for court. Judge Walzl’s 2026 Judicial Survey Report had a mix of individuals responding, with fourteen non-attorneys finding that he met performance standards, two attorneys and one non-attorney finding that he did not meet performance standards, and one non-attorney having no opinion on whether he met performance standards. The Commission reviewed both the survey responses and Judge Walzl’s self-evaluation and decisions, in addition to interviewing Judge Walzl regarding his survey feedback and observing his courtroom. The Commission specifically heard and addressed the ongoing feedback from a small number of attorneys that are critical of his performance, which Judge Walzl responded to with candor and insight. The Commission concluded that such critiques from attorneys were not credible. A breakdown of all of the respondents’ scores of demeanor (3.1), fairness (3.2), ability to communicate (3.5), case management (3.5), and application of the law (3.4) reflected Judge Walzl’s increase in score in several categories from his last retention cycle, including the ability to communicate, case management, and application and knowledge of the law.

Judge Walzl earned his Juris Doctor degree from the University of Colorado in Boulder in 1999. After graduating law school, he served as a law clerk for the Honorable Thomas M. Jahnke in the Superior Court, First Judicial District, Ketchikan, Alaska. After completing his clerkship, he then returned to Colorado and spent the next eleven years working as a deputy state public defender, first in Pueblo and then in Alamosa, before becoming County Court Judge for Alamosa in 2011.

name: Daniel W. Warhola
position: Twenty-Third Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Twenty-Third Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance finds by a vote of 6-0, with one commissioner recusing themselves, one commissioner absent, and two commission vacancies, that Judge Daniel W. Warhola MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Warhola presided over a domestic relations docket when appointed and transitioned to a full-time criminal docket in October 2025. Judge Warhola’s demeanor is described as calm, respectful, and approachable. The commission applauds the work he has done as a new judge to learn the job. His work ethic and preparation are evident to the people who come into his courtroom. Judge Warhola is thorough in his efforts to provide equal treatment and make correct decisions, while also being conscientious about delivering timely rulings. He clearly explains the evidence and legal reasoning that inform his decisions, speaking and writing in language that is understandable to everyone. Judge Warhola demonstrates a strong commitment to ongoing professional development. Commission members observed these qualities during their evaluation and interview. Based on these findings the Commission unanimously agreed that Judge Daniel Warhola meets performance standards.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Warhola, reviewed opinions he authored, observed him in court, interviewed stakeholders, and reviewed judicial performance survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had interaction in Judge Warhola’s court. Among the survey questions was, “Based on your responses to the previous questions related to the performance evaluation criteria, do you think Judge Warhola meets judicial performance standards?” Of the attorneys responding to the survey, 82% answered yes, and 18% answered no. Of the non-attorneys responding to the survey, 67% answered yes, 20% answered no, and 13% had no opinion. A total of fourteen attorneys and fifteen non-attorneys responded to the judicial performance surveys expressing their opinion of Judge Warhola.

Daniel Warhola was appointed to the District Court in August 2024. Prior to his appointment to the bench, Judge Warhola was an Assistant United States Attorney for the District of Colorado from 2022-2024. Previously, he was a Senior Deputy District Attorney (2021-2022) and Deputy District Attorney (2014-2021) in the 18th Judicial District Attorney’s Office; and a Deputy District Attorney in the 17th Judicial District Attorney’s Office (2013-2014). Judge Warhola earned his B.S.B.A. from the University of Richmond and his J.D. from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law. He volunteers as a judge for high school mock trial and speech and debate competitions.

name: Christine A. Washburn
position: Eighteenth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Eighteenth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance agrees by a vote of 8-0, with one member absent and one vacancy on the Commission, that Judge Chirstine A. Washburn MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The Colorado statutory judicial performance criteria are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and to the public.

Judge Washburn’s docket consists entirely of domestic relations matters involving petitions for dissolution of marriage/legal separation and allocation of parental responsibilities. The Commission was unanimous that she meets judicial performance standards. She received praise for her demeanor, diligence and her application and knowledge of the law. Judge Washburn was described as patient, thoughtful, and attentive. While reference was made to Judge Washburn taking too much time to issue orders, the Commission concluded the sheer volume and complex issues in many cases contributed to this dynamic.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Washburn, reviewed opinions she authored, observed her in court, considered comments from interested parties during the evaluation, and assessed survey responses from attorneys and non-attorneys who had experience with Judge Washburn. The survey responses were low in number and did not identify many performance issues. This was consistent with the Commission’s overall findings. Most of the negative feedback came from non-attorneys, which is not surprising to the Commission given the type of docket Judge Washburn handles.

Judge Washburn was appointed to the bench on September 4, 2024. Prior to her appointment, she served as a Magistrate in the 18th Judicial District handling general domestic relations matters and the child support enforcement docket. Judge Washburn has also served as a part-time Magistrate in Denver County Court, handling protection orders, civil, forcible entry and detainer, criminal and general sessions matters. She worked as a Deputy District Attorney, Chief Deputy District Attorney and Senior Chief Deputy District Attorney for the Denver District Attorney’s Office from 1999 to 2021 and then opened a private law practice in 2022. She earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science, summa cum laude, in 1995 and her Juris Doctor in 1998, both from the University of Colorado at Boulder. She is actively involved in the Colorado Women’s Bar Association and a member of the Colorado Bar Association, the Arapahoe County Bar Association, the Asian Pacific Bar Association, the Colorado Hispanic Bar Association, South Asian Bar Association, and the Colorado LGBTQ+ Bar Association. For the Colorado Women’s Bar Association, she served as co-chair of the Professional Advancement Committee and currently serves as the Colorado Bar Association’s Board of Governor’s Representative. Judge Washburn contributes to the community by serving as a volunteer judge for the Colorado Bar Association’s High School Mock Trial Competition and assembling Lunar Year Gift Baskets for Asian families in need through APABA.

name: Gregory Robert Werner
position: Fourth Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The Fourth Judicial District Performance Commission voted 9-0 (with one absence) that Judge Gregory Robert Werner MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

District Court Judge Werner presides over a docket that is made up of predominately civil cases (70%) and probate matters (25%). He also handles certain mental health-related cases. He is the presiding judge in probate, civil, and water court cases, recognized for his deep knowledge and experience in these areas. Judge Werner serves as a resource for other judges, particularly in civil cases. Although he does not currently maintain a criminal docket, Judge Werner has in recent years presided over several high-profile criminal trials. Twenty-two of the 34 attorneys and four of the eight non-attorneys who responded to survey rated Judge Werner as meeting judicial performance standards. Nine opined that Judge Werner did not meet performance standards and two had no opinion. Judge Werner received relatively high scores from the Appellate Judges that responded to the surveys. However, because the response rate to surveys was less than 3% for attorneys (34 of 767) and 1% for non-attorneys (6 of 125), the survey responses are statistically invalid. Judge Werner conducts his courtroom formally, to demonstrate that he has not pre-judged the matter, does not favor any party, and applies the law to the facts without the influence of emotion.

The Commission personally interviewed Judge Werner, observed him in Court, reviewed judicial performance data, a number of his written opinions and orders, as well as written comments from attorneys, non-attorneys and appellate judges. It also met with the Chief Judge of the Fourth Judicial District, and representatives of the District Attorneys’ Office and the Public Defender’s Office. Comments made by both members of the bar and the public include the following: “Judge Werner sets high expectations but does so respectfully;” “Participants are always treated without bias whether represented by an attorney or Pro Se;” and “he’s punctual; gives each side an equal opportunity to present their arguments; and rules quickly. He sets out exactly how he wants counsel to proceed in his courtroom.”

The Governor appointed Judge Werner to the bench on July 10, 2006. Before that he served as a trial attorney in Colorado Springs for approximately 18 years. He is a 1987 graduate of the University of Colorado Law School, having earned his bachelor’s degree from the University of Colorado in 1983. Judge Werner is involved in several community service activities including serving as a judge for both college and high school mock trial competitions and for the Colorado Springs Teen Court. He is a member of the Colorado Supreme Court Rules Committee and has frequently spoken to members of the bar and judges on probate issues that come before Colorado Courts. The Commission highly values Judge Werner and his many years of service to our legal community and the bench.

name: Hollie Wheelwright
position: Twelfth Judicial District - Mineral County Court Judge
narrative: The Twelfth Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously (6-0), with two commission vacancies and two commissioners absent, finds that Judge Hollie Wheelwright MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS. The performance standards contemplate the judge’s integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and the public.

Judge Wheelwright presides over dockets including civil, criminal, misdemeanor cases, traffic and small claims cases in Mineral County. Judge Wheelwright’s self-evaluation reflects her dedication to continuous expansion of her legal knowledge while still striking a balance with being fair and fully present in every proceeding. Judge Wheelwright makes a conscientious effort to ensure that all litigants who appear in court in Mineral County are aware of the nature of the proceedings and understand the purpose and impact of these proceedings. She also ensures that each person in her courtroom is treated fairly and respectfully and is addressed directly. Judge Wheelwright noted she takes special efforts to ensure she approaches each case with as much neutrality as possible and to see each person in her courtroom as someone who is “doing their best” with the same opportunities and possibilities as everyone else. Judge Wheelwright brings a history of dedication to the legal system, especially with her 17 years as a Mineral County Court Clerk. As a Lay Judge who did not follow the “traditional” path or attend law school, Judge Wheelwright prioritizes consulting with other judges on the bench in the 12th Judicial District and with statewide groups. She also strives to attend any educational opportunities that are relevant to current or potential cases in Mineral County.

The Commission interviewed Judge Wheelwright, conducted courtroom observations, and reviewed judicial performance data, her written opinions and orders and self-evaluation. The Commission also discussed Judge Wheelwright’s performance with the 12th Judicial District Chief Judge Hopkins. Survey results were not available for the commission’s review due to an inadequate number of survey responses.

Judge Wheelwright is a native of the San Luis Valley and raised her family in the same community she serves. Before taking the bench, Judge Wheelwright worked for the 12th Judicial District for 26 years in various capacities, 17 of which she served as the Clerk of Court in Mineral County. When she’s not on the bench, Judge Wheelwright enjoys spending time outdoors, reading, and playing the flute. Judge Wheelwright demonstrates a strong commitment to serving her community both on and off the bench.

name: Matthew R. Zehe
position: Eighth Judicial District - Larimer County Court Judge
narrative: The Commission on Judicial Performance for the Eighth Judicial District finds that Judge Mathew R. Zehe MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS by a vote of 8-0 with one commissioner absent and one commission vacancy. The judicial performance standards are integrity, legal knowledge, communication skills, judicial temperament, administrative performance, and service to the legal profession and public.

Judge Zehe strives to conduct an efficient courtroom that meets the needs of those who appear before him and promotes the fair administration of justice. Judge Zehe exhibits great self-awareness, willingness to listen, and receptiveness to ideas and suggestions. Judge Zehe thoughtfully considers the survey comments about his communication style, in both his traditional docket and his Problem-Solving DUI Court and identifies strategies to improve his presentation in court. Judge Zehe expands access to his courtroom through the appropriate use of technology. The Commission believes Judge Zehe performs his duties well and possesses a strong knowledge of the law. The Commission appreciates his commitment and thoughtful approach to self-growth. The Commission believes that Judge Zehe is an asset to the Courts and the State of Colorado.

For this evaluation, the Commission interviewed Judge Zehe, read a selection of his legal opinions, observed him in court (including his problem-solving court docket), reviewed his judicial performance survey report, interviewed the chief judge for the district, the district attorney and head of the public defenders’ office for the district, reviewed case management statistics, and reviewed his self-evaluation. As to the survey data, a total of 24 individuals, 10 attorneys and 14 non-attorneys, completed the survey, which is a markedly low response rate. Given the significantly low response rates to the surveys overall, the Commission gave the appropriate weight to the survey responses in its evaluation.

Matthew Zehe was sworn in as a judge for the County Court in the Eighth Judicial District on November 14, 2022. Previously, Judge Zehe served as a magistrate for the Eighth Judicial District of Colorado since November of 2006. In that role he presided over the juvenile delinquency docket and the Juvenile Recovery Court, the First Appearance Center in Division, and the DUI Recovery Court. Judge Zehe also served as an attorney for the Colorado State Public Defender’s Office from December 1995 to October 2006. He graduated from Indiana University in 1991 with a degree in Philosophy and earned his J.D. from the University of Denver in 1995. Judge Zehe permanently presides at the Loveland County Court, and he continues to preside over the DUI Recovery Court.

name: Christopher C. Zenisek
position: First Judicial District - District Court Judge
narrative: The First Judicial District Commission on Judicial Performance unanimously agrees by a vote of 10-0 that Judge Christopher C. Zenisek MEETS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS.

Judge Zenisek is a District Court Judge in Jefferson County presiding over a mixed docket of criminal, civil, and domestic relations matters. He is consistently described as thoughtful, prepared, thorough, and fair. He has a calm, professional demeanor that promotes respect, efficiency, and control in the courtroom. His rulings are timely, clear, and carefully considered, reflecting strong judgment, impartiality, and accountability, and he manages complex cases with diligence and skill. He is actively engaged in the legal community through service with multiple bar organizations and Colorado Supreme Court committees, participates in mock trials with high school students, and was appointed by the Chief Justice to preside over the Marshall Fire cases while maintaining a full caseload. He was able to manage this additional responsibility without taking a reduced caseload.

The Commission conducted a personal interview with Judge Zenisek, reviewed opinions he authored, observed Judge Zenisek in court, reviewed the 2025 Judicial Performance Survey Report from attorneys and non-attorneys appearing before him and received feedback from the Office of the State Public Defender and the First Judicial District Attorney's Office. Based on the Commission’s evaluation, Judge Zenisek demonstrated that he meets or exceeds performance standards in all categories under review: case management, application and knowledge of the law, communications, diligence, demeanor, and fairness.

Judge Zenisek was appointed to the First Judicial District Court in December 2011. Currently, he serves on the Leadership Committee of that Court. Before his judgeship, Judge Zenisek was an Assistant District Attorney for the 20th Judicial District and worked in private practice with Brownstein Hyatt Farber Shreck, P.C. and as a law clerk to Chief Judge Lewis Babcock (U.S. District Court) prior to that. Judge Zenisek received his undergraduate degree from the University of Colorado and his J.D. from the University of Denver. In 2026, Judge Zenisek was named as one of three finalists nominated for an appointment to the Colorado Supreme Court.
